}}

The game received favorable reviews on all platforms according to the [[Review aggregator|review aggregation]] website [[GameRankings]].<ref name="GRN64"/><ref name="GRPC"/><ref name="GRPS"/> In Japan, where the PlayStation version was ported and published by Acclaim Japan on 2 September 1999, ''[[Famitsu]]'' gave it a score of 24 out of 40.<ref name=Fam/>

Paul Biondich of ''[[AllGame]]'' gave the PC version four-and-a-half stars out of five and argued that although its gameplay was uninventive, its PC version, with its use of  "[[Graphics processing unit#1990s|3D Accelerator]]" [graphics card] and [[Direct3D]], has "utterly impressive technical savvy and attention to detail" few other games had achieved. He highlighted "the quality and generous use of real-time colored lighting effects", "the screen blistering frame rates", explosions, the detail of enemy ships, and smoke trails of missiles.<ref>{{cite web |first=Paul |last=Biondich |url=http://www.allgame.com/game.php?id=9372&tab=review |title=Forsaken (PC) - Review |website=[[AllGame]] |publisher=[[All Media Network]] |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20141115155637/http://www.allgame.com/game.php?id=9372&tab=review |archivedate=15 November 2014 |accessdate=14 June 2018}}</ref>

Lighting effects were highlighted in reviews of all versions. Martin Kitts of ''[[NGC Magazine|N64 Magazine]]'' called the lighting effects the best on the Nintendo 64, "giving heated battles a pleasant lava lamp effect, with shots and explosions bouncing around the room in slow motion."<ref name="N64mag"/> The game's intense action was well-received, but the difficulty was occasionally considered excessive. Kitts explained the N64 port's first stage "will leave most players cold, soon turning into a tedious slog around a nondescript 360° maze".<ref name="N64mag"/>

''Forsaken''{{'}}s PC release significantly exceeded expectations for Joel Durham, writing for the [[PC Gamer#PC Gamer US|American edition]] of ''[[PC Gamer]]''. He expected another PC title that emphasized 3D acceleration effects over gameplay, a la ''[[G-Police]]'' (1997) and ''[[Terracide]]'' (1997).<ref name="PCGamerUS"/>

''[[Edge (magazine)|Edge]]'' gave the PlayStation version eight out of ten in its June 1998 issue, stating that, although it feels familiar to ''[[Descent (video game)|Descent]]'', it refined and updated the formula with features such as its auto-levelling system and orientation aid.<ref>{{cite magazine |author=Edge staff |url=https://retrocdn.net/images/7/77/Edge_UK_059.pdf |title=Forsaken (PS) |magazine=[[Edge (magazine)|Edge]] |publisher=Future Publishing |issue=59 |date=June 1998 |pages=86–87 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20230703200410/https://retrocdn.net/images/7/77/Edge_UK_059.pdf |archivedate=3 July 2023 |url-status=live |accessdate=5 September 2023 |via=RetroCDN}}</ref> An issue later, the magazine gave ''Forsaken 64'' eight out of ten, saying, "With luck, programming of this calibre can become an expectation for all N64 titles developed across multiple formats."<ref>{{cite magazine |author=Edge staff |url=https://retrocdn.net/images/b/b7/Edge_UK_060.pdf |title=Forsaken 64 |magazine=Edge |publisher=Future Publishing |issue=60 |date=July 1998 |page=101 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20230707162704/https://retrocdn.net/images/b/b7/Edge_UK_060.pdf |archivedate=7 July 2023 |url-status=live |accessdate=5 September 2023 |via=RetroCDN}}</ref> Dan Toose of ''[[Hyper (magazine)|Hyper]]'' gave the game 92% and said: "Unless someone pulls some wonder game out of the bag at E3, this one looks like it's going to be the all-formats game of the year.  If you like action shooter games, this is a must-have".<ref name="Hyper">{{cite magazine |first=Dan |last=Toose |url=https://archive.org/details/hyper-056/page/62/mode/2up |title=Forsaken |magazine=[[Hyper (magazine)|Hyper]] |publisher=[[nextmedia|Next Media Pty Ltd]] |issue=56 |date=June 1998 |pages=62–65 |accessdate=20 September 2021 |via=[[Internet Archive]]}}</ref>

Kitts gave the N64 version 87% and compared it to ''[[Quake (video game)|Quake]]'' and ''[[Descent (1995 video game)|Descent]]'' (1995), as well as 2D shooters such as ''[[R-Type]]'' (1987) and ''[[Axelay]]'' (1992).<ref name="N64mag">{{cite magazine |first=Martin |last=Kitts |url=https://archive.org/details/n64magazineukcollection/N64%20Magazine%2016%20-%20june%201998%20%28UK%29%20%28Max-Rez%20version%29/page/50/mode/2up |title=Forsaken |magazine=[[NGC Magazine|N64 Magazine]] |publisher=[[Future plc|Future Publishing]] |issue=16 |date=June 1998 |pages=50–55 |accessdate=November 23, 2021 |via=[[Internet Archive]]}}</ref> He called it the best "serious" Nintendo 64 title since ''[[GoldenEye 007 (1997 video game)|GoldenEye]]'', and "a game that, although not for the fainthearted, holds a genuinely rewarding experience for those who are prepared to persevere".<ref name="N64mag"/> He wrote that the game's best moments were those that required thinking, although did enjoy the more intense parts, such as enemies popping up behind the player and shots from guns hidden in alcoves.<ref name="N64mag"/> Despite the use of static, non-animated character models, he called the visuals impressive nonetheless.<ref name="N64mag"/> He enjoyed how enemy ships, when destroyed, spin out of control, fire random shots, and occasionally dive on the player, adding to the fast-paced gameplay.<ref name="N64mag"/> He also highlighted there being no fogging in the four-playing mode.<ref name="N64mag"/> It did take a little bit of time for him to appreciate the game, however; he was critical of the default control system. He also was disappointed in the multiplayer mode, writing it was hard to tell players from each other and that weapons barely took off hit points of other players, resulting in overly-long matches.<ref name="N64mag"/>

Boba Fatt of ''[[GamePro]]'' described the N64 version as an "endless maze of frustration" wasting "excellent control and four-player split-screen capability". He criticized the lack of radar, which made it difficult to look for the other players in multi-player, and made single-player a chore: "You'll run in perpetual circles looking for your objective or final enemy until you either memorize the level or pass out. Even worse, the unimaginative bad guys blend right into the background, and every level looks just like the previous one."<ref>{{cite magazine |author=Boba Fatt |url=https://retrocdn.net/images/e/e5/GamePro_US_117.pdf |title=Forsaken Review for N64 |magazine=[[GamePro]] |publisher=[[International Data Group|IDG]] |issue=117 |date=June 1998 |page=106 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20041222015808/http://www.gamepro.com/nintendo/n64/games/reviews/206.shtml |archivedate=22 December 2004 |url-status=live |accessdate=10 September 2023}}</ref>{{efn|''[[GamePro]]'' gave the Nintendo 64 version 3.5/5 for graphics, 3/5 for sound, 4.5/5 for control, and 2/5 for fun factor.}} Fatt also said that the PlayStation version's "sharp environmental detail and spectacular real-time lighting effects are just window dressing for a poorly devised game. Unfortunately, bland enemies, derivative gameplay, and squeaky, unappealing sound effects (laser fire on helium—anyone remember [[Atari]]'s ''[[Phoenix (1980 video game)|Phoenix]]''?) run rampant."<ref>{{cite magazine |author=Boba Fatt |title=Forsaken (PS) |magazine=GamePro |publisher=IDG |issue=117 |date=June 1998 |page=118}}</ref>{{efn|''[[GamePro]]'' gave the PlayStation version 3.5/5 for graphics, 2.5/5 for sound, 1.5/5 for control, and 2/5 for fun factor.}}

''[[Next Generation (magazine)|Next Generation]]'' said in its July 1998 issue that the N64 version was "solid, enjoyable stuff with not a hint of originality to cloud the fun";<ref name="NGenN64"/> and called the PlayStation version "a decent title. Probe has mixed together the best elements of ''Descent'' and ''[[Quake (video game)|Quake]]'' and added some pretty tricky enemy AI, resulting in a game that shines, although in slightly different ways, on each platform."<ref name="NGenPS"/> An issue later, the magazine called the PC version "a good game that will provide a nice distraction until players get their hands on the big guns like ''[[Sin (video game)|Sin]]'', ''[[Half-Life (video game)|Half-Life]]'', and ''[[Duke Nukem Forever]]''."<ref name="NGenPC"/>

{{nihongo foot|'''''Front Mission'''''|フロントミッション|Furonto Misshon|group=lower-alpha|lead=yes}} is a [[tactical role-playing game]] developed by [[G-Craft]] and published by [[Square (video game company)|Square]] for the [[Super Famicom]]. It was originally released only in [[Japan]] on February 24, 1995. ''Front Mission'' is the first main entry and the first entry overall in the ''[[Front Mission]]'' series.<ref name="gamespy">{{cite web|url=http://hg101.classicgaming.gamespy.com/frontmission/frontmission.htm |title=Hardcore Gaming 101: Front Mission |last=Kalata |first=Kurt |publisher=Gamespy |access-date=2009-02-22 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090412071829/http://hg101.classicgaming.gamespy.com/frontmission/frontmission.htm |archive-date=April 12, 2009 }}</ref> ''Front Mission'' is part of a serialized storyline that follows the stories of various characters and their struggles involving [[mech]]a known as ''wanzers''.<ref name="dengeki2004">{{cite magazine|magazine=Dengeki GAMES |issue=February 2004 Special Edition |title=100 Year History of Front Mission |editor=Dengeki|publisher=MediaWorks|date=February 2004|language=ja}}</ref> A direct port of the game was released for the [[WonderSwan Color]] in Japan on July 12, 2002.

A remake of the game developed by [[Square Enix|Square Enix Co., Ltd.]] was released for the [[PlayStation (console)|PlayStation]] in Japan on October 23, 2003, titled {{nihongo foot|'''''Front Mission 1st'''''.|フロントミッション ザ・ファスト|group=lower-alpha|lead=yes}} It included new content and offered a new USN scenario to play through. ''Front Mission 1st'' was then ported to the [[Nintendo DS]] with more additional content and was released in Japan on March 22, 2007. Only the Nintendo DS port, renamed as ''Front Mission'', was released in [[North America]] on October 23, 2007.

A further remake of ''Front Mission 1st'', titled '''''Front Mission 1st: Remake''''' (Japanese: フロントミッション ザ・ファースト：リメイク), was developed and published by Forever Entertainment for the [[Nintendo Switch]] on November 30, 2022. Ports to [[PlayStation 4]], [[PlayStation 5]], [[Windows]], [[Xbox One]], and [[Xbox Series X and Series S|Xbox Series X/S]] were released on June 30, 2023.

==Gameplay==
Game progression in ''Front Mission'' proceeds in a linear manner: watch cut-scene events, complete missions, set up wanzers during intermissions, and sortie for the next mission. The player travels to locations on a point-and-click world map. As the player progresses through the plot, new locations are revealed on the world map. Towns and cities act as intermission points where the player can organize and set up their units for the upcoming mission. Battle zones are where the missions take place, though they become inaccessible upon the completion of a mission.

[[File:Front Mission Screenshot.png|thumb|left|220px|Overhead view of world map during a mission]]
In ''Front Mission'', players use playable units called ''wanzers'', a term for mecha derived from the German word ''Wanderpanzer'', or "walking tank".<ref name="gamespy"/> A wanzer differs from the typical combat unit in that it has four [[modular design|modular]] parts: body, left arm, right arm, and legs. Each part has a specific function and its own [[health (gaming)|health]] bar.<ref name="gamespy"/> The legs parts enable movement and evasion, the arm parts are necessary to use hand and shoulder weapons, and the body part maintains the wanzer's operability. In the event the body is destroyed, the wanzer is removed from play completely. Destruction of arm and leg parts does not remove the wanzer from play, but it severely cripples its performance, either through the loss of weapon use (in the case of the arms), or by slowing the movement rate to a single space (in the case of the legs).<ref name="gamespy"/> While the player fights mostly wanzers, vehicles and aircraft, mobile weapon platforms are also featured. These enemy units generally have only one part, the body, and are much stronger than wanzers themselves.

In the customization aspect of ''Front Mission'', wanzers can be customized with a variety of parts, computers, auxiliary backpacks, and weapons. The player has full control over customizing their wanzers and can do so as long as its total weight value does not exceed its given power output. To field a wanzer in battle, it must have a complete frame of parts: body, left arm, right arm, and legs. Parts with built-in weapons in the body or arm sections can also be equipped on a wanzer. Computers improve the accuracy of the weapons equipped on the wanzer, as well as being used to activate special abilities that can be purchased and loaded into them. Auxiliary backpacks and weapons are not mandatory equipment to use wanzers, but are crucial in order to progress through the games. Auxiliary backpacks serve to give a wanzer special features during combat; they allow a wanzer to carry support items such as ammunition reloads and increase the power output of the unit, allowing it to carry heavier gear.

There are four classes of weapons: melee weapons, short-range weapons, long-range weapons, and support fire weapons. Melee weapons are weapons used at melee range and have a tendency to strike the body part of its target. Tonfas and rods are examples of melee weapons. Short-range weapons are weapons used at close range and deal damage to all parts of a target. Machine guns and shotguns are examples of short-range weapons. Long-range weapons are weapons that have long firing ranges and are ideal for avoiding counterattacks. Bazookas are examples of long-range weapons. Support fire weapons are indirect fire weapons; they can never be counterattacked, but have limited ammunition supply and minimum firing ranges. Missile launchers are examples of support fire weapons. Lastly, shields can be equipped on wanzers to absorb some of the damage taken from incoming attacks.

''Front Mission'' has other notable features incorporated into the game. The Arena is a unique feature in which the player can fight [[AI]]-controlled enemy combatants to earn monetary rewards. Likewise, ''Front Mission'' sports a briefing feature that details basic information about the composition of enemy forces for the upcoming mission. Missions in ''Front Mission'' are traditional tactical RPG fare, ranging from destroying all enemy targets or protecting a particular allied target.

==Synopsis==
===Setting===
Set in 2090, the story of ''Front Mission'' takes place on Huffman Island, a fictional Pacific Ocean island roughly the size of [[Oahu]], [[volcanic island|created by volcanic activity]] south of [[Mexico]]'s west coast in 1995.<ref name="matsudaFMC">{{cite book|title=Front Mission Comics|last=Matsuda|first=Taishu|publisher=ASCII Comix|date=1995-07-22|isbn=978-4-7561-1157-9|language=ja}}</ref> In 2002, the land mass was classified as an island, and was ceded to [[United Nations]] control. However, in 2020, the United States of the New Continent (USN), a unification of [[North America]]n and [[South America]]n countries, made a bid for control of the island after withdrawing from the United Nations.<ref>{{cite book|title=Front Mission World Historica - Report of Conflicts 1970-2121|editor=Dengeki PlayStation Editorial, LogicGate|publisher=Mediaworks|date=March 2007|isbn=978-4-8402-3663-8|language=ja|quote=2020, The United States and Canada took the advantage of Latin America's bid for unification, and have proclaimed the birth of 'The United States of the New Continent' (USN). The new nation works toward eliminating the wealth gap between its people, while guaranteeing basic human rights for its citizens. In the same year, the USN withdrew from the United Nations and submitted a motion to the UN, OCU and the 'European Community' (EC) proposing that Huffman Island be treated as USN territory.}}</ref> The Oceania Cooperative Union (OCU), an alliance of the nations of [[South Asia]], [[Southeast Asia]], [[Japan]], [[South Korea]] and [[Australia]] that was created in 2025, dispute this claim when the two superpowers colonized the island in 2065.<ref>{{cite book|title=Front Mission World Historica - Report of Conflicts 1970-2121|editor=Dengeki PlayStation Editorial, LogicGate|publisher=Mediaworks|date=March 2007|isbn=978-4-8402-3663-8|language=ja|quote=In 2019, Australia joins the Bangkok Economic Alliance. Later at a summit, leaders of the alliance voted to change the name to 'Oceania Cooperative Union' (OCU). The new name reflecting the intention of the nations to work towards establishing a union framework for the coalition, originally formed in 2005.}}</ref> The tensions heat up and eventually lead to the 1st Huffman Conflict in 2070, with Huffman Island being divided into two halves at the end of the war: the east becoming OCU territory, and the west becoming USN territory.

===Plot===
An OCU reconnaissance team led by Royd Clive is assigned to investigate a USN [[munitions factory]] in the Larcus district, located on eastern Huffman Island. Upon reaching the factory, the team is ambushed by USN wanzers led by officer Driscoll. He ambushes Karen Meure, Royd's [[fiancée]], and destroys her wanzer. The two forces engage in battle, but it ends with Driscoll detonating explosives inside the plant and he escapes. The USN publicly [[false-flag|frames the event as an enemy attack]], later known as the Larcus Incident, which reignites tensions and begins the 2nd Huffman Conflict. Royd and his team are [[Military discharge|discharged]] and listed as [[killed in action]].

One year later, Royd earns a living at a wanzer fighting arena, and is approached by Guri Olson. Olson, commander of the ''Canyon Crows'' [[private military company|mercenary group]], recruits Royd into the ''Crows'' with the prospect of avenging Karen's death. The ''Crows'' initially consists of Natalie Blakewood, Keith Carabell, Joynas "JJ" Jeriaska, and Ryuji Sakata. Royd is permitted to recruit anyone else he chooses, including [[war journalist]] Frederick Lancaster, and [[child soldier]] Yang Meihua. Royd learns from Meihua and her [[hacker]] friend Hans Goldwin that Karen is possibly alive and recovering at Grey Rock Hospital, but they arrive too late as a USN truck takes the patients elsewhere, and Driscoll demolishes the hospital.

Although Hans finds a conspiratorial connection between Grey Rock Hospital and a mysterious "Nirvana Institute", with no further leads on Karen's fate the ''Crows'' collaborate with the OCU to fight the UCN, and liberate Freedom City, the capital of eastern Huffman. Having reclaimed all former OCU territory, the ''Crows'' and OCU push into western Huffman; this includes an assault on Morgan Fortress, where Driscoll is revealed to be a member of Nirvana. Driscoll deploys wanzers utilising experimental "B-device" technology, though they are defeated by the ''Crows'', and Driscoll again escapes. The ''Crows'' also discover that Nirvana are experimenting on kidnapped soldiers, including Meihua's brother Yeehin, whom they rescue.

Whilst the OCU comes very close to winning the war outright, a peace is brokered by the Peace Mediation Organization (PMO), a group backed by the Republic of Zafra. The ''Crows'' now find themselves working for the PMO, and on neutral terms with USN soldiers. This includes Driscoll, whom Olson prohibits Royd taking vengeance on. The ''Crows'' are now tasked with eliminating the Spirit of Huffman [[terrorist group]], led by Gentz Weizer. The Spirit of Huffman are reportedly attacking civilians, but particularly focused on attacking Sakata Industries, a wanzer manufacturer, and its president Koichi Sakata, Ryuji's brother.

During an attack on the Spirit of Huffman, the ''Crows'' discover that Frederick has already been in close contact with Spirit of Human, who disputes the group's reported attacks on civilians. Gentz claims they are solely targeting Sakata, who are actually the creators of B-device technology, revealed to be the grafting of soldiers' brains into wanzer [[CPU]]s, and that Nirvana is responsible for finding and capturing candidates with extensive combat experience. Believing his story, Royd recruits Gentz, but this causes a split in the ''Crows''; Natalie, Keith, and JJ stay with Olson's faction, whereas the other recruits join Royd's rogue faction to pursue Nirvana and Sakata.

Returning to the Larcus munitions factory, Gentz explains it was actually Nirvana's original B-device factory, and Sakata had arranged the attack to intentionally trigger the war as a means to test and sell the technology. Driscoll appears, revealing Karen is the B-device of his wanzer,<ref>'''Driscoll''': "She controls this machine. [...] Karen has been reborn as one of Sakata's B-device modules. {{cite video game |title=Front Mission 1st: Remake |developer=Forever Entertainment |publisher=Forever Entertainment |date=June 30, 2023 |platform=PC }}</ref> but is killed by Royd's ''Crows''. Upon dying, Driscoll reveals the ''Crows'' were themselves assembled as B-device candidates.<ref>'''Driscoll''': "You and your friends... were assembled... to serve as device materials." {{cite video game |title=Front Mission 1st: Remake |developer=Forever Entertainment |publisher=Forever Entertainment |date=June 30, 2023 |platform=PC }}</ref>

Having attacked Driscoll's squad and thus threatening peace, Olson's ''Crows'' confront Royd's ''Crows'', but Natalie takes pity on the others - having known about the ''Crows'' purpose from the beginning and betraying them to Driscoll<ref>'''Natalie''': "I knew that you'd been selected as B-device candidates. [...] I knew everything. Everything about Driscoll... and Karen. [...] I'm the one who told Driscoll where to find you." {{cite video game |title=Front Mission 1st: Remake |developer=Forever Entertainment |publisher=Forever Entertainment |date=June 30, 2023 |platform=PC }}</ref> - and join's Royd's faction. JJ and Keith do the same, leaving Olson alone. Royd's ''Crows'' hide at Rupidis, the largest [[port]], until they are tracked down by USN/OCU soldiers led by Olson. Willas Blakewood, founder of the ''Crows'' and Natalie's father, arrives to assist Royd's faction, and informs them that Koichi is on a Sakata ship nearby. Ryuji begs his father Reiji, Sakata's founder, to stop Koichi. Reiji attempts it but Koichi is unmoved and Reiji leaves to join Ryuji, but Koichi's ship guns Reiji down. Their conversation reveals that Zafra, despite being PMO's benefactor, is also involved in Sakata's research<ref>'''Reiji''': "You and that cursed country you bow down to!" {{cite video game |title=Front Mission 1st: Remake |developer=Forever Entertainment |publisher=Forever Entertainment |date=June 30, 2023 |platform=PC }}</ref> and they share a secret facility on Longrivers Island (publicly restricted as a [[nature reserve]]) nearby.

The ''Crows'' follow Koichi to the Longrivers Island facility. Zafra, speaking remotely, disregard Koichi's B-device technology as they have already made significant progress with its successor, the S-device. Royd's ''Crows'' kill Koichi as they proceed through the facility, coming across the first S-device: a large weaponised Driscoll [[cyborg]]. Driscoll is once again destroyed by the ''Crows'' and they destroy the facility before escaping. The destruction is framed by the PMO as the [[mass suicide]] of the Spirit of Huffman at their secret base. The ''Crows'' disband, though Royd and Gentz join together as independent [[freedom fighter]]s against the PMO.

Six months later, Frederick releases a public [[exposé (journalism)|exposé]] on the truth of the conflict as discovered by the ''Crows''. Although the OCU and USN admit partial blame, and the PMO suffers reputational damage, Zafra denies any involvement and evades consequences. Some time later during a mission, Royd and Gentz are surprised when many of the ''Crows'' return to rejoin them.

==== USN campaign ====

In the [[PlayStation (console)|PlayStation]] and [[Nintendo DS]] remaster titled ''Front Mission 1st'', the player can also play a second scenario revolving around USN officer Kevin Greenfield. Months before the Larcus Incident, Kevin and his teammates in the ''Black Hounds'' special forces unit are participating in an operation against a terrorist organization known as "The Star of Freedom". Upon finding out the location of their headquarters in the Andes Mountains, the Black Hounds execute an operation to eliminate the group. A grave mistake on Kevin's part gets him fired from the unit and arrested by USN [[military police|MPs]]. In a last-ditch effort to remain in service, Greenfield accepts a post to the USN special weapons research division known as the "Nirvana Institute". He is then deployed to the Nirvana branch on Huffman Island, which is led by Driscoll. After a few operations with the division, the 2nd Huffman Conflict breaks out and Kevin is recalled to active duty. As the new leader of the ''Silver Lynx'' strike force, he aids the USN offensive to defeat the OCU and help end the war quickly.

==Development==
===Concept===
Development of the first ''Front Mission'' started with discussions between software developers Square and G-Craft.<ref name=mup>{{cite web|url= http://shmuplations.com/frontmission/#footnote-1|access-date=May 30, 2020|date=January 1, 1995|title= Front Mission – 1995 Developer Interviews|publisher=Front Mission Official Guidebook}}</ref> Square had never had another developer make a game for them and planning proceeded slowly, but an agreement between the two was finished in the Fall of 1993.<ref name=mup/> Game producer and writer [[Toshiro Tsuchida]] presented a proposal for a game called “100 Mission” to Square through his own development company, Solid, on G-Crafts behalf.<ref name=mup/> When Square producer Shinji Hashimoto first saw the first version of the game proposal, he thought it was “too radical” and usually such proposals would not be approved.<ref name=mup/> Square was not enthusiastic, repeatedly telling Tsuchida “no robots”, and being told by Square that game development couldn't just be driven by a creators passion anymore.<ref name=mup/> Tsuchida also had difficulty explaining how much of a role robots would have in the proposed game, and so he obtained some development hardware to create a prototype of the title.<ref name=mup/> Square was the only publisher at the time willing to consider Tsuchidas’ proposal.<ref name=mup/> They finally agreed to make the game because they thought working in a new genre would be stimulating and it was a title they probably could not do themselves as to that point Square had mostly made fantasy games.<ref name=mup/> Hashimoto insisted that lighter moments be included, such as the characters hanging out and playing cards, in order to balance the mood of the game which was dark and moody.<ref name=mup/>

===Initial development===
Square and G-Craft worked together making the title, including aspects like the games graphics and sound.<ref name=mup/> Because the developers wanted an immersive experience and disliked text-heavy introductions in games, they requested and were allowed to omit the usual Squaresoft branding that always appeared when Square games began.<ref name=mup/> Hironobu Sakaguchi, Shinji Hashimoto, and Toshiro Tsuchida all loved robots and did a lot of brainstorming to discover elements that could be in the game.<ref name=mup/> Hashimoto came up with the idea of the colonel Kirkland being in a fort in Stage 15.<ref name=mup/> Many times Hashimoto would take Tsuchida's ideas and expand upon them.<ref name=mup/> There was debate about whether a game for children should have a brain in the opening scene, but decided to include it anyway.<ref name=mup/> [[Yoshitaka Amano]] painted an illustration for the game, and it was intended to be used as the front cover of the cartridges packaging, but it was too “imposing” and only a portion was used.<ref name=mup/> The development team even went so far as to make a sample movie of the game's intro on a [[Macintosh]] for Hashimoto, which impressed upon him how dedicated and passionate the team was for the game.<ref name=mup/> Sakaguchi loved plastic models, and that led to hiring Kow Yokoyama, who had a reputation for excellent modeling.<ref name=mup/> Yokoyama helped craft models for the wanzer mechs and was able to help design them as though they were real weapons.<ref name=mup/>

===Music===
{{Main|Music of the Front Mission series#Front Mission}}
''Front Mission'''s soundtrack was composed by the joint team of [[Noriko Matsueda]] and [[Yoko Shimomura]]. Shimomura's work on the soundtrack was requested by [[Hironobu Sakaguchi]], the vice-president of Square, due to the need for a more experienced composer to work on the project along with Matsueda. While Shimomura intended to turn down this request due to her preoccupation with the ''[[Super Mario RPG]]'' soundtrack, she changed her mind after encountering the company president, Tetsuo Mizuno, and being embarrassed to decline the request in front of him. Shimomura mainly composed the action themes, as well as the opening theme, describing the soundtrack as "passionate" due to their "motivated" work.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.gamesetwatch.com/2009/08/sound_current_magical_planet.php|title=Sound Current: 'Magical Planet - The Music of Hiroki Kikuta & Yoko Shimomura'|author=Jeriaska|author2=Ryojiro Sato|date=2009-08-19|publisher=GameSetWatch|access-date=26 November 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100611163928/http://www.gamesetwatch.com/2009/08/sound_current_magical_planet.php|archive-date=2010-06-11|url-status=live}}</ref> The score was arranged by [[Hidenori Iwasaki]] for the PlayStation and DS remakes.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.squareenixmusic.com/composers/shimomura/biography.shtml |title=Yoko Shimomura :: Biography |first=Chris |last=Greening |date=2008-08-16 |publisher=Square Enix Music World |access-date=2009-07-23 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090724102258/http://www.squareenixmusic.com/composers/shimomura/biography.shtml |archive-date=July 24, 2009 }}</ref> The promotional album, ''Front Mission 1st Special BGM Selection'', arranged by Isawaki, was released in 2003.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.rpgfan.com/soundtracks/fm1-bgm/index.html|title=Front Mission 1st Special BGM Selection|last=Gann|first=Patrick|publisher=RPGFan|access-date=2009-07-23|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090223231438/http://rpgfan.com/soundtracks/fm1-bgm/index.html|archive-date=2009-02-23|url-status=live}}</ref> Two songs composed by Shimomura from ''Front Mission'', ''Take the Offensive'' and ''Manifold Irons'', were orchestrated for the ''[[Drammatica]]'' album.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.rpgfan.com/soundtracks/drammatica/index.html|title=drammatica - The Very Best of Yoko Shimomura|last=Gann|first=Patrick|publisher=RPGFan|access-date=2009-07-23|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090815191915/http://www.rpgfan.com/soundtracks/drammatica/index.html|archive-date=2009-08-15|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Remakes==
=== ''Front Mission 1st'' ===
''Front Mission'' was remade for the [[PlayStation]] on November 23, 2003 with the title ''Front Mission 1st''. This remake included new content and offered a new USN scenario to play through.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.gamespot.com/ps/strategy/frontmission1st/preview_6076099.html|title=New Front Mission 1st, Front Mission History, and Front Mission 4 Information|last=Niizumi|first=Hirohiko|website=GameSpot|access-date=2010-12-08|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050310075721/http://www.gamespot.com/ps/strategy/frontmission1st/preview_6076099.html|archive-date=2005-03-10|url-status=live}}</ref> ''Front Mission 1st'' also included new characters that would later be seen in ''[[Front Mission 4]]'', namely Darril Traubel and Billy Renges. This remake served as the basis for the [[Nintendo DS]] port, which was released in Japan on March 22, 2007, and in North America (as ''Front Mission'') on October 23, 2007. The PlayStation version was re-released as a [[List of PS one Classics (Japan)|PSOne Classic]] on the [[PlayStation Network]] in Japan on November 12, 2008.

The Nintendo DS version features battle sequences that make use of the console's dual screen setup for an easy view of the action.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://ds.ign.com/articles/829/829426p1.html|title=Front Mission Wanders onto DS|last=Hatfield|first=Daemon|website=IGN|date=23 October 2007 |access-date=2010-12-08|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081010214438/http://ds.ign.com/articles/829/829426p1.html|archive-date=2008-10-10|url-status=live}}</ref>  The port also includes a number of new additions. A number of characters from other ''Front Mission'' titles were added to the game's storyline, such as Griff Burnam and Glen Duval. New parts and weapons from other ''Front Mission'' entries were added. This version also boasted nine secret missions that further expanded the storyline.<ref>{{cite book|title=Front Mission The First Official Complete Guide|publisher=Square Enix|date=March 2007|isbn=978-4-7575-1981-7|language=ja}}</ref>

=== ''Front Mission 1st: Remake'' ===
A further remake of ''Front Mission 1st'', titled ''Front Mission 1st: Remake'', was developed and published by Forever Entertainment for the [[Nintendo Switch]] on November 30, 2022.<ref>{{cite web | author=Romano, Sal| date=November 2, 2022 | title=FRONT MISSION 1st: Remake launches November 30 | url=https://www.gematsu.com/2022/11/front-mission-1st-remake-launches-november-30| work=Gematsu| accessdate=November 3, 2022}}</ref> Ports to [[PlayStation 4]], [[PlayStation 5]], [[Microsoft Windows|Windows]], [[Xbox One]], and [[Xbox Series X and Series S|Xbox Series X/S]] were released on June 30, 2023.<ref>{{cite web|author=Romano, Sal|date=June 1, 2023|title=FRONT MISSION 1st: Remake coming to PS5, Xbox Series, PS4, Xbox One, and PC on June 30|url=https://www.gematsu.com/2023/06/front-mission-1st-remake-coming-to-ps5-xbox-series-ps4-xbox-one-and-pc-on-june-30|work=Gematsu|accessdate=June 1, 2023}}</ref>

In April 1995, ''[[Famitsu]]'' magazine gave the Super Famicom version of the game first a 9 out of 10<ref>読者 クロスレビュー: フロントミッション. Weekly Famicom Tsūshin. No.330. Pg.31. 14 April 1995.</ref> and later an 8 out of 10 in their Reader Cross Review.<ref>読者 クロスレビュー: フロントミッション. Weekly Famicom Tsūshin. No.332. Pg.32. 28 April 1995.</ref> ''Mega Fun'' gave the game a Gold for an import game.<ref name=":2">{{Cite magazine|last=Hellert|first=Stefan|date=June 1995|title=Front Mission|magazine=Mega Fun|language=DE|location=Germany|page=65}}</ref>

The Nintendo DS version received average reviews from critics. ''[[IGN]]'''s Mark Bozon commended the games "options", "depth", and "customization" compared to other DS tactics games, but was disappointed at the lack of online play, calling it a pure port.<ref name=":3">{{cite web|url=http://ds.ign.com/articles/831/831719p1.html|title=IGN: Front Mission Review|last=Bozon|first=Mark|date=2007-10-31|website=IGN|access-date=2009-07-23|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090221182949/http://ds.ign.com/articles/831/831719p1.html|archive-date=2009-02-21|url-status=live}}</ref> ''[[Nintendo Power]]'' called the game "a stark, futuristic ''[[Advance Wars]]'' without the happy combatants and vehicle variety."<ref name=power>{{cite book|title=Nintendo Power|edition=2007-12|page=82|quote=The game is like a stark, futuristic "Advance Wars" without the happy combatants and vehicle variety.}}</ref>

===Sales===
The original ''Front Mission'' was a huge success in Japan, selling over 500,000 copies.<ref name=":0">{{Cite magazine|date=May 1995|title=Import Review: Front Mission|magazine=Super Play|location=United Kingdom|publisher=Future Publishing|issue=31|pages=30–35}}</ref> ''[[Next Generation (magazine)|Next Generation]]'' reported sales of 530,000 copies.<ref>{{cite magazine |title=NG Alphas: Front Mission Alternative |magazine=[[Next Generation (magazine)|Next Generation]]|issue=35 |publisher=[[Imagine Media]] |date=November 1997|page=133}}</ref>

By the end of 2007, the Nintendo DS version sold 57,153 copies in Japan.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.gemaga.com/2008/06/16/famitsu-top-500-of-2007|title=Famitsu Top 500 of 2007|author=Takahashi|date=2008-06-18|work=Gemaga.com|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080619063635/http://www.gemaga.com/2008/06/16/famitsu-top-500-of-2007|archive-date=2008-06-19|url-status=dead|access-date=2009-01-01}}</ref>

The {{nihongo foot|'''Nintendo GameCube'''|ニンテンドーゲームキューブ|Nintendō Gēmukyūbu|lead=yes|group=lower-alpha}}, commonly known as the '''GameCube''',{{efn|Abbreviated in Japan as '''GC''' or '''NGC''' and in North America and Europe as '''GCN'''.}} is a [[home video game console]] developed and marketed by [[Nintendo]]. It was released in Japan on September 14, 2001, in North America on November 18, 2001, in Europe on May 3, 2002, and in Australia on May 17, 2002. Serving as the successor to the [[Nintendo 64]], the system competed primarily against [[Sony Interactive Entertainment|Sony]]'s [[PlayStation 2]], [[Microsoft]]'s [[Xbox (console)|Xbox]], and [[Sega]]'s [[Dreamcast]] as part of the [[sixth generation of video game consoles]].

Nintendo began designing the console in 1998 in partnership with [[ArtX]] for the system logic and [[graphics processing unit]], [[IBM]] for the central processor, and [[Panasonic|Matsushita Electric Industrial]] for the optical drive. The GameCube is the first Nintendo console to use [[Nintendo optical discs|optical discs]] as its primary storage medium instead of [[ROM cartridge]]s, relying on proprietary 8{{nbsp}}cm [[MiniDVD]]-based discs and external [[GameCube accessories#Memory cards|memory cards]] for [[saved game]] data. Unlike its primary sixth-generation competitors, the standard GameCube was designed exclusively for playing games and cannot play standard [[DVD]] movies or [[CD]] audio, although Matsushita released the [[Panasonic Q]] hybrid DVD model in Japan. The system introduced a handlebar-style [[GameCube controller]] with staggered [[analog stick]]s and pressure-sensitive triggers. [[GameCube accessories]] include the [[WaveBird Wireless Controller]], the [[GameCube – Game Boy Advance link cable]] for connecting a [[Game Boy Advance]] (GBA) as a secondary screen or controller, the [[Game Boy Player]] attachment for playing handheld cartridges on a television, and [[GameCube online functionality|broadband and modem adapters]] that enabled network play in a small number of titles.

The GameCube received positive reviews for its ergonomic controller, compact hardware, and exclusive software library, alongside criticism for its toy-like exterior and lack of multimedia capabilities and built-in online infrastructure. Although the hardware and software business remained profitable for Nintendo, lifetime sales reached 21.74{{nbsp}}million units worldwide, falling well short of the PlayStation 2 and trailing the Xbox while outselling the Dreamcast. Analysts attributed its third-place finish to a limited initial software lineup, weak [[third-party developer|third-party]] multiplatform support, the absence of DVD playback, and a brand image that skewed toward younger players during a period when older demographics drove industry growth.

Nintendo succeeded the GameCube with the [[Wii]] in November 2006 and discontinued the console in February 2007. Early Wii models provide native [[backward compatibility]] with GameCube software, memory cards, and controllers. Retrospectively, critics have praised the GameCube for debuting major Nintendo franchises including ''[[Pikmin]]'', ''[[Luigi's Mansion]]'', ''[[Animal Crossing]]'' outside Japan, and the ''[[Metroid Prime]]'' subseries, as well as hosting acclaimed titles such as ''[[Super Smash Bros. Melee]]'' (2001), ''[[Super Mario Sunshine]]'' (2002), ''[[The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker]]'' (2002), and ''[[Resident Evil 4]]'' (2005). The GameCube controller has remained in production through official adapters and wireless reissues across the Wii, [[Wii U]], [[Nintendo Switch]], and [[Nintendo Switch 2]].

==History==
===Development===
In October 1997, following the resignation of [[Silicon Graphics]] (SGI) chief executive officer [[Ed McCracken]], Nintendo reconsidered its hardware partnership with the company.<ref name="A |publisher=Dromble Media}}</ref> Earlier in 1997, twenty former SGI engineers who had worked on the [[Nintendo 64]]'s reality coprocessor founded the graphics hardware company [[ArtX]] under [[Wei Yen]], who had previously led SGI's Nintendo Operations.<ref name="ATI discusses GC graphics">{{Cite interview |last=Buchner |first=Greg |title=ATI Discusses GameCube Graphics |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2001/10/30/ati-discusses-gamecube-graphics |access-date=June 25, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220619083308/https://www.ign.com/articles/2001/10/30/ati-discusses-gamecube-graphics |archive-date=June 19, 2022 |publisher=[[IGN]] |date=October 30, |website=[[IGN]]}}</ref> In May 1998, ArtX partnered with Nintendo to design the system logic and graphics processor, codenamed "Flipper", for Nintendo's sixth-generation home console.<ref name="Nintendo tweaks GC's specs">{{Cite web |last=Parker |first=Sam |date=June 6, 2001 |title=Nintendo Tweaks GameCube's Specs |url=https://www.zdnet.com/article/nintendo-tweaks-gamecubes-specs/ |publisher=[[ZDNet]]}}</ref> Internal working names for the machine included N2000, Star Cube, and Nintendo Advance.<ref name="It's Alive">{{Cite web |date=March 13, 1999 |title=It's Alive! |archive-date=April 1, 2001}}</ref>

On May 12, 1999, prior to [[E3 1999]], Nintendo of America chairman [[Howard Lincoln]] publicly announced the console under the codename "Project Dolphin".<ref name="Nintendo press conference May |website=[[IGN]]}}</ref> Nintendo concurrently announced partnerships with [[IBM]] to manufacture the 486{{nbsp}}MHz PowerPC-based CPU, codenamed "Gekko", and with [[Panasonic|Matsushita Electric Industrial]] to develop the console's proprietary optical disc drive as well as a separate DVD-capable hardware variant.<ref name="A Dolphin's Tale" /><ref name="Nintendo press conference May 1999" /><ref name="Matsushita">{{Cite web |date=May 12, 1999 |title=Matsushita Allies with Nintendo on Next-Generation Game Console |url=http://www.eetimes.com/document.asp?doc_id=1139403 |url-status=live Nintendo subsequently distributed early development kits to studios including [[Rare (company)|Rare]] and [[Retro Studios]].<ref name="A Dolphin's Tale" /> In April 2000, [[ATI Technologies]] acquired 2000]].<ref name="GCN announced">{{Cite web |last=Satterfield |first=Shane |date=August 24, 2000 |title=Nintendo's GameCube Unveiled ===Release===
The GameCube launched in Japan on September 14, 2001, with approximately 500,000 consoles shipped to retailers alongside three launch games: ''Luigi's Mansion'', ''[[Wave Race: Blue Storm]]'', and ''[[Super Monkey Ball (video game)|Super Monkey Ball]]''.<ref name="Launch – BBC">{{Cite news |date=September 14, 2001 |title=GameCube Launches in Japan |work=[[BBC News]] |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/entertainment/1543848.stm |url-status=live |access-date=July 8, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150117054316/http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/entertainment/1543848.stm |archive-date=January 17, 2015}}</ref><ref name="Japan launch – GS">{{Cite web |last=Sato |first=Yukiyoshi Ike |date=September 13, 2001 |title=Nintendo GameCube Launches in Japan |url=http://www.gamespot.com/news/nintendo-gamecube-launches-in-japan-2812298 |access-date=July 8, 2013 |website=[[GameSpot]]}}</ref> Nintendo originally scheduled the North American launch for November 5, 2001, but pushed the date back nearly two weeks to November 18 so factories could supply over 700,000 units alongside twelve launch titles.<ref name="Record launch – CNET" /><ref name="US launch delay">{{Cite web |last=Becker |first=David |date=August 23, 2001 |title=Nintendo Delays U.S. Launch of GameCube |url=http://news.cnet.com/Nintendo-delays-U.S.-launch-of-GameCube/2100-1040_3-272053.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402105211/http://news.cnet.com/Nintendo-delays-U.S.-launch-of-GameCube/2100-1040_3-272053.html |archive-date=April 2, 2015 |access-date=July 8, 2013 |website=CNET}}</ref>

In Europe, the GameCube launched on May 3, 2002, accompanied by twenty launch titles and a last-minute price reduction from €249 to €199 (£129 in the United Kingdom) following a rival price cut by Microsoft on the Xbox.<ref name="BBC EU price" /><ref name="heise" /><ref name="European launch">{{Cite news |date=May 2, 2002 |title=GameCube Gets Midnight Launch |work=[[BBC News]] |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/entertainment/1963749.stm |url-status=live |access-date=July 8, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140502211811/http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/entertainment/1963749.stm |archive-date=May 2, 2014}}</ref> The Australian release followed on May 17, 2002.<ref name="AUS launch" /> In Brazil, [[IGB Eletrônica|Gradiente]] distributed a localized console revision (model DOL-002) that launched on August 23, 2002, for R$1,200 alongside six games.<ref name="BrazilRelease">{{Cite web |url=http://info.abril.com.br/aberto/infonews/082002/23082002-3.shl |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151121221925/http://info.abril.com.br/aberto/infonews/082002/23082002-3.shl |archive-date=November 21, 2015 |title=GameCube chega ao Brasil por R$ 1,2 mil |date=August 23, 2002 |last=Mesquita |first=Renata |publisher=INFO Exame |language=pt-br |access-date=September 20, 2026}}</ref> The console subsequently launched in Taiwan on November 21, 2002,<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://multiplayer.it/notizie/il-gamecube-arriva-a-taiwan.html |title=Il GameCube arriva a Taiwan |language=it |website=Multiplayer.it |access-date=May 12, 2024}}</ref> and in South Korea on December 14, 2002.<ref name="korea">{{cite news |title=닌텐도,「게임큐브」국내 진출 |via=[[Naver News]] |first=Seungeun |last=Myeong|date=5 December 2002 |url=https://n.news.naver.com/mnews/article/092/0000000724?sid=105 |access-date=29 October 2026 |work=ZDnet |language=ko}}</ref> The GameCube was distributed in South Korea by [[Daewon Media|Daewon C.I.]]<ref name=korea/>

|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220822174723/https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB106788619028502300 |archive-date=August 22, 2022}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Fahey |first=Rob |date=November 5, 2003 |title=GameCube's Market Share Doubles in the USA |url=https://www.gamesindustry.biz/gamecubes-market-share-doubles-in-the-usa |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220822174722/https://www.gamesindustry.biz/gamecubes-market-share-doubles-in-the-usa |archive-date=August 22, 2022 |access-date=August 22, 2022 |website=[[GamesIndustry.biz]]}}</ref> A corresponding European price cut in October 2003, combined with bundles and releases such as ''[[Mario Kart: Double Dash]]'' and ''[[Pokémon Colosseum]]'', lifted the GameCube's European market share to 32% by mid-2004, driven primarily by sales in the United Kingdom, France, and Germany.<ref name="Fahey">{{Cite web |date=June 14, 2004 |title=GameCube Market Share Doubles in Europe |url=https://www.gamesindustry.biz/articles/gamecube-market-share-doubles-in-europe |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220630134648/https://www.gamesindustry.biz/articles/gamecube-market-share-doubles-in-europe |archive-date=June 30, 2022 |access-date=June 30, 2022 |website=[[GamesIndustry.biz]]}}</ref><ref name="gamesindustry 3 million">{{Cite web |date=January 20, 2004 |title=GameCube Approaches 3 Million Units in Europe |url=https://www.gamesindustry.biz/articles/gamecube-approaches-3-million-units-in-europe |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220630135027/https://www.gamesindustry.biz/articles/gamecube-approaches-3-million-units-in-europe |archive-date=June 30, 2022 |access-date=June 30, 2022 |website=[[GamesIndustry.biz]]}}</ref> Although the GameCube never matched the profitability of the PlayStation 2 or the Game Boy Advance, Nintendo generated a net profit on the platform overall, contrasting with Microsoft's heavy financial losses on the original Xbox.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Tran |first=Khanh T. L. |date=November 29, 2001 |title=Nintendo's New GameCube Sells Well, But Lower-Priced Game Boy Soars |work=[[The Wall Street Journal]] |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB1006998117720785680 |url-status=live |access-date=August 22, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220822174722/https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB1006998117720785680 |archive-date=August 22, 2022}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Good |first=Dan |title=The Microsoft Story: How the Tech Giant Rebooted Its Culture, Upgraded Its Strategy, and Found Success in the Cloud |publisher=[[HarperCollins]] |year=2020 |pages=110–111}}</ref>

===Discontinuation===
Nintendo launched the GameCube's successor, the [[Wii]], in North America on November 19, 2006, and in Japan, Australia, and Europe the following month. Several first-party projects originally developed for the GameCube were either shifted exclusively to the Wii, such as ''[[Super Paper Mario]]'' and ''[[Donkey Kong Barrel Blast]]'', or released on both platforms, such as ''[[The Legend of Zelda: Twilight Princess]]''.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hatfield |first=Daemon |date=January 23, 2007 |title=Paper Mario Unfolding in April? |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2007/01/23/paper-mario-unfolding-in-april |access-date=March 5, 2026 |website=[[IGN]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Casamassina |first=Matt |date=November 18, 2006 |title=The Legend of Zelda: Twilight Princess Review |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2006/11/18/the-legend-of-zelda-twilight-princess-review-2 |access-date=March 5, 2026 |website=[[IGN]]}}</ref> In February 2007, Nintendo confirmed that hardware manufacturing and first-party software development for the GameCube had ended as the company focused production on the Wii and the [[Nintendo DS]].<ref name=gamespot>{{Cite web |last=Thorsen |first=Tor |date=February 22, 2007 |title=Nintendo Officially Pulls Plug on GameCube? |url=https://www.gamespot.com/articles/nintendo-officially-pulls-plug-on-gamecube/1100-6236024/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230526140312/https://www.gamespot.com/articles/nintendo-officially-pulls-plug-on-gamecube/1100-6236024/ |archive-date=May 26, 2023 |access-date=October 17, 2023 |website=[[GameSpot]]}}</ref><ref name="gcndiscontinued">{{Cite web |last=Parfitt |first=Ben |date=February 22, 2007 |title=Nintendo Ends GameCube Support |url=http://www.mcvuk.com/news/read/nintendo-ends-gamecube-support |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160601030811/http://www.mcvuk.com/news/read/nintendo-ends-gamecube-support |archive-date=June 1, 2016 |access-date=January 16, 2011 |website=[[MCV/Develop|MCV]]}}</ref> The final licensed game released for the console in North America was ''[[Madden NFL 08]]'' on August 14, 2007.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Webster |first=Hilton |date=October 29, 2024 |title=How Many Games Were Made For The GameCube? |url=https://www.thegamer.com/how-many-games-made-released-gamecube/ |access-date=March 5, 2026 |website=[[TheGamer]]}}</ref>

==Hardware==
{{Multiple image
| image1            = GEKKO.jpg
| total_width       = 250
| caption1          = [[Gekko (processor)|Gekko]] CPU
| image2            = FLIPPER.JPG
| caption2          = [[Flipper (graphics chip)|Flipper]] GPU
}}
Nintendo technical director Howard Cheng stated that the company's primary engineering goal was to adopt a clean [[RISC]] architecture that would minimize development bottlenecks and keep hardware costs low.<ref name="It's Alive" /> ArtX vice president Greg Buchner noted that the hardware team spent three years consulting with Nintendo of America and software studios to design a developer-centric architecture that delivered high performance without requiring complex programming workarounds.<ref name="ATI discusses GC graphics" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Gaming Intelligence Agency – Interview with Greg Buchner |url=http://thegia.com/archive/features/f010606.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181125115721/http://thegia.com/archive/features/f010606.html |archive-date=November 25, 2018 |access-date=November 25, 2018 |website=The Gaming Intelligence Agency}}</ref>

The console's central processing unit is the [[Gekko (processor)|Gekko]], a custom 32-bit [[IBM]] [[PowerPC]] microprocessor based on the [[PowerPC 750CXe]] and fabricated on a 180{{nbsp}}nm CMOS process with [[copper interconnects]].<ref name="Nintendo press conference May 1999" /><ref name="Specs – Anandtech">{{Cite web |last=Shimpi |first=Anand Lal |date=December 7, 2001 |title=Hardware Behind the Consoles – Part II: Nintendo's GameCube |url=http://www.anandtech.com/show/858 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130723162237/http://www.anandtech.com/show/858 |archive-date=July 23, 2013 |access-date=July 9, 2013 |publisher=[[AnandTech]]}}</ref> Running at 486{{nbsp}}MHz (1,125{{nbsp}}[[Instructions per second|DMIPS]]), Gekko contains 64{{nbsp}}KB of L1 cache (32{{nbsp}}KB instruction and 32{{nbsp}}KB data, half of which can be locked as a fast scratchpad for [[direct memory access]]) and 256{{nbsp}}KB of on-die L2 cache.<ref name="Specs – Anandtech" /> Its 64-bit [[floating-point unit]] incorporates roughly 50 custom [[SIMD]] "paired singles" instructions tailored for 3D geometry and lighting calculations, yielding a CPU floating-point throughput of 1.9{{nbsp}}[[FLOPS|GFLOPS]] and a system-wide peak of 10.5{{nbsp}}GFLOPS.<ref name="Specs – Anandtech" /><ref name="GC TD NUK">{{Cite web |title=Technical Details |url=https://www.nintendo.co.uk/Corporate/Nintendo-History/Nintendo-GameCube/Technical-Details/Technical-Details-627134.html |access-date=November 7, 2020 |publisher=[[Nintendo of Europe]] |archive-date=July 5, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220705184723/https://www.nintendo.co.uk/Corporate/Nintendo-History/Nintendo-GameCube/Technical-Details/Technical-Details-627134.html |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Specs – ExtremeTech">{{Cite news |last=Hackman |first=Mark |date=June 12, 2001 |title=Nintendo GameCube Unwrapped |work=[[ExtremeTech]] |url=http://www.extremetech.com/extreme/49118-nintendo-gamecube-unwrapped |url-status=live |access-date=July 9, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131203141509/http://www.extremetech.com/extreme/49118-nintendo-gamecube-unwrapped |archive-date=December 3, 2013}}</ref> Gekko communicates with the system's northbridge over a 64-bit, 162{{nbsp}}MHz [[Front-side bus|front-side bus]] with a peak bandwidth of 1.3{{nbsp}}GB/s.<ref name="Specs – Anandtech" />

The ArtX-designed ATI "Flipper" [[application-specific integrated circuit|ASIC]], clocked at 162{{nbsp}}MHz on an 180{{nbsp}}nm [[NEC]] [[eDRAM]] process, integrates the graphics processor, northbridge, I/O controller, and audio processor on a single die.<ref name="Specs – Anandtech" /><ref name="Specs – PC World">{{Cite magazine |last=Gray |first=Douglas F. |date=June 14, 2001 |title=GameCube Uncovered – IBM, ATI Inside |url=http://www.pcworld.idg.com.au/article/28028/gamecube_uncovered_-_ibm_ati_inside/ |magazine=[[PC World]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140104204321/https://www.pcworld.idg.com.au/article/28028/gamecube_uncovered_-_ibm_ati_ati_inside/ |archive-date=January 4, 2014 |access-date=July 9, 2013}}</ref> Flipper contains 3{{nbsp}}MB of embedded [[MoSys]] [[1T-SRAM]] split between a 2{{nbsp}}MB [[framebuffer]]/[[Z-buffering|Z-buffer]] (7.8{{nbsp}}GB/s bandwidth) and a 1{{nbsp}}MB [[Texture memory|texture cache]] (10.4{{nbsp}}GB/s bandwidth), both operating at latencies under 6.2{{nbsp}}nanoseconds.<ref name="Specs – Anandtech" /><ref name="NintendoGCNspecs">{{Cite web |access-date=March 28, 2008 |url=http://register.nintendo.com/techspecgcn |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080502201300/http://register.nintendo.com/techspecgcn |archive-date=May 2, 2008 |title=GCN Technical Specifications |publisher=[[Nintendo]]}}</ref> The console features 43{{nbsp}}MB of total non-unified RAM: in addition to the 3{{nbsp}}MB of embedded 1T-SRAM on Flipper, the motherboard includes 24{{nbsp}}MB of external 1T-SRAM main system memory running at 324{{nbsp}}MHz across a 64-bit bus (2.6{{nbsp}}GB/s bandwidth) and 16{{nbsp}}MB of 81{{nbsp}}MHz [[DRAM]] serving as an auxiliary buffer for audio and optical drive data.<ref name="Specs – Anandtech" /><ref name="NintendoGCNspecs" /> Flipper integrates a custom 81{{nbsp}}MHz [[Macronix]] 16-bit [[digital signal processor]] capable of processing 64 simultaneous [[Adaptive differential pulse-code modulation|ADPCM]] audio channels at a 48{{nbsp}}kHz sampling rate.<ref name="Specs – Anandtech" /> On April 22, 2002, [[Factor 5]] and [[Dolby Laboratories]] released the MusyX 3D audio [[software development kit]] for the console, enabling real-time motion-based surround sound encoded in [[Dolby Pro Logic#Dolby Pro Logic II|Dolby Pro Logic II]].<ref name="Factor 5 on DPL2">{{Cite interview |last=Eggebrecht |first=Julian |title=Factor 5 on Dolby Pro Logic II |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2002/04/22/factor-5-on-dolby-pro-logic-ii |access-date=June 24, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141116141940/http://www.ign.com/articles/2002/04/22/factor-5-on-dolby-pro-logic-ii |archive-date=November 16, 2014 |url-status=live |work=[[IGN]] |date=April 22, 2002}}</ref>

===Storage and memory cards===
[[File:Nintendo GameCube memory card.png|thumb|right|upright|Memory Card 59]]
Following earlier cartridge-complementing magnetic and optical experiments such as the [[Famicom Disk System]], [[SNES-CD]], and [[64DD]], the GameCube became Nintendo's first console to rely exclusively on optical discs for primary retail distribution.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Bonsor |first=Kevin |date=December 4, 2000 |title=How GameCube Works |url=http://electronics.howstuffworks.com/gamecube2.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140106041121/http://electronics.howstuffworks.com/gamecube2.htm |archive-date=January 6, 2014 |access-date=July 8, 2013 |publisher=[[HowStuffWorks]]}}</ref> The proprietary 8{{nbsp}}cm [[GameCube Game Disc]], developed by Matsushita based on the [[MiniDVD]] standard, operates in [[constant angular velocity]] mode at transfer rates of 16 to 25{{nbsp}}Mbit/s and holds up to 1.5{{nbsp}}GB of data.<ref name="miniDVD – IGN">{{Cite web |date=August 23, 2000 |title=GameCube: A Digital Wonder |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2000/08/24/gamecube-a-digital-wonder |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200625172833/https://www.ign.com/articles/2000/08/24/gamecube-a-digital-wonder |archive-date=June 25, 2020 |access-date=July 8, 2013 |website=[[IGN]]}}</ref><ref name="Specs – Anandtech" /> Nintendo chose the smaller format to combat software piracy through a proprietary copy-protection scheme rather than the standard [[Content Scramble System]] used on commercial DVDs, to avoid paying DVD Forum licensing fees for movie playback, and to reduce disc access times.<ref name="Matsushita" /><ref name="miniDVD – IGN" /> While 1.5{{nbsp}}GB accommodated most software, certain content-heavy games required two discs, higher video compression, or trimmed audio compared to the 4.7{{nbsp}}GB single-layer and 8.5{{nbsp}}GB dual-layer standard DVDs used by the PlayStation 2 and Xbox.<ref name="miniDVD – IGN" />

Because the console contains no internal non-volatile storage for game saves, players must insert a proprietary [[GameCube accessories#Memory cards|Memory Card]] into one of the two front memory card slots to record progress, with save files measured in 8{{nbsp}}KB "blocks".<ref name="Memory card issues">{{Cite web |title=Nintendo GameCube Memory Card 1019 |url=https://www.nintendo.com/consumer/memorycard1019.jsp |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130702181148/http://www.nintendo.com/consumer/memorycard1019.jsp |archive-date=July 2, 2013 |access-date=July 12, 2013 |publisher=[[Nintendo]]}}</ref> Nintendo released three official capacities coded by casing color: the gray Memory Card 59 (512{{nbsp}}KB or 4{{nbsp}}Mb), the black Memory Card 251 (2{{nbsp}}MB or 16{{nbsp}}Mb), and the white Memory Card 1019 (8{{nbsp}}MB or 64{{nbsp}}Mb), alongside higher-capacity cards manufactured by third-party companies.<ref name="Memory card issues" /> Official GameCube game cases include a molded interior clip above the disc hub to store a memory card.

===Console design===
[[File:GameCube-Silver-Optional-Set.jpg|thumb|A Platinum GameCube with a [[WaveBird Wireless Controller]] and [[Game Boy Player]] attached]]
Measuring {{cvt|150|xx|161|xx|110|mm}}, the GameCube has a cube-shaped shell with a rear carrying handle, four front controller ports, two memory card slots, and three top buttons for Power, Reset, and opening the top-loading disc lid.<ref name="Specs" /><ref name="Manual101">{{Cite web |title=Nintendo GameCube Instruction Booklet |url=https://www.nintendo.com/consumer/downloads/gcn101_manual_english.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040717074259/https://www.nintendo.com/consumer/downloads/gcn101_manual_english.pdf |archive-date=July 17, 2004 |access-date=August 25, 2022 |website=Nintendo of America Support |publisher=[[Nintendo of America]] |page=15}}</ref> The console launched in "Indigo" (the signature color featured in Nintendo's branding) and "Jet Black".<ref name="Standard colors">{{Cite web |date=August 22, 2001 |title=Spaceworld 2001: Spicing GameCube Up |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2001/08/22/spaceworld-2001-spicing-gamecube-up |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141101082232/http://www.ign.com/articles/2001/08/22/spaceworld-2001-spicing-gamecube-up |archive-date=November 1, 2014 |access-date=July 9, 2013 |website=[[IGN]]}}</ref> A "Spice" orange console launched in Japan in late 2001, though other territories received only the Spice orange controller,<ref name="Spice Orange">{{Cite web |date=December 3, 2001 |title=Spice Up Your Life |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2001/12/04/spice-up-your-life |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402180702/http://www.ign.com/articles/2001/12/04/spice-up-your-life |archive-date=April 2, 2015 |access-date=July 9, 2013 |website=[[IGN]]}}</ref> and a silver "Platinum" edition was released worldwide in late 2002.<ref name="Platinum edition">{{Cite web |last=Berghammer |first=Billy |date=July 24, 2002 |title=Nintendo Announces Platinum GameCube |url=http://www.nintendoworldreport.com/news/7586 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131105103600/http://www.nintendoworldreport.com/news/7586 |archive-date=November 5, 2013 |access-date=July 9, 2013 |publisher=Nintendo World Report}}</ref> Several limited-edition themed consoles were also produced, such as a North American Platinum bundle featuring a custom ''[[Pokémon XD: Gale of Darkness]]'' faceplate in 2005.

The GameCube is the first Nintendo home console to include a built-in [[graphical user interface|system menu]] and an internal battery-backed [[real-time clock]].<ref name="Manual101" /> Players access the menu by powering on the console without a Game Disc inserted or by holding down the A button on Controller 1 during boot-up.<ref name="Manual101" /> The menu presents a rotating 3D cube whose faces are selected by tilting the analog stick in four directions: tilting up boots the inserted game, tilting right accesses the internal date and time settings, tilting down opens the Memory Card manager to view, copy, move, or erase save data blocks, and tilting left opens the Options screen for mono or stereo audio, screen position adjustment, and system language.<ref name="Manual101" /> The boot sequence includes two hidden audio [[Easter egg (media)|Easter eggs]] triggered by holding down the Z button on Controller 1 (replacing the startup xylophone chime with squeaks and a child's laugh) or on all four connected controllers simultaneously (playing a traditional Japanese percussion cadence).<ref name="Easter Eggs">{{Cite magazine |last=Taljonick |first=Ryan |date=April 3, 2013 |title=The 100 Best Easter Eggs of All Time |url=https://www.gamesradar.com/100-best-easter-eggs-all-time/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130908223145/http://www.gamesradar.com/100-best-easter-eggs-all-time/ |archive-date=September 8, 2013 |access-date=July 16, 2013 |magazine=[[GamesRadar+]]}}</ref> Furthermore, when the ambient background music of the main system menu is sped up 16 times, it plays the startup fanfare of the 1986 [[Famicom Disk System]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=September 8, 2021 |title=Talking Point: Which Nintendo Console Has The Best Start-Up Sound? |url=https://www.nintendolife.com/features/talking-point-which-nintendo-console-has-the-best-start-up-sound |access-date=October 18, 2026 |website=[[Nintendo Life]]}}</ref>

Original DOL-001 consoles feature both an "Analog AV Out" port and a "Digital AV Out" port on the rear panel.<ref name="Component FAQ">{{Cite web |access-date=March 27, 2008 |url=https://www.nintendo.com/consumer/systems/nintendogamecube/component_faq.jsp |title=Nintendo GameCube Component Video Questions |publisher=[[Nintendo]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160409142100/https://www.nintendo.com/consumer/systems/nintendogamecube/component_faq.jsp |archive-date=April 9, 2016}}</ref> The Analog AV Out port uses the same multi-out connector introduced on the Super NES and Nintendo 64, outputting 480i composite video and [[S-Video]] on NTSC consoles or 576i composite and [[SCART|RGB SCART]] video on PAL consoles, while always carrying analog stereo audio.<ref name="Component FAQ" /><ref name="Eurogamer 60Hz">{{Cite web| last=Bramwell |first=Tom |date=January 26, 2002 |title=From Rags to Riches |url=https://www.eurogamer.net/article-31674 |access-date=October 18, 2026 |website=[[Eurogamer]]}}</ref> The Digital AV Out port supports [[Component video|component]] cables (sold exclusively through Nintendo's online store in North America and at retail in Japan) and Japanese [[D-Terminal]] cables, which contain a custom digital-to-analog converter chip to enable 480p [[progressive scan]] output.<ref name="Component FAQ" /><ref name="GameSpy Guide">{{Cite web |date=July 30, 2003 |title=Beginner's Guide: GameCube |url=http://cube.gamespy.com/articles/500/500516p1.html |access-date=October 18, 2026 |website=[[GameSpy]]}}</ref> In compatible NTSC titles, players activate 480p progressive scan by holding down the B button during game boot-up, while in PAL releases the same command activates a 60{{nbsp}}Hz "PAL60" display mode.<ref name="Eurogamer 60Hz" /><ref name="GameSpy Guide" /> The GameCube hardware also contains built-in circuitry for [[stereoscopic 3D]] output, which was tested in ''Luigi's Mansion'', but Nintendo never released the required liquid-crystal display accessory because 3D-capable displays were prohibitively expensive at the time.<ref name="IwataAsks3DS">{{Cite web |title=Iwata Asks: Nintendo 3DS |url=https://iwataasks.nintendo.com/interviews/3ds/how-nintendo-3ds-made/0/2/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230224032834/https://iwataasks.nintendo.com/interviews/3ds/how-nintendo-3ds-made/0/2/ |archive-date=February 24, 2023 |access-date=January 11, 2011 |publisher=[[Nintendo]]}}</ref>

===Panasonic Q===
[[File:Panasonic-Q-Console-Set.png|thumb|The Panasonic Q integrates a front-loading DVD player with GameCube hardware.]]
As part of Matsushita's May 1999 optical drive agreement with Nintendo, Matsushita developed the {{nihongo foot|'''Panasonic Q'''|パナソニックQ|Panasonikku Kyū|lead=yes|group=lower-alpha}} (model SL-GC10), an officially licensed hybrid system combining GameCube hardware with a commercial DVD and CD player.<ref name="Q Christmas – NWR">{{Cite news |last=Lake |first=Max |date=October 19, 2001 |title=Q for Christmas in Japan |work=Nintendo World Report |agency=[[Reuters]] |url=https://www.nintendoworldreport.com/news/6618/q-for-christmas-in-japan |url-status=live |access-date=March 29, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210125230928/https://www.nintendoworldreport.com/news/6618/q-for-christmas-in-japan |archive-date=January 25, 2021}}</ref> Encased in a mirrored [[stainless steel]] chassis with a front-loading motorized disc tray, a backlit LCD screen, optical digital audio output, and top-mounted playback controls, the Panasonic Q launched exclusively in Japan on December 14, 2001, at ¥39,800, after Panasonic confirmed in November 2001 that it had no plans for a North American release.<ref name="Q Christmas – NWR" /><ref name="PanasonicQ-IGN">{{Cite web |last=Mirabella III |first=Fran |date=April 9, 2002 |title=Panasonic Q Review |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2002/04/09/panasonic-q-review |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190414182159/https://www.ign.com/articles/2002/04/09/panasonic-q-review |archive-date=April 14, 2019 |access-date=May 1, 2019 |website=[[IGN]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=November 2, 2001 |title=No Q for the U.S. |url=http://www.nintendoworldreport.com/news/6687/no-q-for-the-us |access-date=February 27, 2017 |website=Nintendo World Report}}</ref> Because its bottom feet obstructed the standard [[Game Boy Player]], Panasonic released a specialized Game Boy Player attachment (model SH-GB10-H) tailored to the Q's chassis. Despite a price cut in July 2002 following reductions on the standard GameCube, the Q's high price relative to buying a standard console and a standalone DVD player resulted in low sales, and Panasonic discontinued the unit in December 2003.<ref>{{Cite web |date=July 1, 2002 |title=Panasonic Drops Q Price |url=http://www.nintendoworldreport.com/news/7507/panasonic-drops-q-price |access-date=February 27, 2017 |website=Nintendo World Report}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Cole |first=Michael |date=December 17, 2003 |title=Panasonic Q Discontinued – News |url=http://www.nintendoworldreport.com/news/9283/panasonic-q-discontinued |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304084816/http://www.nintendoworldreport.com/news/9283/panasonic-q-discontinued |archive-date=March 4, 2016 |access-date=July 28, 2015 |website=Nintendo World Report}}</ref>

===Technical specs===
In May 2004, Nintendo introduced a cost-reduced hardware revision designated model DOL-101.<ref name="Component FAQ" /> After determining that fewer than one percent of owners used progressive scan output, Nintendo removed the Digital AV Out port from the rear of the DOL-101.<ref name="Component FAQ" /> The DOL-101 revision also removed the unused Serial Port 2 expansion bay from the underside of the console, replaced the removable circular nameplate on the disc lid with a fixed nameplate, and paired the unit with a 48-watt AC adapter in place of the original 46-watt adapter.<ref name="Manual101" /><ref name="nwr">{{Cite web |last=Bivens |first=Danny |date=October 31, 2001 |title=GameCube Broadband/Modem Adapter – Feature |url=http://www.nintendoworldreport.com/feature/27672/nintendos-expansion-ports-gamecube-broadbandmodem-adapter |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160406003238/http://www.nintendoworldreport.com/feature/27672/nintendos-expansion-ports-gamecube-broadbandmodem-adapter |archive-date=April 6, 2016 |access-date=November 18, 2017 |website=Nintendo World Report}}</ref>
