* [[32-bit]] 486&nbsp;MHz [[IBM]] "[[Gekko (processor)|Gekko]]" [[PowerPC]] CPU (based on the [[PowerPC 750CXe|750CXe]] and [[PowerPC 750FX|750FX]]){{citation needed|date=April 2016}}
** [[180 nm]] IBM six-layer, copper-wire process, 43{{nbsp}}mm<sup>2</sup> [[Die (integrated circuit)|die]] with 4.9 watts dissipation
** 1.8 [[Volt|V]] for logic and [[I/O]]
** 27×27&nbsp;mm [[Ball grid array|PBGA]] package with 256 contacts
** 18.6 million transistors; of which 6.35 million transistors are for logic
* [[Superscalar]] 3 issue (2 plus branch folding)
* [[Out-of-order execution]]
* Two 4-stage [[Arithmetic logic unit|integer units]]: IU1 and IU2, 32-bit
* [[Front-side bus]]:
** 162&nbsp;MHz 64-bit enhanced [[PowerPC 600#60x bus|60x bus]] northbridge to Flipper
** 1.3 GB/s peak bandwidth (32-bit address, 64-bit data bus)
* On-chip caches:
** 32{{nbsp}}KB 8-way [[CPU cache#Associativity|set-associative]] [[CPU cache|L1 instruction cache]]
** 32{{nbsp}}KB 8-way set-associative [[CPU cache|L1 data cache]]
*** Half of L1 data cache (16{{nbsp}}KB) can be locked for fast [[Direct memory access|DMA]]-from-cache in parallel with instruction execution
** 256{{nbsp}}KB 2-way set-associative [[CPU cache#Multi-level caches|L2 cache]]
* 64-bit [[Floating Point Unit]] (FPU) [[coprocessor]]:
** PowerPC 750 + roughly 50 new [[SIMD]] instructions, geared toward [[3D graphics]]
** 7-stage pipeline
** 32x 64-bit FPR registers
** Usable as 1x 64-bit ([[Double-precision floating-point format|double-precision]]) or 2× 32-bit (paired [[Single-precision floating-point format|singles]]) [[SIMD]] per clock cycle.
** 1.9 [[GFLOPS]] (single precision 32-bit floating point)
** [[IEEE 754|IEEE compliant]]
* [[Data Compression]]
** 2:1 and 4:1 compression for graphics data yields 5.2 GB/s peak effective bus bandwidth
** Load Q instruction: converts 8-bit or 16-bit, signed or unsigned [[Integer (computer science)|integers]] to SP [[Floating-point arithmetic|floating point]]
** Store Q instruction: converts SP floating point to 8-bit or 16-bit, signed or unsigned integer
* Branch Prediction Unit (BPU)
* Load-Store Unit (LSU)
* System Register Unit (SRU)
* Memory Management Unit (MMU)
* Branch Target Instruction Cache (BTIC)
* CPU performance: 1125 [[DMIPS]] (Dhrystone 2.1)
| style="text-align:center" | <ref name="Specs - Anandtech">{{cite web|url=http://www.anandtech.com/show/858|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100703144640/http://www.anandtech.com/show/858|url-status=dead|archive-date=July 3, 2010|title=Hardware Behind the Consoles - Part II: Nintendo's GameCube|last=Shimpi|first=Anand Lal|date=December 7, 2001|publisher=AnandTech|access-date=July 9, 2013}}</ref><ref name="AcesHardwareGCN">{{cite web|access-date=March 27, 2008|url=http://www.aceshardware.com/read.jsp?id=60000288|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040208044032/http://www.aceshardware.com/read.jsp?id=60000288|archive-date=February 8, 2004|title=Game Consoles: A Look Ahead|date=December 14, 2003|publisher=Ace's Hardware}}</ref>
|-
! [[Graphics processing unit|GPU]]
|
* 162&nbsp;MHz [[ArtX]]-designed [[ATI Technologies|ATI]] "Flipper" [[ASIC]] (9.4&nbsp;[[GFLOPS]])
* 180&nbsp;nm [[NEC]] [[eDRAM]] manufacturing process, 51 million [[transistor]]s (approximately half dedicated to 1T-SRAM), 106&nbsp;mm<sup>2</sup> die
* Contains GPU, audio DSP, I/O controller and northbridge
* 3&nbsp;[[Mebibyte|MB]] of on-chip [[1T-SRAM]] (2&nbsp;MB [[Z-buffering|Z-buffer]]/[[framebuffer]] + 1&nbsp;MB [[texture cache]]) with ~18 GB/s total bandwidth
** Embedded 24-bit Z-buffer/framebuffer RAM: 2&nbsp;MB (4× 512&nbsp;KB)
*** Bus width: 384-bit (4 buses, each 96-bit wide) 
*** Bandwidth: 7.8 GB/s
*** Sustainable latency: Under 5&nbsp;ns
** Embedded [[Texture memory|texture]] [[GPU cache|cache]]: 1&nbsp;MB (32× 256&nbsp;Kb)
*** Bus width: 512-bit (32 buses, each 16-bit wide)
*** Bandwidth: 10.4 GB/s
*** Sustainable latency: Under 5&nbsp;ns
* 24&nbsp;MB (2× 12&nbsp;MB) 1T-SRAM main memory @ 324&nbsp;MHz, 64-bit bus, 2.6 GB/s bandwidth 
**
* 1 vertex pipeline, 4 [[pixel pipeline]]s with 1 [[texture mapping unit]] (TMU) each and 4 [[render output unit]]s (ROPs)
* Simultaneous textures per pass: 4
* [[Color depth]]: 16-bit [[RGB color model|RGB]], 32-bit [[RGBA color space|RGBA]]
*System [[floating-point]] arithmetic capability: 11 GFLOPS (peak) (MPU, Geometry Engine, Hardware Lighting Total)
* [[Fillrate]]: 648 [[megapixel]]s/sec, with [[Z-buffering]], [[alpha blending]], [[Distance fog|fogging]], [[texture mapping]], [[trilinear filtering]], [[mipmap]]ping and [[S3 Texture Compression]]<ref name="IGN3">[https://www.ign.com/articles/2001/03/17/graphics-processor-specifications Graphics Processor Specifications], [[IGN]], 2001</ref>
*Raw [[Polygon (computer graphics)|polygon]] performance: 60  million polygons/sec<ref name="IGN1">{{cite web|url=http://ign.com/articles/2001/01/17/gamecube-101-graphics|title=GameCube 101: Graphics|author=IGN Staff|date=January 17, 2001|work=IGN|access-date=November 22, 2015}}</ref>
**40 million polygons/sec, with fogging, Z-buffering, alpha blending and [[Gouraud shading]]<ref name="IGN3"/>
**30 million polygons/sec, with fogging, Z-buffering, alpha blending and texture mapping<ref name="IGN3"/>
**25 million polygons/sec, with fogging, Z-buffering, alpha blending, texture mapping and lighting<ref name="IGN3"/>
**6-12 million polygons/sec,<ref name="IGN2">{{cite web|url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2001/01/09/x-ing-things-out|website=IGN|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20010123223800/http://cube.ign.com/news/29756.html|title=X-ing Things Out|date=January 9, 2001 |archive-date=January 23, 2001|access-date=November 12, 2021|df=mdy-all}}</ref> assuming actual game conditions, with complex models, fully textured, fully lit, etc.
*16-stage TEV fixed-function texture combiner unit (4 inputs, 1 output)[http://amnoid.de/gc/tev.html]
*Indirect texturing unit with 4 dedicated stages using a 2x3 transformation matrix to scale and rotate texture coordinate offsets, enabling per-pixel effects like bump mapping and refraction<ref>{{cite magazine |last=Engel |first=Thomas |date=October 2002 |title=Shader Integration: Merging Shading Technologies on the Nintendo GameCube |url=https://www.gamedeveloper.com/programming/shader-integration-merging-shading-technologies-on-the-nintendo-gamecube |magazine=[[Game Developer (magazine)|Game Developer]] |access-date=June 5, 2024}}</ref>
*Image processing functions: [[Volumetric lighting|Volumetric]] fog, [[heat haze]], [[motion blur]], [[Bloom (shader effect)|bloom]], subpixel [[anti-aliasing]], [[per-vertex lighting]], 8 hardware [[Computer graphics lighting|lights]], alpha blending, hardware [[transform and lighting]] (T&L), virtual texture design, multi-texturing, emboss [[bump mapping]], Dot3 bump mapping ([[normal mapping]]), [[lightmap]]ping, [[shadow map]]ping, [[shadow volume]]s, planar projection shadows, [[environment mapping]], mipmapping, [[Level of detail (computer graphics)|LOD]], [[depth of field]], perspective-correct texture mapping, [[bilinear filtering]], trilinear filtering, [[anisotropic filtering]], real-time hardware texture decompression (S3TC) (6:1 ratio), 8 simultaneous texture layers, 256 levels of transparency, [[Clipping (computer graphics)|clipping]], [[hidden surface removal]]/culling, Zfreeze, Zcomploc/early-Z reject, [[bounding box]], destination alpha test, alpha test, depth test, render to texture, TEV compare, color combiners, alpha combiners, texture combiners, transparency effects, framebuffer effects, post-processing effects, [[Gouraud shading]], [[cel shading]], [[dither]]ing, can emulate 1-bit [[stencil buffer]] through a Zfreeze function
*Other: Real-time decompression of [[display list]], hardware motion compensation capability, HW 3-line deflickering filter
| style="text-align:center" | <ref name="Specs - Anandtech"/><ref name="AcesHardwareGCN"/><ref name="eetimes">[http://www.eetimes.com/document.asp?doc_id=1227977 GameCube clears path for game developers], ''[[EE Times]]'', 5/16/2001</ref>

! System memory
| 
* 43&nbsp;[[Mebibyte|MB]] total non-unified [[Random-access memory|RAM]]
** 24&nbsp;MB (2× 12&nbsp;MB) [[MoSys]] [[1T-SRAM]] @ 324&nbsp;MHz (codenamed "Splash") as main system RAM
** 3&nbsp;MB [[eDRAM|embedded]] 1T-SRAM cache within "Flipper" GPU (2&nbsp;MB [[framebuffer]]/[[Z-buffer]], 1&nbsp;MB [[Texture memory|texture cache]])
** 16&nbsp;MB [[DRAM]] used as [[Input/output|I/O]] buffer for audio and DVD drive
* [[Memory bus]] width: 64-bit main system RAM, 896-bit internal GPU memory, 8-bit ARAM
* [[Memory bandwidth]]: 1.3&nbsp;[[GB/s]] Gekko to Northbridge, 2.6&nbsp;[[GB/s]] Flipper to main system RAM, 10.4&nbsp;GB/s texture cache, 7.8&nbsp;GB/s framebuffer/Z-buffer, 81 MB/s auxiliary RAM<ref name="Specs - Anandtech"/>
* [[CAS latency|Latency]]: Under 10&nbsp;[[Nanosecond|ns]] main memory, 5&nbsp;ns texture cache, 5&nbsp;ns [[framebuffer]] memory

! Audio
|
* Audio processor integrated into Flipper: custom 81&nbsp;MHz [[Macronix]] 16-bit DSP
** Sampling frequency: 48&nbsp;kHz 
** 64 simultaneous channels, [[Adaptive differential pulse-code modulation|ADPCM]] encoding
** Instruction memory: 8&nbsp;KB RAM, 8&nbsp;KB [[Read-only memory|ROM]]
** Data memory: 8&nbsp;KB RAM, 4&nbsp;KB ROM
* External auxiliary RAM: 16&nbsp;MB DRAM @ 81&nbsp;MHz
** Auxiliary RAM bus: 8-bit
** Auxiliary RAM bus bandwidth: 81 MB/s<ref name="Specs - Anandtech"/>
** CPU can read/write blocks from RAM to ARAM through DMA; ARAM can be used for miscellaneous low-bandwidth purposes [https://blog.lse.epita.fr/articles/38-emulating-the-gamecube-audio-processing-in-dolphin.html]
* Stereo output (may contain 5.1-channel surround via [[Pro Logic|Dolby Pro Logic II]])

===Controllers and accessories===
{{Main|GameCube controller|WaveBird Wireless Controller|GameCube accessories}}
[[File:Gamecube-controller-breakdown.jpg|thumb|Indigo GameCube controller]]
Departing from the three-pronged Nintendo 64 gamepad, Nintendo adopted a two-grip handlebar layout for the standard [[GameCube controller]].<ref name="Controller – ZDNet">{{Cite news |last=Satterfield |first=Shane |date=November 16, 2001 |title=What's Inside the GameCube? |work=[[ZDNet]] |url=https://www.zdnet.com/article/whats-inside-the-gamecube/ |url-status=live |access-date=July 15, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120307005736/http://www.zdnet.com/news/whats-inside-the-gamecube/117056 |archive-date=March 7, 2012}}</ref> The controller includes a built-in [[Haptic technology|rumble motor]], staggered dual [[analog stick]]s (a rubberized primary control stick on the upper left and a yellow "C-Stick" on the lower right that replaced the Nintendo 64's four C-buttons), a small directional pad identical in size to that of the original Game Boy Advance, a central Start/Pause button, and an asymmetric face-button cluster with a large green A button flanked by a red B button and kidney-shaped X and Y buttons.<ref name="Controller – ZDNet" /><ref name="Controller – Nintendojo">{{Cite web |last=England |first=Kyle |date=April 5, 2012 |title=The Legend of the Gamepad: A Brief History of Nintendo Consoles Told with Buttons and Joysticks |url=http://www.nintendojo.com/features/editorials/the-legend-of-the-gamepad |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121130073145/http://www.nintendojo.com/features/editorials/the-legend-of-the-gamepad |archive-date=November 30, 2012 |access-date=July 15, 2013 |publisher=Nintendojo}}</ref> The shoulder inputs consist of a digital purple Z button on the right and dual hybrid L and R triggers that register progressive analog travel before clicking a digital contact at full depression.<ref name="Controller – L & R">{{Cite web |date=July 27, 2001 |title=GCN Controller: See It in Action |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2001/07/27/gcn-controller-see-it-in-action |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141116122312/http://www.ign.com/articles/2001/07/27/gcn-controller-see-it-in-action |archive-date=November 16, 2014 |access-date=July 15, 2013 |website=[[IGN]]}}</ref> In June 2002, Nintendo launched the [[WaveBird Wireless Controller]], the first [[Radio frequency|radio-frequency]] wireless gamepad developed by a first-party console manufacturer, which runs on two AA batteries and communicates via a plug-in receiver dongle while omitting the rumble motor to conserve battery life.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Wiley |first=M. |date=June 11, 2002 |title=Nintendo WaveBird Review |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2002/06/11/nintendo-wavebird-review |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130923231827/http://www.ign.com/articles/2002/06/11/nintendo-wavebird-review |archive-date=September 23, 2013 |access-date=July 15, 2013 |website=[[IGN]]}}</ref> In June 2003, [[LodgeNet]] partnered with Nintendo to deploy on-demand GameCube games to North American hotel rooms through its Signeture TV system, utilizing a black, tamper-resistant hotel controller variant equipped with television menu navigation buttons.<ref>{{Cite web |date=June 23, 2003 |title=LodgeNet Upgrading to Gamecube |url=https://www.gamedeveloper.com/game-platforms/lodgenet-upgrading-to-gamecube |access-date=October 18, 2026 |website=[[Game Developer (website)|Game Developer]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Rodriguez |first=Steven |date=June 24, 2003 |title=Play GameCube Games in Your Hotel Room |url=http://www.nintendoworldreport.com/news/8763/play-gamecube-games-in-your-hotel-room |access-date=October 18, 2026 |website=Nintendo World Report}}</ref>

[[File:GameCube-GBA-Link-Cable.jpg|thumb|The [[GameCube – Game Boy Advance link cable]] connects a [[Game Boy Advance]] to a controller port.]]
Nintendo and third-party manufacturers released several specialized input peripherals and hardware attachments. The [[GameCube – Game Boy Advance link cable]] connects a GBA or [[Nintendo e-Reader|e-Reader]] to a GameCube controller port to transfer unlockable content, download minigames, or use the handheld as a personal screen and controller in titles such as ''[[The Legend of Zelda: Four Swords Adventures]]'' and ''[[Final Fantasy Crystal Chronicles (video game)|Final Fantasy Crystal Chronicles]]''.<ref name="Months before GameCube – IGN" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Schneider |first=Peer |date=June 2, 2004 |title=The Legend of Zelda: Four Swords Adventures |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2004/06/02/the-legend-of-zelda-four-swords-adventures |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131012030528/http://www.ign.com/articles/2004/06/02/the-legend-of-zelda-four-swords-adventures |archive-date=October 12, 2013 |access-date=July 8, 2013 |website=[[IGN]]}}</ref> Released in 2003, the [[Game Boy Player]] attaches to the high-speed parallel port on the underside of the console and uses internal GBA hardware and a boot disc to play [[Game Boy]], [[Game Boy Color]], and GBA cartridges on a television, providing an on-screen Z-button menu for display borders, screen sizing, filters, and controller mapping, although cartridges with built-in tilt sensors such as ''[[WarioWare: Twisted!]]'' and ''[[Yoshi Topsy-Turvy]]'' are awkward to use because they require tilting the console itself.<ref name="GB Player">{{Cite web |date=November 18, 2002 |title=Nintendo GameCube Game Boy Player |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2002/11/18/nintendo-gamecube-game-boy-player |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131224011252/http://www.ign.com/articles/2002/11/18/nintendo-gamecube-game-boy-player |archive-date=December 24, 2013 |access-date=July 16, 2013 |website=[[IGN]]}}</ref> Game-specific controllers include the [[DK Bongos]] (known as the ''TaruKonga'' in Japan), a pair of barrel-shaped drums with a Start/Pause button and an internal clap-detecting microphone used for the ''[[Donkey Konga]]'' series and ''[[Donkey Kong Jungle Beat]]'', the Nintendo GameCube Microphone, which plugs into a memory card slot to process voice commands in ''[[Mario Party 6]]'', ''[[Mario Party 7]]'', ''Karaoke Revolution Party'', and ''[[Odama]]'' (which included a controller microphone clip), the Action Pad dance mat produced by [[Konami]] for ''[[Dance Dance Revolution: Mario Mix]]'', and the Japan-exclusive [[ASCII Corporation|ASCII]] Keyboard Controller, which embeds a full keyboard inside an elongated GameCube controller shell and plugs into two controller ports for text chat in ''[[Phantasy Star Online]]''.

===Backward compatibility and emulation===
Original [[Wii]] models (RVL-001) feature native hardware [[backward compatibility]] with all official GameCube Game Discs, memory cards, and controller-port peripherals via four built-in GameCube controller ports and two memory card slots beneath hinged top panels, including 480p progressive scan output over Wii component cables, although the Wii lacks the bottom expansion ports required for the Game Boy Player or the Broadband and Modem Adapters.<ref name="Family Edition">{{Cite web |last=Humphries |first=Matthew |date=August 17, 2011 |title=Nintendo's New Wii Drops GameCube Compatibility, Bundles More Games |url=http://www.geek.com/games/nintendos-new-wii-console-drops-gamecube-compatibility-bundles-more-games-1413513/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130612050210/http://www.geek.com/games/nintendos-new-wii-console-drops-gamecube-compatibility-bundles-more-games-1413513/ |archive-date=June 12, 2013 |access-date=July 16, 2013 |publisher=Geek.com}}</ref> Nintendo removed GameCube software and accessory support from the 2011 Wii Family Edition (RVL-101) and the 2012 [[Wii Mini]].<ref name="Family Edition" /><ref name="Wii Mini">{{Cite web |last=Plunkett |first=Luke |date=December 13, 2012 |title=Tearing Open the New Wii Reveals Some Crazy Nintendo Decisions |url=https://kotaku.com/tearing-open-the-new-wii-reveals-some-crazy-nintendo-de-5968014 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130514082125/http://kotaku.com/5968014/tearing-open-the-new-wii-reveals-some-crazy-nintendo-decisions |archive-date=May 14, 2013 |access-date=July 16, 2013 |publisher=[[Kotaku]]}}</ref> On June 5, 2025, Nintendo began re-releasing emulated GameCube titles through the ''[[Nintendo Classics|Nintendo GameCube – Nintendo Classics]]'' application exclusively for the [[Nintendo Switch 2]] as part of the [[Nintendo Switch Online]] + Expansion Pack subscription tier.<ref name="NSO Switch 2">{{Cite web |title=What's new with Nintendo Switch Online on Nintendo Switch 2? |url=https://www.nintendo.com/us/whatsnew/whats-new-with-nintendo-switch-online-on-nintendo-switch-2/ |access-date=April 8, 2025 |website=[[Nintendo]] |archive-date=April 11, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250411221410/https://www.nintendo.com/us/whatsnew/whats-new-with-nintendo-switch-online-on-nintendo-switch-2/?srsltid=AfmBOor5XKQECwK6475YbGFAK57GEiHkfVNJMYBHnIwhn3JzEnYNSvVN |url-status=live}}</ref> Outside of official hardware, GameCube games are widely emulated on personal computers and mobile devices using the open-source [[Dolphin (emulator)|Dolphin]] emulator, first released in 2003.

==Games==
{{See also|List of GameCube games|List of best-selling GameCube video games|List of cancelled GameCube games}}
More than 600 licensed games were released for the GameCube during its lifespan between 2001 and 2007.<ref name="GC History – Nintendo Life">{{Cite web |last=Reece |first=Mark |date=November 18, 2011 |title=Feature: Remembering the GameCube |url=http://www.nintendolife.com/news/2011/11/feature_remembering_the_gamecube |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130910195802/http://www.nintendolife.com/news/2011/11/feature_remembering_the_gamecube |archive-date=September 10, 2013 |access-date=July 19, 2013 |website=[[Nintendo Life]]}}</ref><ref name="Year One">{{Cite web |last=Hinkle |first=David |date=November 19, 2007 |title=Year One: GameCube vs. Wii |url=https://www.engadget.com/2007/11/19/year-one-gamecube-vs-wii/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181125115528/https://www.engadget.com/2007/11/19/year-one-gamecube-vs-wii/ |archive-date=November 25, 2018 |access-date=November 24, 2018 |website=[[Engadget]]}}</ref> Although Nintendo faced criticism for a slow first-year release schedule and the absence of a launch ''Mario'' platformer,<ref name="Year One" /> the company introduced several new intellectual properties on the system, including ''[[Pikmin]]'', ''[[Luigi's Mansion]]'', ''[[Chibi-Robo!]]'', and the Western debut of ''[[Animal Crossing (video game)|Animal Crossing]]'' (originally released on the Nintendo 64 in Japan as ''Dōbutsu no Mori''), while reviving the ''[[Metroid]]'' series after an eight-year hiatus with Retro Studios' ''[[Metroid Prime]]'' (2002) and ''[[Metroid Prime 2: Echoes]]'' (2004).<ref name="GC History – Nintendo Life" /> First-party sequels to established Nintendo franchises included the platform's best-selling title ''[[Super Smash Bros. Melee]]'' (7.09{{nbsp}}million copies sold), ''[[Mario Kart: Double Dash]]'', ''[[Super Mario Sunshine]]'', ''[[The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker]]'', ''[[Paper Mario: The Thousand-Year Door]]'', ''[[F-Zero GX]]'', ''[[Mario Golf: Toadstool Tour]]'', ''[[Mario Power Tennis]]'', and four entries in the ''[[Mario Party]]'' series (''[[Mario Party 4|4]]'' through ''[[Mario Party 7|7]]'').<ref name="Melee 7.09" /><ref name="GC History – Nintendo Life" />

To counter perceptions that its consoles catered exclusively to children, Nintendo published and courted several mature-rated and teen-oriented exclusives.<ref name="chicagotribune 2001" /><ref>{{Cite news |last=Chu |first=Showwei |date=October 30, 2002 |title=Nintendo Targeting New Video Games at Young Adults |url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/report-on-business/nintendo-targeting-new-video-games-at-young-adults/article25424723/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220822174722/https://www.theglobeandmail.com/report-on-business/nintendo-targeting-new-video-games-at-young-adults/article25424723/ |archive-date=August 22, 2022 |access-date=August 22, 2022 |work=[[The Globe and Mail]]}}</ref> Nintendo published [[Silicon Knights]]' psychological horror game ''[[Eternal Darkness: Sanity's Requiem]]'' (2002), which achieved modest commercial sales but earned critical acclaim,<ref>{{Cite news |last=Haines |first=Rob |date=March 9, 2014 |title=Eternal Darkness: Sanity's Requiem Retrospective |work=[[Eurogamer]] |url=https://www.eurogamer.net/eternal-darkness-sanitys-requiem-retrospective |url-status=live |access-date=August 27, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220827144203/https://www.eurogamer.net/eternal-darkness-sanitys-requiem-retrospective |archive-date=August 27, 2022}}</ref> and collaborated with [[Konami]] and Silicon Knights on ''[[Metal Gear Solid: The Twin Snakes]]'' (2004).<ref>{{Cite web |last=Rodriguez |first=Steven |date=March 18, 2004 |title=Metal Gear Solid: The Twin Snakes Review |url=http://www.nintendoworldreport.com/review/4218/metal-gear-solid-the-twin-snakes-gamecube |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220822174641/http://www.nintendoworldreport.com/review/4218/metal-gear-solid-the-twin-snakes-gamecube |archive-date=August 22, 2022 |access-date=August 22, 2022 |website=Nintendo World Report}}</ref>

===Third-party support===
After high cartridge manufacturing costs on the Nintendo 64 drove many publishers to Sony's CD-based PlayStation during the 1990s, Nintendo designed the GameCube's optical disc format and development tools to win back third-party support.<ref name="3rd-party – NMagUK">{{Cite web |last=East |first=Tom |date=November 4, 2009 |title=History of Nintendo: GameCube |url=http://www.officialnintendomagazine.co.uk/12990/features/history-of-nintendo-gamecube/?page=1 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141010144232/http://www.officialnintendomagazine.co.uk/12990/features/history-of-nintendo-gamecube/?page=1 |archive-date=October 10, 2014 |access-date=July 19, 2013 |publisher=[[Official Nintendo Magazine]]}}</ref> Longtime second-party partner [[Rare (company)|Rare]] completed only one GameCube title, ''[[Star Fox Adventures]]'' (2002), before Microsoft acquired the studio in September 2002.<ref name="GC History – Nintendo Life" /> To expand its software output, Nintendo commissioned external studios to develop entries in its own franchises, partnering with [[Sega]]'s [[Amusement Vision]] on ''F-Zero GX'', [[Namco]] on ''[[Donkey Konga]]'' and ''[[Star Fox: Assault]]'', [[Treasure (company)|Treasure]] on ''[[Wario World]]'', and [[Square Enix]] on ''Final Fantasy Crystal Chronicles''.<ref name="GC History – Nintendo Life" />

Following the discontinuation of the Dreamcast in 2001, Sega became one of the most prolific third-party publishers on the GameCube, achieving strong commercial sales with ''Super Monkey Ball'', ''[[Sonic Adventure 2|Sonic Adventure 2: Battle]]'', ''[[Sonic Adventure|Sonic Adventure DX: Director's Cut]]'', ''[[Sonic Heroes]]'', and ''[[Phantasy Star Online Episode I & II]]''.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Buchanan |first=Levi |date=March 5, 2002 |title=Teaming Up with Nintendo, the Ship Comes In for Sega |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/news/ct-xpm-2002-03-05-0203050005-story.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220808160132/https://www.chicagotribune.com/news/ct-xpm-2002-03-05-0203050005-story.html |archive-date=August 8, 2022 |access-date=August 8, 2022 |newspaper=[[Chicago Tribune]]}}</ref><ref name="ign sonic">{{Cite web |author=IGN Staff |date=February 25, 2002 |title=Sonic Nabs Strong Sales |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2002/02/25/sonic-nabs-strong-sales |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220701145225/https://www.ign.com/articles/2002/02/25/sonic-nabs-strong-sales |archive-date=July 1, 2022 |access-date=August 23, 2022 |website=[[IGN]]}}</ref> [[Capcom]] also formed a close partnership with Nintendo, releasing the remake of ''[[Resident Evil (2002 video game)|Resident Evil]]'' and ''[[Resident Evil Zero]]'' in 2002 before announcing the [[Capcom Five]] lineup in November 2002: ''[[P.N.03]]'', ''[[Viewtiful Joe (video game)|Viewtiful Joe]]'', ''[[Dead Phoenix]]'' (later cancelled), ''[[Killer7]]'', and ''[[Resident Evil 4]]'', though Capcom subsequently ported ''Viewtiful Joe'', ''Killer7'', and ''Resident Evil 4'' to the PlayStation 2.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Thompson |first=Scott |date=November 10, 2011 |title=Observing the Course and Wake of the Capcom Five – Feature |url=http://www.nintendoworldreport.com/feature/28394/observing-the-course-and-wake-of-the-capcom-five |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220822174723/http://www.nintendoworldreport.com/feature/28394/observing-the-course-and-wake-of-the-capcom-five |archive-date=August 22, 2022 |access-date=August 22, 2022 |website=Nintendo World Report}}</ref><ref name="kotaku re4">{{Cite web |date=December 14, 2012 |title=Why Resident Evil 4 Became a Nintendo Exclusive |url=https://kotaku.com/why-resident-evil-4-became-a-nintendo-exclusive-5968398 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220822174722/https://kotaku.com/why-resident-evil-4-became-a-nintendo-exclusive-5968398 |archive-date=August 22, 2022 |access-date=August 22, 2022 |website=[[Kotaku]]}}</ref> Other notable third-party collaborations included Namco including Link from ''The Legend of Zelda'' as an exclusive guest fighter in the GameCube version of ''[[Soulcalibur II]]'', and [[Electronic Arts]] incorporating Mario, Luigi, and Princess Peach into the GameCube versions of ''[[NBA Street V3]]'' and ''[[SSX on Tour]]''.<ref>{{Cite news |date=March 7, 2003 |title=Nintendo Teams Up With Electronic Arts |work=[[The Wall Street Journal]] |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB104706206680368100 |url-status=live |access-date=August 23, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220823150420/https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB104706206680368100 |archive-date=August 23, 2022}}</ref> Major Western publishers including Electronic Arts, [[Activision]], [[Ubisoft]], [[THQ]], and [[Midway Games]] supported the console through 2007, although several multiplatform titles sold fewer copies on the GameCube than on the PlayStation 2 and Xbox, leading some studios to scale back support during the second half of the console's life.<ref name="A Dolphin's Tale" />

===Online gaming===
{{Main|GameCube online functionality}}
[[File:GameCube online setup.png|thumb|right|A GameCube equipped with a Broadband Adapter and the Japan-exclusive [[ASCII Corporation|ASCII]] Keyboard Controller for ''[[Phantasy Star Online]]''.]]
Unlike Microsoft with [[Xbox Live]] and Sony with the [[PlayStation 2 Expansion Bay|PlayStation 2 Network Adaptor]], Nintendo remained skeptical of consumer demand for subscription online console gaming and did not establish a unified first-party online network for the GameCube.<ref name="GCN jumps online2" /> Instead, network connectivity required purchasing the official [[Nintendo GameCube Broadband Adapter and Modem Adapter|Broadband Adapter or Modem Adapter]], which were released in autumn 2002 and fit into Serial Port 1 on the underside of the console, while individual publishers managed their own servers.<ref name="GCN jumps online2" /><ref name="nwr" />

Only eight GameCube titles officially supported network functionality.<ref name="nwr" /><ref name="konami.jp-2005">{{Cite web |date=November 19, 2005 |title=ダウンロード |url=http://www.konami.jp:80/gs/game/pawa/10_gc/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20051119025520/http://www.konami.jp/gs/game/pawa/10_gc/ |archive-date=November 19, 2005 |access-date=November 25, 2017 |website=Konami}}</ref> In Western territories, Internet play was limited to three Sega role-playing games: ''[[Phantasy Star Online Episode I & II]]'', ''Phantasy Star Online Episode I & II Plus'', and ''[[Phantasy Star Online Episode III: C.A.R.D. Revolution]]'', whose official servers operated until 2007.<ref name="nwr" /> Japan received two additional Internet-enabled titles: [[Chunsoft]]'s cooperative role-playing game ''[[Homeland (video game)|Homeland]]'' (which allowed a player's console to act as a host server for up to 35 other players) and Konami's ''Jikkyō Powerful Pro Yakyū 10'', which supported downloadable roster updates.<ref name="nwr" /><ref name="konami.jp-2005" /> Three first-party racing games—''[[Mario Kart: Double Dash]]'', ''[[1080° Avalanche]]'', and ''[[Kirby Air Ride]]''—supported local area network (LAN) multiplayer across up to eight linked consoles using the Broadband Adapter, which enthusiasts also routed over the Internet using PC [[Tunneling protocol|tunneling]] software.<ref name="nwr" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Thorsen |first=Tor |date=October 28, 2003 |title=DIY Developers Bring GameCube Online |url=https://www.gamespot.com/articles/diy-developers-bring-gamecube-online/1100-6077489/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171117122528/https://www.gamespot.com/articles/diy-developers-bring-gamecube-online/1100-6077489/ |archive-date=November 17, 2017 |access-date=November 27, 2017 |website=[[GameSpot]]}}</ref>

==Reception==

===Critical reception===
The GameCube received generally positive reviews from hardware critics at launch. ''[[PC Magazine]]'' praised the console's compact industrial design, fast loading times, and launch software quality.<ref name="PCMag Review">{{Cite web |last=Ryan |first=Michael E. |date=November 15, 2001 |title=Nintendo GameCube: Review |url=https://www.pcmag.com/article2/0,2817,7344,00.asp |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130710201253/http://www.pcmag.com/article2/0,2817,7344,00.asp |archive-date=July 10, 2013 |access-date=July 22, 2013 |website=[[PCMag|PC Magazine]]}}</ref> ''[[CNET]]'' highlighted the $199 launch price and the ergonomics of the controller while noting the lack of DVD playback and audio CD support compared to the PlayStation 2 and Xbox.<ref name="CNET Review">{{Cite web |date=November 18, 2001 |title=Nintendo GameCube |url=http://reviews.cnet.com/consoles/nintendo-gamecube-black/4505-10109_7-8688672.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131002153039/http://reviews.cnet.com/consoles/nintendo-gamecube-black/4505-10109_7-8688672.html |archive-date=October 2, 2013 |access-date=July 22, 2013 |website=[[CNET]]}}</ref> Later hardware assessments frequently criticized the Indigo console's lunchbox-like handle and plastic casing as "toy-ish" in comparison to the home-theater styling of its rivals.<ref name="igntop25">{{Cite web |title=Nintendo GameCube Is Number 16 |url=https://www.ign.com/top-25-consoles/16.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090906014845/http://www.ign.com/top-25-consoles/16.html |archive-date=September 6, 2009 |access-date=October 15, 2009 |website=[[IGN]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=December 7, 2004 |title=Xbox Vs. GameCube Vs. PlayStation 2: Torture-Testing All the Video Game Consoles--in One Room, at One Time |url=http://www.popularmechanics.com/technology/gadgets/1278831 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130804101308/http://www.popularmechanics.com/technology/gadgets/1278831 |archive-date=August 4, 2013 |access-date=July 22, 2013 |website=[[Popular Mechanics]]}}</ref> Looking back at the console's commercial trajectory, ''[[Joystiq]]'' attributed the GameCube's market share struggles to software droughts during its first year and its sparse online support.<ref name="Year One" />

===Sales===
In Japan, consumers purchased between 280,000 and 300,000 GameCube units during its first three days on the market out of an initial shipment of 450,000 consoles.<ref name="gamespot sales">{{Cite web |title=Japanese GameCube Sales Figures |url=https://www.gamespot.com/articles/japanese-gamecube-sales-figures/1100-2812925/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171209043936/https://www.gamespot.com/articles/japanese-gamecube-sales-figures/1100-2812925/ |archive-date=December 9, 2017 |access-date=July 15, 2022 |website=[[GameSpot]]}}</ref> In North America, Nintendo generated over $100{{nbsp}}million in GameCube hardware and software revenue during its launch weekend and sold 600,000 consoles by early December 2001, with ''Luigi's Mansion'', ''Star Wars Rogue Squadron II: Rogue Leader'', and ''Wave Race: Blue Storm'' leading initial software sales.<ref name="BBC">{{Cite news |date=November 21, 2001 |title=GameCube Sales Hit $100m |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/entertainment/1666671.stm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171208231544/http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/entertainment/1666671.stm |archive-date=December 8, 2017 |access-date=December 8, 2017 |work=[[BBC News]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Smith |first=Tony |date=December 4, 2001 |title=Nintendo GameCube Sales on Target to Beat Initial Forecast |url=https://www.theregister.co.uk/2001/12/04/nintendo_gamecube_sales_on_target/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171208231500/https://www.theregister.co.uk/2001/12/04/nintendo_gamecube_sales_on_target/ |archive-date=December 8, 2017 |access-date=December 8, 2017 |website=[[The Register]]}}</ref>

Sales momentum slowed significantly in 2002 and early 2003. By March 31, 2003, worldwide hardware sales stood at 9.55{{nbsp}}million units, missing Nintendo's fiscal target of 10{{nbsp}}million.<ref>{{Cite news |date=May 22, 2003 |title=Profit Decline at Nintendo Blamed on GameCube Sales |url=http://www.seattlepi.com/business/amp/Profit-decline-at-Nintendo-blamed-on-GameCube-1115364.php |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171208231711/http://www.seattlepi.com/business/amp/Profit-decline-at-Nintendo-blamed-on-GameCube-1115364.php |archive-date=December 8, 2017 |access-date=December 8, 2017 |newspaper=[[Seattle Post-Intelligencer]]}}</ref> Faced with millions of unsold consoles in warehouse inventory, Nintendo president [[Satoru Iwata]] halted GameCube factory production for the first nine months of 2003.<ref name="Frederick Sekiguchi" /> In the United Kingdom, retailer [[Dixons Retail|Dixons]] removed GameCube hardware and software from its stores in March 2003, while [[Argos (retailer)|Argos]] slashed prices to clear stock before restocking the console in October 2003 after Nintendo cut the official retail price and bundled the console with ''[[The Legend of Zelda: Collector's Edition]]''.<ref>{{Cite news |date=March 18, 2003 |title=Argos to Drop GameCube |work=[[Eurogamer]] |url=https://www.eurogamer.net/articles/article_47584 |url-status=live |access-date=November 24, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181124220314/https://www.eurogamer.net/articles/article_47584 |archive-date=November 24, 2018}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Fahey |first=Rob |date=October 10, 2003 |title=Argos Re-Introduces GameCube Following Price Cut |url=https://www.gamesindustry.biz/articles/argos-re-introduces-gamecube-following-price-cut |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220701160553/https://www.gamesindustry.biz/articles/argos-re-introduces-gamecube-following-price-cut |archive-date=July 1, 2022 |access-date=July 1, 2022 |website=[[GamesIndustry.biz]]}}</ref> During the same period, [[Acclaim Entertainment]] chief executive Rod Cousens publicly questioned the console's profitability in June 2003 prior to Acclaim's 2004 bankruptcy,<ref>{{Cite web |date=June 23, 2003 |title=Acclaim to Pull GameCube Support |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2003/06/23/acclaim-to-pull-gamecube-support |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210711010507/https://www.ign.com/articles/2003/06/23/acclaim-to-pull-gamecube-support |archive-date=July 11, 2021 |access-date=July 26, 2021 |website=[[IGN]]}}</ref> and [[Eidos Interactive]] suspended GameCube development in September 2003 before returning to the platform following its 2005 acquisition by [[SCi Games|SCi Entertainment]] to publish ''[[Lego Star Wars: The Video Game]]'' and ''[[Tomb Raider: Legend]]''.<ref>{{Cite web |date=September 5, 2003 |title=Eidos to Pull GCN Support |url=http://cube.ign.com/articles/436/436915p1.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120204083334/http://cube.ign.com/articles/436/436915p1.html |archive-date=February 4, 2012 |access-date=July 12, 2007 |website=[[IGN]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=October 26, 2005 |title=Eidos Brings "The Force" to the Nintendo GameCube with LEGO Star Wars: The Video Game |url=https://www.gamesindustry.biz/articles/eidos-brings-the-force-to-the-nintendo-gamecuber-with-lego-star-wars-the-video-game |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210711162141/https://www.gamesindustry.biz/articles/eidos-brings-the-force-to-the-nintendo-gamecuber-with-lego-star-wars-the-video-game |archive-date=July 11, 2021 |access-date=July 26, 2021 |website=[[GamesIndustry.biz]]}}</ref>

Although Nintendo had projected lifetime sales of 50{{nbsp}}million consoles by 2005,<ref>{{Cite web |date=June 12, 2002 |title=Nintendo Targets 50 Million GameCubes – News |url=http://www.nintendoworldreport.com/news/7448/nintendo-targets-50-million-gamecubes |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220702190158/http://www.nintendoworldreport.com/news/7448/nintendo-targets-50-million-gamecubes |archive-date=July 2, 2022 |access-date=June 30, 2022 |website=Nintendo World Report}}</ref> the GameCube finished its commercial run with 21.74{{nbsp}}million hardware units and 208.57{{nbsp}}million software units sold worldwide, consisting of 12.94{{nbsp}}million consoles in the Americas, 4.04{{nbsp}}million in Japan, and 4.77{{nbsp}}million in Europe, Australia, and other regions.<ref name="Sales">{{Cite web |date=June 2011 |title=Consolidated Sales Transition by Region |url=https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ir/library/historical_data/pdf/consolidated_sales_e1106.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111027052007/http://www.nintendo.co.jp/ir/library/historical_data/pdf/consolidated_sales_e1106.pdf |archive-date=October 27, 2011 |access-date=September 4, 2011 |publisher=[[Nintendo]]}}</ref> In sixth-generation console sales, it placed ahead of Sega's Dreamcast (9.13{{nbsp}}million),<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Zackariasson |first1=Peter |title=The Video Game Industry: Formation, Present State, and Future |last2=Wilson |first2=Timothy L. |last3=Ernkvist |first3=Mirko |publisher=[[Routledge]] |year=2012 |isbn=978-1-138-80383-1 |page=158 |chapter=Console Hardware: The Development of Nintendo Wii}}</ref> slightly behind Microsoft's Xbox (24{{nbsp}}million worldwide, though the GameCube outsold the Xbox in Japan),<ref name="Xbox sales">{{Cite web |last=Dyer |first=Mitch |date=November 15, 2011 |title=Ten Incredible Gifts Xbox Gave Modern Gaming |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2011/11/15/ten-incredible-gifts-xbox-gave-modern-gaming?page=2 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140407071245/http://www.ign.com/articles/2011/11/15/ten-incredible-gifts-xbox-gave-modern-gaming?page=2 |archive-date=April 7, 2014 |access-date=July 22, 2013 |website=[[IGN]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=November 17, 2013 |title=Why Xbox Failed in Japan |work=[[Eurogamer]] |url=https://www.eurogamer.net/why-xbox-failed-in-japan |url-status=live |access-date=July 1, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220701152720/https://www.eurogamer.net/why-xbox-failed-in-japan |archive-date=July 1, 2022}}</ref> and far behind Sony's PlayStation 2 (over 155{{nbsp}}million).<ref name="PS2 sales">{{Cite web |last=Moriarty |first=Colin |date=February 16, 2013 |title=Sony's Documentary on PlayStation 2's Retail Dominance |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2013/02/17/sonys-documentary-on-playstation-2s-retail-dominance |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130221035859/http://www.ign.com/articles/2013/02/17/sonys-documentary-on-playstation-2s-retail-dominance |archive-date=February 21, 2013 |access-date=July 22, 2013 |website=[[IGN]]}}</ref> It also sold fewer units than its predecessor, the Nintendo 64 (32.93{{nbsp}}million), and remained Nintendo's lowest-selling major home console until the [[Wii U]] ended production in 2017 with 13.56{{nbsp}}million units sold.<ref name="Sales" /><ref name="Moriarty numbers">{{Cite web |last=Moriarty |first=Colin |date=January 29, 2014 |title=These Are Nintendo's Lifetime Hardware and Software Numbers |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2014/01/29/these-are-nintendos-lifetime-hardware-and-software-numbers |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220701151349/https://www.ign.com/articles/2014/01/29/these-are-nintendos-lifetime-hardware-and-software-numbers |archive-date=July 1, 2022 |access-date=July 15, 2022 |website=[[IGN]]}}</ref> Despite its third-place hardware finish, the GameCube achieved a high software [[attach rate]] of 9.59 games per console.<ref name="Moriarty numbers" />

===Legacy===
Many games and series that debuted on the GameCube—including ''Pikmin'', ''Luigi's Mansion'', ''Chibi-Robo!'', and the ''Metroid Prime'' subseries—became enduring pillars of Nintendo's software catalog.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Vuckovic |first=Daniel |date=May 21, 2012 |title=The GameCube's Legacy to Nintendo and Gaming |url=http://www.vooks.net/the-gamecubes-legacy-to-nintendo-and-gaming/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170627200417/http://www.vooks.net/the-gamecubes-legacy-to-nintendo-and-gaming/ |archive-date=June 27, 2017 |access-date=March 9, 2017 |website=Vooks}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=October 17, 2018 |title=How Luigi's Mansion Went from an Underwhelming Launch Title to a Beloved Classic |url=https://www.gamerevolution.com/features/445173-luigis-mansion-became-beloved-classic |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201027175050/https://www.gamerevolution.com/features/445173-luigis-mansion-became-beloved-classic |archive-date=October 27, 2020 |access-date=July 4, 2022 |website=[[GameRevolution]]}}</ref> In retrospective hardware rankings, ''IGN'' named the GameCube the 16th best video game console of all time in 2009,<ref name="igntop25" /> ''[[GamesRadar+]]'' ranked it 11th in 2021,<ref name="GamesRadar+ranking">{{Cite web |last=West |first=Josh |title=The 20 Best Video Game Consoles and Hardware of All Time |url=https://www.gamesradar.com/best-video-game-consoles-hardware-of-all-time/ |date=November 23, 2021 |access-date=March 26, 2024 |website=[[GamesRadar+]] |archive-date=March 26, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240326205729/https://www.gamesradar.com/best-video-game-consoles-hardware-of-all-time/ |url-status=live}}</ref> and ''[[Den of Geek]]'' ranked it 12th in 2023.<ref name="DenOfGeek">{{Cite web |last=Byrd |first=Matthew |title=The 25 Best Video Game Consoles Ever, Ranked |url=https://www.denofgeek.com/games/best-video-game-consoles-ever-ranked/ |date=July 8, 2023 |access-date=March 26, 2024 |website=[[Den of Geek]] |archive-date=March 26, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240326211208/https://www.denofgeek.com/games/best-video-game-consoles-ever-ranked/ |url-status=live}}</ref>

The [[GameCube controller]] has been officially supported across five generations of Nintendo home consoles, more than any other Nintendo gamepad. Following native controller ports on early Wii consoles (used in titles such as ''[[Super Smash Bros. Brawl]]'' and ''[[Mario Kart Wii]]''), Nintendo released a four-port USB GameCube Controller Adapter alongside [[Super Smash Bros. for Nintendo 3DS and Wii U|''Super Smash Bros. for Wii U'']] in 2014.<ref name="Controller circulation">{{Cite web |last=Perlmutter |first=Zachary |date=May 20, 2019 |title=How Nintendo Kept the GameCube Controller in Constant Circulation |url=https://www.nintendoenthusiast.com/2019/05/20/nintendo-gamecube-controller-constant-circulation/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190602224752/https://www.nintendoenthusiast.com/2019/05/20/nintendo-gamecube-controller-constant-circulation/ |archive-date=June 2, 2019 |access-date=June 2, 2019 |website=Nintendo Enthusiast}}</ref> System software update 4.0.0 for the [[Nintendo Switch]] in October 2017 enabled the USB adapter to recognize original GameCube controllers across compatible Switch software and specifically in ''[[Super Smash Bros. Ultimate]]'' (2018), which was accompanied by a new production run of wired GameCube controllers.<ref name="Controller circulation" /> For the launch of the [[Nintendo Switch 2]] in June 2025, Nintendo maintained support for the USB adapter and released a new official wireless GameCube controller featuring a rechargeable battery, motion-sensing gyroscope controls, and extra system buttons designed for ''Nintendo GameCube – Nintendo Classics''.<ref name="NSO Switch 2" /><ref>{{Cite web |date=June 6, 2025 |title=Surprise! GameCube Controller for Nintendo Switch 2 Has Gyro Controls |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/surprise-gamecube-controller-for-nintendo-switch-2-has-gyro-controls-and-fans-are-having-fun-working-out-what-its-compatible-with |access-date=October 18, 2026 |website=[[IGN]]}}</ref>

WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Glossary of video game terms

{{mi|
