NEO Project for N64 Dev kit }}</ref> Ukrainian developer krikzz, later to be known for his Everdrive line of flash cartridges, began to develop a flash cartridge for the N64 as early as July 2009<ref>{{cite web|url=http://krikzz.com/cart64.html|title=N64 flash cartridge|website=krikzz.com|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090906161606/http://krikzz.com/cart64.html|archive-date=2009-09-06|access-date=2026-08-14}}</ref> before releasing it as the Everdrive 64 in June 2011;<ref>{{cite web|url=http://krikzz.com/ed64.html|title=Super Everdrive<!--This title name is a misnomer, as a later version of the page (https://web.archive.org/web/20110903051131/http://krikzz.com/ed64.html) fixes the title to EverDrive 64-->|website=krikzz.com|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110623102007/http://krikzz.com/ed64.html|archive-date=2011-06-23|access-date=2026-08-14}}</ref> this flash cart was also used for homebrew development.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://krikzz.com/index.php?route=product%2Fproduct&product_id=54 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130105024957/http://krikzz.com/index.php?route=product%2Fproduct&product_id=54 | archive-date=2013-01-05 | title=Everdrive 64 }}</ref> In April 2010, the 64drive, a developer-friendly flash cartridge for running custom programs and code, was released by developer Marshall H.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://64drive.retroactive.be/faq.php | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110511002309/http://64drive.retroactive.be/faq.php | archive-date=2011-05-11 | title=64drive by Retroactive }}</ref> Hobbyist Jennifer Taylor also started work on an [[Open-source software|open-source]] [[Software development kit|SDK]] for N64 homebrew development known as "LibDragon" beginning in May 2009.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.dragonminded.com/n64dev/|title=DragonMinded.com :: N64DEV|date=December 1, 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101201013422/http://www.dragonminded.com/n64dev/ |archive-date=2010-12-01 }}</ref>

In August 2020, members of the N64 homebrew scene established a [[wiki]] known as the N64Brew Wiki, providing accurate documentation of the N64, its peripherals, and related software.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://n64brew.dev/wiki/Main_Page|title=Main Page|date=February 15, 2023|website=N64brew Wiki}}</ref> The site also hosted annual [[game jam]] development competitions since its inception,<ref>{{cite web | last=Wilds | first=Anastasia | title=10 Best Modern Video Games Inspired By The Nintendo 64 | website=ScreenRant | date=2022-08-21 | url=https://screenrant.com/best-modern-video-games-nintendo-64-inspired/ | access-date=2025-12-08}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | last=Yarwood | first=Jack | title=N64Brew Is Putting On A Summer-Themed Game Jam To Raise Money For Charity | website=Time Extension | date=2023-06-30 | url=https://www.timeextension.com/news/2023/06/n64brew-is-putting-on-a-summer-themed-game-jam-to-raise-money-for-charity | access-date=2025-12-08}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | last=Yarwood | first=Jack | title=The Theme For N64Brew's Next Charity Game Jam Has Been Announced | website=Time Extension | date=2024-10-28 | url=https://www.timeextension.com/news/2024/10/the-theme-for-n64brews-next-charity-game-jam-has-been-announced | access-date=2025-12-08}}</ref> which focused on game creation rather than the demoscene of the old POM competitions in the late 1990s. It also held interviews with the judges and developers behind the games they worked on, including former N64 developers such as Allan Findlay, [[David Doak]], [[Neil Voss]], and [[Giles Goddard (video game programmer)|Giles Goddard]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VixNMSLTv-o|title=N64brew Jam 2020 - Interviews! (David Doak, Allan Findlay, Neil Voss, Snooplax, Buu342, Jammers)|date=21 December 2020 |via=www.youtube.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0yxd2s-0t-s|title=N64brew Jam 2021 - Interviews! (Giles Goddard, Kaiser, Kaze, LuigiBlood, Buu342, Jammers)|date=14 December 2021 |via=www.youtube.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=19JOcCS3_vs|title=N64brew Spooky Game Jam 2022 - Interviews! (BehindTheCode, N64 Squid, Buu342, Jammers)|date=7 November 2022 |via=www.youtube.com}}</ref>
[[File:Junk Runner 64 gameplay.webm|thumb|''Junk Runner 64'', an [[open world]] tech demo by [[James Lambert (programmer)|James Lambert]]]]
{{as of|2022|12}}, the N64 still has an active homebrew community, moreso than its early days in the late 1990s and early 2000s, and continues to receive various games and utilities created by members of the community, with over 6,000 members being active in the hacking and homebrew scene.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IptOoeUDzps|title=The State of Nintendo 64 Homebrew|date=31 December 2022 |via=www.youtube.com}}</ref> Prominent [[technology demonstration|tech demo]]s for the N64 have also been created by a handful of homebrew and demoscene members that pushed the limits of the console as well as showcasing some technical feats running on stock hardware, including those by hobbyist [[James Lambert (programmer)|James Lambert]], who implemented [[Clipmap|clipmapping]] (including [[MegaTexture]]s),<ref name="n64-megatextures" /> [[virtual reality headset]] support<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hector |first=Hamish |date=2024-03-14 |title=This N64-powered VR setup is the complete opposite of an Apple Vison Pro |url=https://www.techradar.com/computing/virtual-reality-augmented-reality/this-n64-powered-vr-setup-is-the-complete-opposite-of-an-apple-vison-pro |access-date=2026-03-30 |website=TechRadar |language=en}}</ref> and a modern-sized [[open world]] comparable to that of ''[[The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim]]''.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Yarwood |first=Jack |date=2026-03-27 |title=N64 Dev Spills The Secrets Of His "Skyrim-Sized" Open World Game |url=https://www.timeextension.com/news/2026/03/n64-dev-spills-the-secrets-of-his-skyrim-sized-open-world-game |access-date=2026-03-30 |website=Time Extension |language=en-GB}}</ref>

The 16-bit top-down shooter ''[[Xeno Crisis]]'' has received a version for the N64, released on physical ROM cartridge.<ref name="xeno-n64-gcn">{{cite web|url=https://gonintendo.com/contents/18440-xeno-crisis-seeing-n64-gamecube-release|title=Xeno Crisis seeing N64, GameCube release|website=gonintendo|date=2 April 2023 |access-date=2023-04-09}}</ref>

A number of homebrew emulators for older gaming systems and computers are also available for the N64, including the NES, SNES, Neo Geo, Game Boy and Game Boy Color. [[ScummVM]] also received a port for the N64.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://github.com/hcs64/neon64v2|title=Neon64 2.0 source notes|date=June 6, 2023|via=GitHub}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://github.com/Hydr8gon/sodium64|title=sodium64|date=June 21, 2023|via=GitHub}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://github.com/rasky/mvs64|title=rasky/mvs64|date=June 8, 2023|via=GitHub}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://github.com/lambertjamesd/gb64|title=lambertjamesd/gb64|date=May 7, 2023|via=GitHub}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://micro-64.com/features/scummvm64.shtml|title=Micro-64|website=micro-64.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://krikzz.com/forum/index.php?topic=2396.0|title=list of emulators for ed64 v3|website=krikzz.com}}</ref>{{Excessive citations inline|date=March 2026}}

==Sixth generation consoles==

===Dreamcast===
Despite its short commercial lifespan of less than two years in North America, the [[Dreamcast]] benefits from an active homebrew scene even ten years after its discontinuation. Due to a flaw in the Dreamcast's [[BIOS]], which was intended for use with [[MIL-CD]]'s, the console can run software from a [[CD-R]] without the use of a modchip. Sega responded to this by removing MIL-CD support from the BIOS on all Dreamcast consoles manufactured from November 2000 onwards.

The console is especially notable for its commercial homebrew scene. One notable project was the [[Bleemcast!]] emulator, which was a series of bootdisks made to play [[PlayStation]] games on the system, featuring visual enhancements over the original console. Newer independent releases include ''[[Last Hope (video game)|Last Hope]]'', released by RedSpotGames, and ''[[DUX (video game)|DUX]]'',<ref name="AVClub" /> both [[Shoot 'em up]] style games. These releases were written using the KallistiOS development system. A port of the freeware high-level development language Fenix and [[BennuGD]] is available for use in game development; many DIV Games Studio games have been ported and others were originally written for the system.

===PlayStation 2===
Early versions of the [[PlayStation 2]] have a [[buffer overflow]] bug in the part of the BIOS that handles PS1 game compatibility; hackers found a way to turn this into a loophole called the PS2 Independence Exploit (released in August 2003), allowing the use of homebrew software. Other options for homebrew development would be the use of a [[modchip]] or the utilization of a PS2 hard drive and [[HD Loader]]. In [[Europe]] and Australia, the PS2 came with a free [[Yabasic]] interpreter on the bundled demo disc for some time. This allows simple programs to be created for the PS2 by the end-user. This was included in a failed attempt to circumvent a UK tax by defining the console as a "computer" if it contained certain software.<ref name="PS2ComputerTrial">{{cite web|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100504212929/http://www.gamedaily.com/articles/features/uk-court-ps2-not-a-computer/69084/?biz=1|title=U.K. Court: PS2 Not a Computer|archive-date = May 4, 2010|date=June 20, 2006|publisher=[[GameDaily]]|first=James|last=Brightman|url=http://www.gamedaily.com/articles/features/uk-court-ps2-not-a-computer/69084/?biz=1}}</ref> A port of the [[NetBSD]] project and [[BlackRhino GNU/Linux]], an alternative [[Debian]]-based distribution, are also available for the PS2.

Sony released an official [[Linux for PlayStation 2|Linux-based operating system for the PS2]] in 2002, with the contents of the kit including a [[computer keyboard|keyboard]], [[computer mouse|mouse]], [[PlayStation 2 online functionality#Adapter|Network Adaptor]] and HDD. The North American versions were discontinued a year after the kits quickly went out of stock not too long afterwards, however the European version was still available for quite some time. The kit boots by installing a proprietary interface (the [[run-time environment]]) from a region-encoded [[DVD]], meaning that the North American and European kits would only work with PS2 systems from their respective regions.

A more recent development called Free McBoot or FMCB (first released in May 2008) allows homebrew programs to be launched without a trigger disc required by the older exploit (Independence Exploit), and also allows the use of homebrew on unmodded systems without a functional disc drive. Installation of the exploit to each individual memory card however requires either an already exploited/modded system in order to launch the installer, or a boot image that can load an app to boot into [[Executable and Linkable Format]] (ELF) binaries (a network adapter and HDD is also required). The installation is keyed to the Memory Card and will only be usable on the same version consoles that it was originally installed on, unless a Multi-Install is performed. The only drawback to this exploit is that it needs to be installed/compiled on each individual memory card. Simply copying from one memory card to another will not work. This exploit does not work on the latest slimline PS2s manufactured since late 2008 (the later SCPH-9000x models with BIOS 2.30 and newer), but will work on all models prior to that. The newest versions of Free McBoot (version 1.90 and newer) also have the ability to install and boot from both Sony and non-Sony HDDs when using an original "fat" model PS2 and network adapter;<ref>FMCB 1.9 series release thread - http://psx-scene.com/forums/f153/fmcb-v1-9-series-release-thread-116247/ {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191109055857/http://psx-scene.com/forums/f153/fmcb-v1-9-series-release-thread-116247/ |date=2019-11-09 }}</ref> this support is called Free HDBoot or FHDB. With a few minor issues, it is now possible to play games entirely from the HDD without the need to use an optical disc drive nor a physical memory card. Free McBoot and Free HDBoot is also notable for allowing the user to copy PS1/PS2 save files from a Memory Card to a USB drive, a functionality normally only possible with tools such as [[DexDrive]].

After installing an exploit, unsigned executables (in ELF format) may be launched from a Memory Card or a USB drive. Such programs include emulators, media players, hard drive management tools, and PC-based or NAS-based file shares. Using homebrew programs (e.g. 'SMS Media Player'<ref>Simple Media System for PlayStation 2 – http://home.casema.nl/eugene_plotnikov/ {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090517093230/http://home.casema.nl/eugene_plotnikov/ |date=2009-05-17 }}</ref>) it is possible to listen to various audio file formats ([[MP3]], [[OpenMG Audio|OMA]], [[Ogg Vorbis]], [[Advanced Audio Coding|AAC]], [[FLAC]], [[Dolby AC-3|AC3]]), and watch various video formats ([[DivX]]/[[XviD]], [[MPEG1]], [[MPEG2]], [[MPEG-4 Part 2|MPEG4-ASP]] in [[Audio Video Interleave|AVI Container]]) using the console. Games and other unsigned software can also be played and run on any device connected to the console (i.e. external [[USB]]/[[FireWire]] [[thumb drive]]/hard disk drive ([[FAT32]] and [[exFAT]] only), internal hard disk drive on early revision consoles, network shares ([[Server Message Block|Windows Network]] or PS2 host: protocol), and CD-R(W)/DVD±R(W) optical discs (modded systems or patched discs)). A number of homebrew emulators of older computer and gaming systems have also been developed for the PS2.<ref>PS2 Emulators – http://www.sksapps.com/index.php?page=emus.html {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080612091242/http://sksapps.com/index.php?page=emus.html |date=2008-06-12 }}</ref>

===GameCube===
Homebrew development on the Nintendo [[GameCube]] tended to be difficult, since it uses a proprietary [[MiniDVD]]-based drive and media as opposed to the standard DVD drives of the PS2 and Xbox for piracy protection. Also, its connectivity is limited, as it does not feature a USB port or an HDD port like the PlayStation 2.

The barrier to burning Nintendo GameCube discs with a consumer DVD burner is the [[Burst Cutting Area]], a "barcode" in the innermost ring of the disc, an area inaccessible to most burners and writeable only by very expensive disc pressing machines. For a long time the only way to run homebrew software on Nintendo GameCube was through a patching-system exploit of ''[[Phantasy Star Online Episode I & II]]'', requiring users to find the game and a Broadband Adapter. Both of these are difficult to find because a follow-up has been released (under the name ''[[Phantasy Star Online Episode I & II Plus]]'') and thus the original PSO was rarely sold after then, and because the Broadband Adapter was not often carried in stores due to the Nintendo GameCube's very limited selection of online games.

As of August 2019, the most common method is to use an Action Replay in conjunction with an SD card adapter inserted into the memory card slot, allowing the user to run homebrew from the SD card, or over Ethernet. Another method involves using a modchip to allow the GameCube to run homebrew from a MiniDVD-R via the disc drive. Another method uses a save game exploit which involves transferring modified game save files to a GameCube memory card that triggers arbitrary code execution when loaded by an official game, allowing custom software to be run from a memory card, SD card, or other media.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.gc-forever.com/wiki/index.php?title=Booting_Homebrew|title=Booting homebrew - GC-Forever Wiki|website=www.gc-forever.com|accessdate=8 May 2023}}</ref> As the Nintendo GameCube's case does not fit a full-size DVD-R, third party replacement cases are available.

Homebrew software for the Nintendo GameCube mainly consist of emulators for other systems, as well as several popular homebrew utilities. Swiss is an "all-in-one homebrew utility" that has a file browser, as well as the ability to force software to use different video modes that aren't officially supported such as progressive scan or 16:9 widescreen.<ref>{{Citation|last=emukidid|title=GitHub - emukidid/swiss-gc: Swiss: The swiss army knife of GameCube homebrew.|date=2019-05-27|url=https://github.com/emukidid/swiss-gc|access-date=2019-05-27}}</ref> The Game Boy Interface is a homebrew software frontend for the Game Boy Player peripheral, often used for capturing high-quality footage from Game Boy, Game Boy Color, and Game Boy Advance games.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.gc-forever.com/wiki/index.php?title=Game_Boy_Interface|title=Game Boy Interface - GC-Forever Wiki|website=www.gc-forever.com|access-date=2019-05-27}}</ref>

The 16-bit top-down shooter ''[[Xeno Crisis]]'' has received a version for the GameCube, released on physical optical disc.<ref name="xeno-n64-gcn" /> Though unlike the earlier  Action Replay disc which can run on unmodified GameCubes despite being unlicensed software, ''Xeno Crisis'' requires a modified console.<ref name="McFerran">{{Cite web |last=McFerran |first=Damien |date=April 28, 2023 |title=Hands On: Xeno Crisis Continues Its Quest To Be Released On Every Gaming System Ever Made |url=https://www.timeextension.com/features/hands-on-xeno-crisis-continues-its-quest-to-be-released-on-every-gaming-system-ever-made |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260728003948/https://www.timeextension.com/features/hands-on-xeno-crisis-continues-its-quest-to-be-released-on-every-gaming-system-ever-made |archive-date=July 28, 2026 |access-date=2026-08-24 |website=Time Extension |language=en-US}}</ref>

===Xbox===
{{See also|Xbox (console)#Modding}}
[[File:Xboxinside01.jpg|thumb|right|Microsoft [[Xbox (console)|Xbox]] with a modchip installed]]
The [[Xbox (console)|Xbox]] console uses several measures, including cryptographically signed code to obfuscate firmware. The primary method of executing homebrew code required installing a [[mod chip]] which could be flashed with a modified Microsoft [[BIOS]]. This BIOS allowed the system to boot unsigned executables (XBEs) and control several hardware variables, such as region coding and video mode. With the leak of Microsoft's official development kit ([[Xbox Development Kit|XDK]]), homebrew coders were able to write replacement Xbox GUIs (known as dashboards), games and applications for the Xbox.

A [[softmod]], which uses a commercial game such as ''[[007: Agent Under Fire]]'', ''[[Mech Assault]]'', or ''[[Tom Clancy's Splinter Cell (video game)|Tom Clancy's Splinter Cell]]'', had been created to execute a persistent softmod installer without modification of the hardware. This method utilizes modified font and sound files to cause the Xbox to cause a [[stack buffer overflow]] and load a homebrew dashboard. Once in this condition, the Xbox is able to execute homebrew games and applications upon boot up. Such softmods include the Rocky5 soft modding tool (which has methods that the retail games needed are optional).

Due to the Xbox using standard PC libraries, writing homebrew games is relatively easy and the vast majority of libraries available for a PC programmer are available to an Xbox homebrew programmer.

One of the more common type of homebrew games for the Xbox are ports of PC games whose source has been publicly released or leaked. Many classic PC games have been released for Xbox, but most are created with the XDK which limits their availability. The only places to find these ports are through [[IRC]] or [[peer-to-peer]] browsers.

The Xbox system is also very adept at running [[emulators]] ported from the PC given its high processing power. It is able to emulate systems up to the previous generation, including the [[Nintendo 64]] and the [[PlayStation]]. For this reason, many different emulators have been created for or ported to the Xbox.

A community-run replacement for its now-discontinued Xbox Live service is known as Insignia, which provides many of the features that were supported by the former service in select games (see below).<ref name=insignia />

===Game Boy Advance===
Homebrew development for the [[Game Boy Advance]] has been popular due to the availability of C compilers and ready-made, high-quality code libraries, as well as debugging features for several Game Boy Advance emulators such as [[VisualBoyAdvance]] (including VisualBoyAdvance-M), mGBA, NO$GBA, and Mesen. The ''[[Pokémon]]'' [[ROM hacking]] community and the wide availability of [[flash cartridge]]s and ROM copiers for the system also influenced homebrew development for the system.

==Seventh generation consoles==

===PlayStation Portable===
{{Main|PlayStation Portable homebrew}}

===Nintendo DS===
[[File:SuperCard DS Lite 01.JPG|thumb|Nintendo DS Lite with SuperCard DS Lite flash cartridge and microSD card]]
Since the release of the Nintendo DS, a great deal of hacking has occurred involving the DS's fully rewritable firmware, Wi-Fi connection, [[flash cartridge]]s with support for [[SD card|SD]] storage (such as [[R4 cartridge]]s), and software use.{{Citation needed|date=October 2020}} There are now many emulators for the DS, as well as the NES, SNES, Sega Master System, Sega Mega Drive, Neo-Geo Pocket, the Neo-Geo MVS arcade platform, and older handheld consoles like the Game Boy Color.<ref>{{Cite web|title=List of DS homebrew emulators - GameBrew - a wiki dedicated to Video Game Homebrew.|url=https://gamebrew.org/wiki/List_of_DS_homebrew_emulators|access-date=2021-05-29|website=gamebrew.org}}</ref>

There are a number of flash cartridges or cards which either have built-in flash memory or an [[SD card]] slot (in both standard and "micro" formats). These typically enable DS gamers to use their system to play MP3s and videos, as well as other non-gaming functions traditionally reserved for separate devices.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nintendodscards.com/what-are-nintendo-ds-dsi-cards/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110203141105/http://www.nintendodscards.com/what-are-nintendo-ds-dsi-cards/|archive-date=February 3, 2011|title=What Are Nintendo DS and DSi Cards?|publisher=Nintendo DS Cards|date=June 27, 2010|access-date=September 23, 2010}}</ref>

In South Korea, many video game consumers exploit illegal copies of video games, including for the Nintendo DS. In 2007, 500,000 copies of DS games were sold, while the sales of the DS hardware units was 800,000.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.chosunonline.com/article/20071211000038|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100207215151/http://www.chosunonline.com/article/20071211000038|archive-date=February 7, 2010|title=ニンテンドーDSの違法コピーにご注意！|publisher=[[The Chosun Ilbo]]|language=ja|date=December 11, 2007|access-date=September 10, 2008}}</ref>

Another modification device called [[Action Replay]], manufactured by the company Datel, is a device which allows the user to input cheat codes that allows it to hack games, granting the player infinite [[Health points|health]], [[power-ups]], access to any part of the game, infinite in game currency, the ability to walk through walls, and various other abilities depending on the game and code used.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2012-11-14|title=DSi Action Replay - Codejunkies US|url=http://us.codejunkies.com/Products/DSi-Action-Replay-now-compatible-with-3DS__EF001012.aspx|access-date=2021-05-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121114002622/http://us.codejunkies.com/Products/DSi-Action-Replay-now-compatible-with-3DS__EF001012.aspx|archive-date=2012-11-14}}</ref>

Photographer Steve Chapman, looking for other ways to continue his photography work with smaller equipment, created DS-DSLR, an application that allowed him to control his camera without his bulky laptop. When his camera was connected to the DS through the GBA cartridge slot, DS-DSLR allowed him to execute many tasks, including controlled bracketing, custom interval shots, and timed long exposures. DS-DSLR even had a noise-activated shutter control which was activated when the DS mic detected noise.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://gizmodo.com/homebrew-ds-dslr-uses-nintendo-ds-as-a-canon-eos-remote-5051117|title=Homebrew DS-DSLR Uses Nintendo DS as a Canon EOS Remote|date=17 September 2008 }} Retrieved 2019-10-05.</ref>

The DSi also has some homebrew exploits, some of which use DSiWare apps such as Flipnote Studio (aka ugopwn), sudokuhax, using a game called ''Sudoku'' by EA Games, grtpwn, exidiahax, fieldrunhax, 4swordhax, UNO*hax, and an exploit using [[Petit Computer]] called petit-compwner. There is also systemflaaw, which uses the DSi-exclusive game ''System Flaw''.

A user by the name of shutterbug2000 on GBAtemp has released two DSi exploits, one being called Memory Pit, an exploit using the [[DSi Camera]] app,<ref>{{Cite web|date=2019-05-28|title=Memory Pit Exploit for DSi - All DSi Can Now Be Hacked via The Camera|url=https://www.thenerdmag.com/memory-pit-exploit-for-dsi-all-dsi-can-now-be-hacked/|access-date=2021-05-29|website=TheNerdMag|language=en-US}}</ref> and the other known as the Flipnote Lenny exploit (aka ugopwn), using [[Flipnote Studio]].

===Xbox 360===
[[Microsoft]] has released a version of its proprietary Software Development Kit (SDK) for free, to would-be homebrew programmers. This [[Software development kit|SDK]], called [[Microsoft XNA|XNA Game Studio]], is a free version of the SDK available to professional development companies and college students. However, to create Xbox 360 games one must pay for a premium membership to the XNA Creators Club. Once the games are verified, the games written with XNA Studio can be made available for 80, 240, or 400 Microsoft Points to all [[Xbox 360]] owners (through [[Xbox Live]]). This allows creators of homebrew content access to their target audience of Xbox 360 owners. This content is available under the Indie Games section of the New Xbox Experience.

On March 20, 2007, it was announced that a hack using the previously discovered hypervisor vulnerability in the Xbox 360 kernel versions 4532 and 4548 had been developed to allow users to run XeLL, a Linux bootloader. The initial hack was beyond the average user and required an Xbox serial cable to be installed and a flashed DVD Drive firmware. Felix Domke, the programmer behind XeLL, has since announced a live bootable Linux CD suitable for novice users, with the capabilities to be installed to the SATA hard drive of the Xbox 360. Despite the availability of such a distribution, the Xbox 360 still isn't considered a popular platform for homebrew development, given the dependence of the exploit on the DVD-ROM being able to load a burnt DVD game, a modified version of the game ''[[Peter Jackson's King Kong]]'', and two older kernel revisions of the console itself. A group independent of Microsoft was working on the means to run homebrew code, as part of the [[Free60]] project.

''Note: The hypervisor vulnerability in the Xbox 360 kernel versions 4532 and 4548 was addressed by Microsoft with the release of the NXE system and dashboard update in 2008.''{{Citation needed|date=July 2009}}

Homebrew was since re-enabled on any Xbox 360 with dash 2.0.7371.0 or lower via an exploit referred to as the JTAG / SMC hack but was promptly patched again by Microsoft with the 2.0.8495.0 update.

Homebrew has now become available on most Xbox 360 consoles due to the Reset Glitch Hack. It works on all current dashboards up to the latest revision. Because the Reset Glitch Hack required a modchip, soldering skills are a necessity when attempting to use this exploit. It was patched in the Winchester revisions of the Xbox 360 with mitigations in the hardware.

In early 2025, a software-based exploit known as Bad Update was introduced, which involves a race condition with the hypervisor in software. It depends on an exploit found in ''[[Tony Hawk's American Wasteland]]'' and ''[[Rock Band Blitz]]'', and works on all Xbox 360 consoles up to the latest Winchester revisions without the need of a modchip or directly modifying the console's hardware (as what was previously done with the JTAG and Reset Glitch Hack exploits).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://github.com/grimdoomer/Xbox360BadUpdate|title=grimdoomer/Xbox360BadUpdate|via=GitHub}}</ref> A [[Fork (software development)|fork]] of Bad Update, ABadAvatar, was introduced later that year, which involves a race condition with the [[Xbox Avatar|Xbox Live Avatar]] sign-in system after the console has booted up rather than the hypervisor, and does not depend on a game to trigger the exploit.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://github.com/shutterbug2000/ABadAvatar|title=shutterbug2000/ABadAvatar|via=GitHub}}</ref> Both Bad Update and ABadAvatar are non-persistent exploits however, and will revert back to a stock configuration once it has been turned off, meaning that the exploit must be rerun every time the Xbox 360 is turned on.

Though hardware-based exploits such as the JTAG and Reset Glitch Hack are still the preferred methods of hacking the Xbox 360 for homebrew, Bad Update and ABadAvatar allowed for easier accessibility to homebrew for users who are not experienced with hardware modding or soldering skills, and also allowed homebrew to work on the later Winchester revisions of the console which patched out the Reset Glitch Hack exploit.

===PlayStation 3===
{{main|PlayStation 3 homebrew}}

The [[PlayStation 3]] was designed to run other [[operating system]]s from day one. Very soon after launch, the first users managed to install [[Fedora Linux|Fedora Linux Core 5]] onto the PlayStation 3 via the "Install [[OtherOS|Other OS]]" option in the system's [[XrossMediaBar]] (XMB), which also allows configuring the PlayStation 3 to boot into the other OS installed by default. So far, several [[Linux distribution]]s have been made to install successfully on the PlayStation 3, including Fedora Core 5 and 6, [[Gentoo Linux|Gentoo]], [[Ubuntu]], and [[Yellow Dog Linux]] (YDL). The latter comes installed with the [[Cell (processor)|Cell]] SDK by default, allowing a low cost entry into Cell programming.

Originally, graphics support was limited to [[framebuffer]] access only, with no access to the [[RSX Reality Synthesizer]] graphics processor chip, however some access to the RSX was achieved, which was blocked with firmware update 2.10. Homebrew developers do have access to the [[Cell (processor)|Cell microprocessor]], including 6 of its 7 active Synergistic Processing Elements (SPEs). The Game OS resides under a [[hypervisor]] and prevents users from taking full control of the PlayStation 3's hardware. This is a security measure which helps Sony feel secure enough to allow users to install other operating systems on the PS3.

The [[Sixaxis]] controller has also been exposed to Linux and Windows,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://forums.ps2dev.org/viewtopic.php?t=7099|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070901074640/http://forums.ps2dev.org/viewtopic.php?t=7099|url-status=dead|archive-date=2007-09-01|title=Sixaxis driver for Windows XP}}</ref> but no driver seems to have been successfully created yet that exposes its [[accelerometer]] functions, except for Motioninjoy. However, other drivers have successfully used it as a controller for gaming and other uses. Drivers for the succeeding DualShock 3 were made available through software such as DsHidMini and DS4Windows (initially created for the DualShock 4), and the [[Steam (software)|Steam]] client features built-in support for the controller.

In May 2008, a vulnerability was found in the PlayStation 3 allowing users to install a partial debug firmware on a regular console. However, the debug functions are disabled, so homebrew applications and backup games cannot be run yet.

Another exploit was found on August 14, 2008, allowing users to boot some backup games from the PlayStation 3's [[Hard disk drive|HDD]], although the exact instructions on how to do this were not released at that time. However, a different person posted instructions 10 days later, which explained the exploit.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://forums.maxconsole.net/showthread.php?t=122140|title=How to run a PS3 game backup|access-date=8 May 2023|archive-date=14 April 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090414030609/http://forums.maxconsole.net/showthread.php?t=122140|url-status=dead}}</ref>

On January 6, 2009, a hacking ring named ''Sh4d0ws'' leaked the jig files needed to launch the PlayStation 3 into service mode. Although the PlayStation 3 can be triggered into service mode, it is not yet of any use because the files needed to make changes to the console have not been leaked.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.ps3news.com/PS3Dev/playstation-3-service-mode-jig-set-up-files-leaked|title=ps3news.com|website=www.ps3news.com|access-date=8 May 2023}}</ref>

"Other OS" functionality was removed in firmware update 3.21 in April 2010; Sony has stated that this was in response to several "security concerns". The removal of OtherOS, an advertised functionality, led to a lawsuit.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.joystiq.com/2010/04/01/psa-ps3-firmware-update-3-21-available-now |title=Sony blocks OtherOS in firmware 3.21 |access-date=2012-04-14}}</ref>

On August 31, 2010, PSGroove, an exploit for the PS3 through the USB port, was released and made open source. This exploit works on all of the PS3 models released up until then.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.ps3-hacks.com/2010/08/31/diy-ps-jailbreak-may-be-available-soon/ |title=Open Source PS JailBreak Clone "PSGroove" Available Now! – PS3-Hacks: Hack your PlayStation 3 |publisher=PS3-Hacks |access-date=2012-04-03}}</ref> A guide for the creation of the PSGroove is available through several online sources.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://howtohackps3.com/ |title=Web hosting, domain name registration and web services by 1&1 Internet |publisher=Howtohackps3.com |access-date=2012-04-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120402124144/http://howtohackps3.com/ |archive-date=2012-04-02 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

[[George Hotz]], better known under his nickname "geohot", appeared on ''[[Attack of the Show!]]'' because he released the PlayStation 3's encryption keys, therefore any homebrew or custom firmware can be signed. Once signed, homebrew can be natively run. It would be difficult for Sony to fix this because it would most likely require a voluntary recall and the costliest parts would need replacing.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.geohot.com/|title=geohot|website=www.geohot.com|access-date=8 May 2023}}</ref> In 2011, Sony, with help from law firm [[Kilpatrick Stockton]], sued Hotz and associates of the group fail0verflow for their jailbreaking activities. Charges included violating the [[Digital Millennium Copyright Act|DMCA]], [[Computer Fraud and Abuse Act|CFAA]], [[Contributory liability|copyright law]], and [[California Comprehensive Computer Data Access and Fraud Act|California's CCDAFA]], and for [[breach of contract]] (related to the [[PlayStation Network]] [[Terms of service|User Agreement]]), [[tortious interference]], [[misappropriation]], and [[trespass]].<ref>[https://www.engadget.com/2011/01/12/sony-follows-up-officially-sues-geohot-and-fail0verflow-over-ps/ Sony follows up, officially sues Geohot and fail0verflow over PS3 jailbreak]. Nilay Patel, Engadget (2011-01-12). Retrieved on 2011-02-16.</ref>

Recent homebrew efforts included the development of ''PS3HEN'', which allows for the execution of homebrew. It exploits certain unpatched system files that are installed through the system updater, and must be re-enabled after powering off the system. ''PS3HEN'' is compatible with all PlayStation 3 models, including later patched ''Slim'' and ''Super Slim'' models, as an alternative for those that cannot install conventional custom firmware.

===Wii===
{{See also|Wii system software}}
[[File:Homebrew channel logo.png|right|thumb|The Homebrew Channel banner appearing on the [[Wii Menu]]]]
In advance of the Wii's release, WiiCade was the first site to host [[Adobe Flash]] homebrew games specifically designed for the Wii and its remote, which could be played without any exploits using the Wii's [[Opera (web browser)|Opera]] web browser.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.engadget.com/2006/11/17/for-your-enjoyment-wiicade/|title=For your enjoyment: WiiCade|date=18 November 2006 |author-first1=Kevin|author-last1=Kelly|work=Engadget}}</ref> The Wii Opera software development kit lets developers make their own games for the Wii via JavaScript.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.engadget.com/2007/07/17/revolutionary-web-wii-wares/|title=Revolutionary: Web Wii Wares|date=17 July 2007 |author-first1=Mike|author-last1=Sylvester|work=Engadget}}</ref>

The Wii was hacked in December 2007, via a method that involves a pair of [[tweezers]] to bridge pins in the Wii's memory module in order to access parts of Wii system memory in GameCube mode and obtain the console's [[encryption key]]s, as well as a custom serial interface.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hall |first=Charlie |date=29 October 2019|title=The key to unlocking the Nintendo Wii's copy protection was a simple pair of tweezers |url=https://www.polygon.com/2019/10/29/20938279/nintendo-wii-hack-tweezers/ |access-date=3 July 2026|website=[[Polygon (website)|Polygon]]|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://gizmodo.com/338897/nintendo-wii-hacked-the-video|title=Nintendo Wii Hacked, The Video|first=Mark|last=Wilson|date=29 December 2007|access-date=9 September 2017|archive-date=31 December 2007|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071231040224/https://gizmodo.com/338897/nintendo-wii-hacked-the-video|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Breaking analysis: Wii Hacked. > Console Games > Game > Features > Atomic |url=http://www.atomicmpc.com.au/Feature/102072,breaking-analysis-wii-hacked.aspx |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081207165217/http://www.atomicmpc.com.au/Feature/102072,breaking-analysis-wii-hacked.aspx |archive-date=2008-12-07 |access-date=2026-05-06 |website=www.atomicmpc.com.au}}</ref> In 2008, Team Twiizers (named after the aforementioned hack, now known as fail0verflow) released an exploit called the Twilight Hack which takes advantage of a [[Buffer overflow|buffer overflow vulnerability]] found in the Wii version of ''[[The Legend of Zelda: Twilight Princess]]'' that utilizes a malformed [[Saved game|save file]] to load an [[Executable and Linkable Format|ELF]] file (boot.elf) into memory (if present in the root directory of the SD card), which will then run unsigned code.

The goal of most Wii exploits today is to install The Homebrew Channel, a custom channel that lets users run homebrew software on the console. Its first full release was in December 2008.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.engadget.com/2008/12/10/wii-homebrew-channel-turns-1-0/|title=Wii Homebrew Channel turns 1.0|date=10 December 2008 }}</ref> Though Nintendo has successfully patched various older exploits to install The Homebrew Channel, many exploits to run the channel on current firmware exist. Note that only exploits that use disc games are compatible with installing The Homebrew Channel on the vWii (virtual Wii) mode on a Wii U (with the exception of "wuphax", an exploit that installs the channel via Wii U-specific system permission exploits). The console's controller was also a popular target for modification.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB117772630151685703|title=Magic Wand: How Hackers Make Use Of Their Wii-motes|first=Jamin|last=Brophy-Warren|date=29 April 2007|newspaper=Wall Street Journal}}</ref>

{{as of|2025}}, various other exploits other than the Twilight Hack exist that can hack the [[Wii]] for homebrew and allow for the installation of The Homebrew Channel from supported games and on specific system software revisions, including (but not limited to) Smash Stack (using an exploit found within the game's stage editor in [[NTSC]] releases of ''[[Super Smash Bros. Brawl]]''), BannerBomb (using a malformed Channel; patched in firmware version 4.3), LetterBomb (using the Wii's [[Wii system software#Wii Message Board|Messaging Board]]),<ref name="LetterBomb">{{cite web |url=https://letterbomb.readthedocs.io/en/latest/how_it_works.html |title=How It Works |author=<!--Not stated--> |website=LetterBomb |access-date=2023-09-27}}</ref> WilBrand (LetterBomb alternative that supports firmware versions 3.0 to 4.3), FlashHax (using the Internet Channel),<ref name="FlashHax">{{Cite news|url=https://gbatemp.net/threads/new-free-homebrew-entry-point-flashhax.491674/|title=New free homebrew entry point. FlashHax|work=GBAtemp.net - The Independent Video Game Community|access-date=2018-06-14|language=en-US}}</ref> str2hax (using a DNS exploit in the Wii's EULA), and BlueBomb (using Bluetooth).

Most exploits for the console typically requires the use of an SD card as they expect the ELF loader file (boot.elf) to be present on the root of the medium. However, some exploits such as FlashHax, str2hax and BlueBomb do not require the use of an SD card in order to exploit the Wii as they can download the ELF loader file directly off the internet (depending on the console model) if the SD card itself or the ELF loader file on the SD card is not present. BlueBomb in particular also allowed for the Wii Mini to become hackable for the first time, which was a hardware revision of the Wii released late in its lifecycle that was deemed "unhackable" by many users prior to the exploit's release, mainly due to the lack of an SD card slot and internet connectivity on the Wii Mini.

==Eighth/ninth generation consoles==
===Nintendo 3DS===
[[File:3DS Homebrew Launcher.jpg|thumb|right|A [[New Nintendo 3DS XL]] running The Homebrew Launcher]]

To directly install custom software onto the Nintendo 3DS' home menu, [[custom firmware]] is needed. There are several custom firmware releases available, the most popular being Luma3DS. Requirements to install [[custom firmware]] involve using various exploits to run a boot ROM exploit called boot9strap, which executes custom code before boot ROM lockout. Similar to Wii, the 3DS has its own custom software known as The Homebrew Launcher, which allows homebrew software to run on the system. The Homebrew Launcher can be installed after performing an exploit.

The first public homebrew exploit for the 3DS, ninjhax, originally called ssspwn, allowed the user to scan a [[QR Code]] to exploit the game ''[[Cubic Ninja]]''. Other ways to run The Homebrew Launcher have been discovered since then, including (but not limited to) freakyhax, an exploit in the Deluxe edition of ''[[Freakyforms: Your Creations, Alive!]]'';<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://plutooo.github.io/freakyhax/|title=freakyhax - 3DS homebrew exploit|website=plutooo.github.io|accessdate=8 May 2023}}</ref> Doodlebomb, an exploit in the 1.1.1 and older versions of ''[[Swapdoodle]]'';<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://mrnbayoh.github.io/doodlebomb/|title=doodlebomb by MrNbaYoh|website=mrnbayoh.github.io|accessdate=8 May 2023}}</ref> browserhax, broswerhax-xl,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://github.com/zoogie/old-browserhax|title=Old-browserhax |website=[[GitHub]] |date=13 June 2022 }}</ref> SSloth browser, and super-skaterhax (all of which used the 3DS' [[Internet Browser (Nintendo 3DS)|Internet Browser]] with the latter exclusive to New 3DS models); soundhax, using the [[Nintendo 3DS Sound]] app; pichaxx, using ''[[Pokémon Picross]]''; unSAFE_MODE, which injects a corrupted WiFi profile into the SAFE_MODE firmware; kartdlphax and Kartminer7, both using ''[[Mario Kart 7]]''; MSET9, which utilizes an exploit in the System Settings application; ntrboot, using an NDS/DSi flash cart; and smashbroshax, a New 3DS exclusive exploit for ''[[Super Smash Bros. for Nintendo 3DS and Wii U|Super Smash Bros. for Nintendo 3DS]]''.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://github.com/yellows8/3ds_smashbroshax|title=yellows8/3ds_smashbroshax|website=[[GitHub]] |date=25 March 2021}}</ref>

After installing custom firmware, several things can be done on the system, such as being able to play games that were [[Region lock|region-locked]] on any regional system, install and launch games, homebrew apps, emulators and other unsigned software directly from the home menu, and also obtain [[ROM image]]s of games from [[Nintendo Game Card#Nintendo 3DS Game Card|game card]]s inserted directly into the system. Homebrew applications for the 3DS often include features that are only available on exploited/modded systems; for instance, PC games can be streamed on the 3DS via a homebrew streaming application called Moonlight, which is built on an open-source version of the [[Nvidia]] GameStream protocol, allowing games to be controlled via the system with the top screen acting as a computer display, the bottom screen as a keyboard, and the buttons acting as the buttons on a game controller.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.gamesradar.com/games/assassin-s-creed/assassins-creed-shadows-is-shown-running-on-a-nintendo-3ds-in-an-impressive-bit-of-fan-homebrew/|title=Assassin's Creed Shadows is shown running on a Nintendo 3DS in an impressive bit of fan homebrew|first=Scott|last=McCrae|date=March 26, 2025|website=GamesRadar+|access-date=November 9, 2025}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.gamingbible.com/news/assassins-creed-shadows-lands-last-platform-expected-939211-20250326|title=Assassin's Creed Shadows quietly lands on the last platform we expected|website=GAMINGbible|date=26 March 2025 |access-date=November 9, 2025}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cbr.com/final-fantasy-14-playable-3ds/|title=Final Fantasy XIV Is Playable on 3DS, But There's a Catch|first=Scott|last=Baird|date=October 11, 2025|website=CBR|access-date=November 9, 2025}}</ref> Other homebrew applications can also allow for the 3DS to be used as a game controller for the same reason as well. Various homebrew emulators are also available for the 3DS, including the [[RetroArch]] frontend and Red Viper, the latter of which is a [[Virtual Boy]] emulator for the 3DS.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://arstechnica.com/gaming/2024/02/virtual-boy-finally-comes-to-nintendo-3ds-but-not-in-the-way-youd-think/|title=Nintendo's lost 1990s "VR" console comes to 3DS thanks to a remarkable emulator|first=Kevin|last=Purdy|date=February 27, 2024|website=Ars Technica|access-date=November 9, 2025}}</ref>

Unsigned software can be launched from the SD card without having to install custom firmware on the device by using an exploit to run The Homebrew Launcher. The Homebrew Launcher itself can be launched on system versions 9.0-11.16 on any 3DS system. However, without installing custom firmware, the user will need to run the exploit each time they want to access The Homebrew Launcher.

The majority of system updates that have "Further improvements to overall system stability and other minor adjustments have been made to enhance the user experience" in their changelog are simply to patch Homebrew Launcher (userland) exploits. Those that require a specific version of a game or application are often patched in these updates by adding exploited application versions to the "IsTitleAllowed" blacklist, which prevents outdated applications on the list from launching and forces users to update those applications to the latest version to launch the application.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://3dbrew.org/wiki/APT:IsTitleAllowed|title=APT:IsTitleAllowed - 3dbrew|website=3dbrew.org|accessdate=8 May 2023}}</ref> For example, notehax only works on outdated versions of Flipnote Studio 3D. In the 11.6.0-39 system update, all regions of Flipnote Studio version <=1.0.1 in USA, <=1.2.0 in EUR, and <=1.3.1 in JPN were blocked from launching the application, patching the exploit on current firmware.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://3dbrew.org/wiki/11.6.0-39|title=11.6.0-39 - 3dbrew|website=3dbrew.org|accessdate=8 May 2023}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://mrnbayoh.github.io/notehax/|title=Notehax|website=notehax|accessdate=8 May 2023}}</ref>

In December 2020, an exploit was released that used an oversight in [[DSiWare]], which can run custom code from the DSiWare menu in the 3DS settings app to install the 3DS hacks.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Homebrew|first=Nintendo|title=Seedminer|url=https://3ds.hacks.guide/seedminer.html|access-date=2020-12-16|website=3DS Hacks Guide|language=en}}</ref> The majority of exploits for the system were patched out by the 11.17.0-50 system update {{as of|lc=y|2023|05}},<ref>{{Cite web |last=Orland |first=Kyle |date=2023-05-23 |title=Unexpected 3DS update breaks many common homebrew hacking methods |url=https://arstechnica.com/gaming/2023/05/nintendo-is-still-trying-to-patch-hacking-exploits-for-the-defunct-3ds/ |access-date=2023-05-29 |website=Ars Technica |language=en-us}}</ref> with the exception of MSET9 (for all 3DS models), super-skaterhax (for New 3DS models) and ntrboot (for all 3DS models as a fallback for the MSET9 and super-skaterhax exploits).

===PlayStation 4===
In 2015, an [[exploit (computer security)|exploit]] for the PlayStation 4 was released for firmware 1.76 and below which grants kernel access. It was the first known public exploit for the PS4.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://wololo.net/2015/12/06/ps4-hack-cturt-confirms-ps4-kernel-exploit/|title=PS4 hack: CTurt confirms PS4 Kernel exploit|website=wololo.net|date=6 December 2015 |access-date=2022-12-31}}</ref> The userland exploit targeted the native PlayStation web browser and was colloquially referred to as a "webkit exploit". This was chained with the kernel exploit named "BadIRET" allowing it to execute unsigned code and access the kernel through exploiting the PS4's kernel vulnerabilities previously discovered in [[Linux]] and [[FreeBSD]]. This exploit took advantage of the webkit entrypoint and its "just-in-time" execution to gain kernel access to the PS4 and enable homebrew.

Over time, further exploits have been found that grant kernel level modifications to the system. All firmware versions except the latest that being 13.02 and 13.04 have been exploited to enable homebrew.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://wololo.net/2018/05/28/ps4-specterdev-releases-ps4-5-05-kernel-exploit/|title=PS4: SpecterDev releases PS4 5.05 kernel exploit|website=wololo.net|date=27 May 2018 |access-date=2023-01-02}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://wololo.net/2020/07/17/ps4-6-72-jailbreak-released-by-sleirsgoevy/|title=PS4 6.72 Jailbreak released by Sleirsgoevy|website=wololo.net|date=16 July 2020 |access-date=2023-01-02}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://wololo.net/2020/12/19/playstation-4-ps4hen-released-for-firmware-7-02-following-the-firmware-being-fully-cracked-open/|title=PlayStation 4: PS4HEN released for Firmware 7.02 following the firmware being fully cracked open!|website=wololo.net|date=19 December 2020 |access-date=2023-01-02}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://wololo.net/2021/03/15/release-mira-custom-firmware-for-ps4-7-55-updated-jailbreak/|title=Release: Mira (Custom firmware) for PS4 7.55 (+ updated jailbreak)|website=wololo.net|date=15 March 2021 |access-date=2023-01-02}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://wololo.net/2021/12/13/ps4-9-00-jailbreak-poobs4-released/|title=PS4 9.00 Jailbreak "pOOBs4" released!|website=wololo.net|date=13 December 2021 |access-date=2023-01-02}}</ref> Most of these use a webkit exploit as the entry point, but the PPPwn exploit targeting firmwares up to 11.00 uses a vulnerability found in the PlayStation 4 network settings and a computer to send payloads. The PSVue [[User space and kernel space|userland exploit]] targets the discontinued Sony streaming app [[PlayStation Vue]] and works by bridging the gap between low-privilege application code and high-privilege kernel memory, using the initial user-mode access to trigger vulnerabilities within kernel-mode drivers or system calls to enable homebrew. The exploit targets all firmware up to 13.02 and enables homebrew on all firmwares except 13.02 due to it not having a kernel exploit available. The PPPwn and PSVue exploits were patched in 11.02 and 13.04 respectively.

Homebrew on the PS4 includes being able to boot the PS4 into a [[Linux distribution]], although this is not permanent and the console will revert to Orbis OS on reboot.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://wololo.net/2018/03/02/linux-released-ps4-4-55/|title=Linux released for PS4 4.55|website=wololo.net|date=2 March 2018 |access-date=2023-01-02}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://wololo.net/2022/12/17/ps4-linux-psxitarch-v3-released-with-mesa-22-2-0-support-lightweight-ram-usage-and-preinstalled-emulators/|title=PS4 Linux: Psxitarch v3 released, with Mesa 22.2.0 support, lightweight RAM usage, and preinstalled emulators|website=wololo.net|date=17 December 2022 |access-date=2023-01-02}}</ref> Some payloads can patch games on the fly, such as 60 FPS for games that were never given official patches, character mods, and removal of intros and cutscenes.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://wololo.net/2022/11/15/you-can-now-load-ps4-game-patches-60fps-etc-directly-with-goldhen-2-2-5b7-goldhen-cheats-manager-1-0-0/|title=You can now load PS4 Game patches (60FPS, etc…) directly with GoldHEN 2.2.5b7 + GoldHEN Cheats Manager 1.0.0|website=wololo.net|date=15 November 2022 |access-date=2023-01-02}}</ref> These patches can even work on physical retail discs inserted into the console; they are done at runtime in RAM and such leave the physical disc data intact.

=== PlayStation Vita ===
[[File:PS Vita HENlo jailbreak.png|thumb|right|Screenshot of HENlo, a WebKit-based jailbreak for the [[PlayStation Vita]]]]
In 2016, an [[exploit (computer security)|exploit]] for the PlayStation Vita was released named "HENkaku".<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://henkaku.xyz/changes|title=HENkaku|website=henkaku.xyz|access-date=2018-10-16}}</ref>  This exploit used a bug found on the 3.60 system firmware, allowing users to run unsigned software. It was installed by visiting a website and clicking on the install button on the PlayStation Vita web browser. This had to be done every time the user turned the system on, and was patched in firmware version 3.61. However, in 2018, [[computer science]] student TheFloW (Andy Nguyen) found a kernel bug in firmware versions 3.65, 3.67, and 3.68 that allowed unsigned code to be run. Eventually, he developed an exploit called "h-encore" which allowed one to install the HENkaku hack on later PS Vita versions. The kernel bug was patched in firmware version 3.69, but the [[user space|userland]] bug still works. Because HENkaku needs to be reinstalled every time the device is turned on, a program named ensō, which permanently flashes any custom firmware (including HENkaku) into the software, was created.

On February 13, 2019, TheFloW released a downgrader tool that can downgrade any Vita console to an older firmware down to its factory firmware.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://github.com/TheOfficialFloW/modoru|title=Modoru|website=GitHub|access-date=2019-06-24}}</ref>

On December 26, 2022, TheFloW released HENlo, a [[WebKit]]-based exploit chain for developers and security researchers on his GitHub page; a working implementation of the exploit which can be used on all Vita firmware versions was released by SKGleba.<ref name="henlo">{{Cite web |last=TheGuardian |date=2022-12-28 |title=PS Vita: TheFloW releases new kernel exploit "HENlo" (compatible with 3.74) |url=https://wololo.net/2022/12/28/ps-vita-theflow-releases-new-kernel-exploit-henlo-compatible-with-3-74/ |access-date=2023-01-02 |website=Wololo.net |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== Wii U ===
The most common way to execute code on the Wii U for 5.5.6 and below is through vulnerabilities in the Wii U's built-in web browser. Websites specifically made to exploit these vulnerabilities usually use them to run the Homebrew Launcher from the user's SD card, allowing for other unsigned programs to be run. The Homebrew Launcher could also be used to run or install custom firmware, such as Mocha or Haxchi. Haxchi could optionally be enabled on boot using Coldboot Haxchi, a modified version of Haxchi that runs the Virtual Console game it is installed to on boot.

In January 2022, Tiramisu and the EnvironmentLoader were released.<ref>{{cite web|title = Tiramisu| date=31 December 2021| url=https://maschell.github.io/homebrew/2021/12/31/tiramisu.html|access-date=2023-08-28}}</ref> EnvironmentLoader allows custom firmware, such as Tiramisu, to be automatically loaded on boot (similar to Coldboot Haxchi), but uses the console's Health and Safety Information app to run the exploit instead of a Virtual Console game. This removes the requirement to purchase a compatible Virtual Console game as well as reducing the risks of [[Brick (electronics)|bricking]] the console. Later in September of that year, Aroma received its first public beta release, which uses the same exploit that EnvironmentLoader used, allowing for easier migration between the two.<ref>{{cite web|title = Aroma| date=5 September 2022| url=https://maschell.github.io/homebrew/2022/09/05/aroma.html|access-date=2023-08-28}}</ref> It also introduced modules, a new plugin system, and a new homebrew app format known as WUHB (shorthand for "Wii U HomeBrew") and RPX, the latter two of which negated the need for the Homebrew Launcher as ELF binaries are unsupported under Aroma. As such, unsigned software (in WUHB and RPX format) can only be installed and run via the Wii U's home menu, in a similar manner to the custom firmware on the 3DS. Many homebrew applications that run via the Homebrew Launcher (or by the Wii U's home menu in the case of Aroma) have been collected and hosted on [https://apps.fortheusers.org/wiiu fortheusers.org]. These hosted applications can be downloaded directly on the Wii U using The Homebrew App Store app in the repository.

The Wii U's built-in Wii sandbox environment (often nicknamed vWii or Wii Mode) is capable of running Wii homebrew, such as The Homebrew Channel.<ref>{{Cite web|url = http://wiiubrew.org/wiki/WiiMode#Homebrew_Channel|title = WiiMode|date = 3 February 2016|access-date = 20 February 2016}}</ref> However, due to changes made to the Wii operating system that runs in vWii mode, previous exploits that utilized the Wii Menu to load the HackMii Installer, such as Letterbomb, do not work. The only way to hack the vWii without using one of the exploit games is by using Wii U homebrew applications, such as wuphax or Compat Installer. The operating system changes also prevent some homebrew applications from functioning properly, requiring developers to create alternate versions to run on vWii.

===Nintendo Switch===
On March 14, 2017, 11 days after the release of the [[Nintendo Switch]], the console was exploited by a team named ReSwitched with their exploit called PegaSwitch. It did not allow true homebrew to run on the system at the time, but it did let developers look for other security bugs in the system. Later on October 1 of that year, ReSwitched announced new exploits and tools that allowed homebrew developers to start working on homebrew programs for the system before they could be launched.<ref>{{Cite web |date=1 October 2017 |title=octrelease |url=https://reswitched.tech/octrelease |access-date=4 February 2018}}</ref> At the 34th Chaos Communication Congress, hackers Plutoo, Derrek, and Naehrwert announced a kernel exploit for the system (which they explicitly said they would not release it to the public) and said that a homebrew launcher was coming soon.<ref>{{Cite web |date=29 December 2017 |title=Nintendo Switch Kernel exploit 34c3 presentation: "Nvidia Backdoored themselves" |url=http://wololo.net/2017/12/29/nintendo-switch-kernel-exploit-34c3-presentation-nvidia-backdoored/ |access-date=4 February 2018}}</ref>

The Nintendo Switch has both a homebrew launcher and custom firmware. The most notable, ''Atmosphère'', is being developed alongside new system updates. The ability to install homebrew on the Nintendo Switch is dependent on the version of the console; access to a Japanese copy of ''[[Puyo Puyo Tetris]]'' was needed to install CFW on version 1.0.0. Original Switch models released before June 2018 had a full control TrustZone exploit that allows a custom-made RCM jig to be inserted into the right [[Joy-Con]] rail, allowing the system to enter a recovery mode that would otherwise not be accessible to regular users and thus access custom payloads that are sent through another device. Consoles that were released after June 2018 with version 4.1.0 shipped have their boot ROMs patched against this exploit that would allow for homebrew to be installed,<ref>{{cite web |title=ReiNX |url=https://reinx.guide/firsttime |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181019071537/http://reinx.guide/firsttime |archive-date=2018-10-19}}</ref> so it is currently not possible to install homebrew to the original HAC-001 Nintendo Switch models with version 4.1.0 or higher installed (units manufactured after June 2018), the HAC-001(-01) revision of the Nintendo Switch (newer models with the Tegra X1+ SOC which patched the TrustZone exploit completely), the Nintendo Switch Lite and the OLED model of the Nintendo Switch officially known as the "Nintendo Switch – OLED Model" without the purchase and installation of a specialized modchip which replicates the vulnerability of the [[Tegra#Tegra X1|Tegra X1]] chip. The installation requires soldering the modchip as opposed to utilizing an RCM jig on earlier models. In addition to running game backups, homebrewed Switches allow for the execution of homebrew, [[Android (operating system)|Android]] (up to [[Android 15]] through [[LineageOS]]), and [[Linux]] distributions, allowing the system to be used as a fully-fledged Android tablet or ARM64 Linux computer - the latter in the same vein as the [[Steam Deck]], though requiring extra software to run [[Microsoft Windows|Windows]] games - respectively.

The succeeding [[Nintendo Switch 2]] features hardened security measures that makes it significantly more difficult to install homebrew.

=== Xbox One, Series X, and Series S ===
The [[Xbox One]] and [[Xbox Series X and Series S|Series X/S]] have a Dev Mode which, though intended to be used for retail game development, can be used to run unsigned homebrew software.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://support.xbox.com/en-AU/xbox-one/apps/developer-mode-activation-app-faq|title=Developer Mode Activation App FAQ|website=support.xbox.com|language=en|access-date=2018-07-04}}</ref> It can be enabled on any retail Xbox console. Dev Mode disables retail games and software while enabled. Homebrew software can be developed as [[Universal Windows Platform]] applications, allowing many programs designed to run on desktop editions of [[Windows 10]] to run on the console including console emulators. In order to activate developer mode, one has to first register for an app developer account, which has a fee of $19.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://developer.microsoft.com/en-us/store/register/|title=Register as an app developer|website=developer.microsoft.com|language=en|access-date=2021-05-16}}</ref>

===PlayStation 5===
The [[PlayStation 5]] is capable of running unsigned code on earlier firmware versions. A userland, kernel (and optionally hypervisor) exploit chain is required to be able to load homebrew on the PS5. As of April 2024, firmwares 3.00 to 4.51 is exploitable using an IPv6 kernel exploit that was originally patched on the PS4 but later resurfaced on the PS5. This exploit chain does not contain a hypervisor exploit, although a payload was created that works as a partial bypass to defeat enough security to run homebrew, dubbed libhijacker.<ref>{{cite web|title=astrelsky/libhijacker|website=[[GitHub]]|url=https://github.com/astrelsky/libhijacker|accessdate=24 June 2023}}</ref> Homebrew on the console includes patches (including unofficial 60/120 FPS patches for backwards-compatible PS4 games), cheats and fan speed adjustments. Like the PlayStation 4, original model PlayStation 5 systems with certain firmware versions installed can boot into Linux, though the process will need to be repeated should the system be powered off or restarted.

== Unofficial online services ==
In recent years, there have been several attempts at restoring old and defunct online services and servers for some online-capable game consoles and video games, typically those from the sixth generation onward. As many of these were shut down over time, hackers and modders have attempted to unofficially restore these via private, community-run servers or projects that are aimed at replicating or restoring online functionalities to various discontinued services and servers.

Access to these services typically requires a homebrew-enabled system to work, however there are some that can be accessed on an unmodified system such as private servers which can be accessed by adjusting [[Domain Name System|DNS]] settings. For instance, several online-capable games for the [[PlayStation 2]] and [[Dreamcast]] had their online functionalities restored via private servers, some of which require bypassing of authentication services such as the DNAS (Dynamic Network Authentication System) used on most [[PlayStation 2 online functionality|online-capable PlayStation 2 games]].

===Xbox (original)===
Insignia is a community-run online server for the [[original Xbox]] consoles in 2022 that served as a replacement for its now-defunct [[Xbox Live]] service (which was shut down in April 2010). It aims to replicate many of the features that were previously available on the now-discontinued service for the platform, and can be accessed by adjusting DNS settings on the console.<ref name=insignia>{{Cite web|url=https://www.gamesradar.com/og-xbox-live-is-being-resurrected-by-insignia/|title=OG Xbox Live is being resurrected by Insignia|first=Dustin|last=Bailey|date=July 18, 2022|website=GamesRadar+|access-date=November 9, 2025}}</ref>

===Wii===
The [[Wii]] has its now-discontinued [[WiiConnect24]] service (which was shut down in June 2013) restored by a project known as RiiConnect24 in 2015 that primarily aims to restore the WiiConnect24 service for Wii consoles that have been opened up for homebrew. WiiLink was another project in 2020 that restores WiiConnect24 as well as other online functionalities to homebrewed Wii consoles, of which was eventually merged with RiiConnect24 in 2023.

===Nintendo 3DS and Wii U===
Ahead of the discontinuation of the [[Nintendo Network]] for the [[Nintendo 3DS]] and [[Wii U]] in 2024, an unofficial fan-made project aimed at preserving most functionalities of the now-discontinued service known as Pretendo Network (or just Pretendo) emerged, providing several features such as online multiplayer, friends list, matchmaking and other online services such as [[Miiverse]], and remains in active development. Initially, access to Pretendo requires a homebrew-enabled system (which is still the case for the 3DS {{as of|lc=y|2026}}), {{as of|2024|04|lc=y}} that is no longer the case, specifically in the case of the Wii U.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.engadget.com/the-bootleg-nintendo-network-replacement-no-longer-requires-jailbreaking-192749406.html|title=The bootleg Nintendo Network replacement no longer requires jailbreaking|first=Will|last=Shanklin|date=April 9, 2024|website=Engadget|access-date=November 12, 2025}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nintendolife.com/news/2024/04/fan-made-nintendo-network-replacement-pretendo-no-longer-requires-hacked-wii-u|title=Fan-Made Nintendo Network Replacement 'Pretendo' No Longer Requires Hacked Wii U|first=Jim|last=Norman|date=April 9, 2024|website=Nintendo Life|access-date=November 12, 2025}}</ref> The most notable games currently supported by Pretendo are ''[[Mario Kart 7]]'', ''[[Mario Kart 8]]'', ''[[Splatoon (video game)|Splatoon]]'' and ''[[Kid Icarus: Uprising]]'', with other titles such as ''[[Steel Diver: Sub Wars]]'', ''[[Pikmin 3]]'' and ''[[Pokémon Rumble World]]'' being worked on for Pretendo support.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ign.com/articles/3ds-wii-u-project-pretendo|title=Nintendo Shuts Down Online Services for Wii U and 3DS, but Fan Project Pretendo Is Keeping Them Alive|first=Michael|last=Cripe|date=April 9, 2024|website=IGN|access-date=November 9, 2025}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.gonintendo.com/contents/34143-pretendo-network-fan-group-hoping-to-restore-wii-u-3ds-online-services|title=Pretendo Network hoping to restore Wii U/3DS online services|date=April 9, 2024|website=www.gonintendo.com|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240520095454/https://www.gonintendo.com/contents/34143-pretendo-network-fan-group-hoping-to-restore-wii-u-3ds-online-services|archive-date=May 20, 2024|access-date=November 9, 2025}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://pretendo.network/|title=Pretendo Network|website=Pretendo Network|access-date=November 9, 2025}}</ref>

The Miiverse-like clone provided by Pretendo uses a different interface than the original; as a result, another Miiverse revival project called Roseverse was created, which aimed at preserving Miiverse functionality as close as possible to the official (and now discontinued) service and is generally preferred to be the "better" version over Pretendo's version.{{cn|date=July 2026}}

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: List of commercial failures in video and arcade games
======================================================================

{{Short description|none}}
<!--In addition to the definition given in the article, it's levied according to consensus of [[WP:RS|reliable sources]]. This definition should be applied internationally, and not based strictly on the performance of a platform in any one given market (e.g. North America). -->

As a hit-driven business, the great majority of the [[video game industry]]'s software releases have been [[failure#In business|commercial disappointments]]. In the early 21st century, industry commentators made these general estimates: 10% of published games generated 90% of revenue;<ref>[http://publish.uwo.ca/~ncdyerwi/Mapping-Queens.pdf Mapping the Canadian Video and Computer Game Industry] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160316095149/http://publish.uwo.ca/~ncdyerwi/Mapping-Queens.pdf |date=March 16, 2016 }} from The Canadian Video Game Industry with data from the ([[Portable Document Format|PDF]])</ref> that around 3% of PC games and 15% of console games have global sales of more than 100,000 units per year, with even this level insufficient to make high-budget games profitable;<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VFHOSRrMH5kC&q=video+game+%22hit-driven%22&pg=PA43|title=Secrets of the Game Business|first=Francois Dominic|last=Laramee|date=8 January 2018|publisher=Charles River Media|isbn=978-1-58450-282-1|via=Google Books}}</ref> and that about 20% of games make any profit.<ref>[https://www.nytimes.com/2004/08/22/business/news-and-analysis-video-game-makers-go-hollywood-uh-oh.html Video Game Makers Go Hollywood. Uh-Oh.] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150528044335/http://www.nytimes.com/2004/08/22/business/news-and-analysis-video-game-makers-go-hollywood-uh-oh.html |date=May 28, 2015 }} from The New York Times</ref> Within years after [[Steam (service)|Steam]] relaxed limits on which games could be digitally distributed on its service, they reported that around 80% of games failed to reach $5000 in revenue in their first two weeks of sales.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Orland |first=Kyle |date=April 7, 2020 |title=Ars analysis: ~80% of Steam games earn under $5K in first two weeks |url=https://arstechnica.com/gaming/2020/04/ars-analysis-80-of-steam-games-earn-under-5k-in-first-two-weeks/}}</ref>

Some of these failure events have drastically changed the video game market since its origin in the late 1970s. For example, the failure of ''[[E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial (video game)|E.T.]]'' contributed to the [[video game crash of 1983]]. Some games, though commercial failures, are well received by certain groups of [[gamer]]s and are considered [[Cult video game|cult games]].

The following list includes any video game software on any platform where the commercial failure has been documented as such by the manufacture or published, or affirmed through industry sales trackers (in alphabetical order).

== Video game software failures ==
{{See also|List of video games notable for negative reception}}

The following is an incomplete list of software that have been deemed commercial failures by industry sources.

{{Incomplete List|date=May 2025}}

===''Afro Samurai 2: Revenge of Kuma''===
{{Main|Afro Samurai 2}}
''Afro Samurai 2: Revenge of Kuma'' is a [[Third-person (video games)|third-person]] [[Action-adventure game|action-adventure]] [[video game]] published by [[Versus Evil]] and developed by Redacted Studios. The game was released for [[PlayStation 4]] via [[PlayStation Network]] and [[Windows]] in September 2015, with an [[Xbox One]] version planned for October. The sequel to 2009's ''[[Afro Samurai (video game)|Afro Samurai]]'', originally a [[Afro Samurai|manga series]] by [[Takashi Okazaki]], the player controls Kuma, a swordsman who seeks revenge on Afro.

The game received widely negative reviews from critics. Originally planned to be released in three volumes, Versus Evil pulled ''Revenge of Kuma'' from all platforms, issued refunds, and canceled the other two volumes. The [[Xbox One]] version was also never released, while the [[PlayStation 4]] version is one of the few titles from that platform to not be [[PlayStation 5#Backward compatibility|backward compatible with]] the [[PlayStation 5]].

[[Polygon (website)|Polygon]] called it one of the worst games of 2015.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.polygon.com/2015/12/30/10689844/the-worst-video-games-of-2015 |title=The worst video games of 2015 |last=Frank |first=Allegra |work=[[Polygon (website)|Polygon]] |publisher=[[Vox Media]] |date=December 30, 2015 |access-date=December 31, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151231200730/http://www.polygon.com/2015/12/30/10689844/the-worst-video-games-of-2015 |archive-date=December 31, 2015 |url-status=live}}</ref> [[Giant Bomb]] called it the worst game of the year.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.giantbomb.com/articles/giant-bombs-2015-game-of-the-year-awards-day-four-/1100-5319/ | title=Giant Bomb's 2015 Game of the Year Awards: Day Four Text Recap | work=[[Giant Bomb]] | publisher=[[CBS Interactive]] | date=December 31, 2015 | access-date=January 24, 2016}}</ref> It was the second worst-reviewed game of 2015 according to aggregate review website [[Metacritic]].<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.metacritic.com/pictures/worst-videogames-of-2015 | title=The 10 Worst Video Games of 2015 | work=[[Metacritic]] | publisher=[[CBS Interactive]] | first=Jason | last=Dietz | date=December 21, 2015 | access-date=January 24, 2016}}</ref> In November 2015, ''Afro Samurai 2'' was pulled from the [[PSN]] and [[Steam (service)|Steam]]. In an interview with CGMagazine on the game's withdrawal, Versus Evil's Steve Escalante called the game "a failure" and announced the cancellation of the other two volumes and refunds for customers.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Versus Evil Explains the Disappearance of Afro Samurai 2|date=19 November 2015|url=https://www.cgmagonline.com/news/versus-evil-exafro-samurai-2/|access-date=2021-11-18|language=en-CA}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.polygon.com/2015/11/20/9770612/afro-samurai-2-pulled-steam-ps4-failure|title=Afro Samurai 2 pulled from retail, deemed 'a failure'|last=Frank|first=Allegra|work=[[Polygon (website)|Polygon]]|publisher=[[Vox Media]]|date=November 20, 2015|access-date=December 17, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151122165430/http://www.polygon.com/2015/11/20/9770612/afro-samurai-2-pulled-steam-ps4-failure|archive-date=November 22, 2015|url-status=live}}</ref> Escalante later expanded on the decision in an interview with [[Gamasutra]], saying, "Given the game quality was not what people were expecting, it didn't sell like hot cakes, let's just put it like that."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.gamasutra.com/view/news/260138/Indepth_The_decision_to_unpublish_Afro_Samurai_2_and_refund_buyers.php |title=In-depth: The decision to un-publish Afro Samurai 2 and refund buyers |last=Graft |first=Kris |work=[[Gamasutra]] |publisher=[[UBM plc]] |date=November 23, 2015 |access-date=December 14, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151231215237/http://www.gamasutra.com/view/news/260138/Indepth_The_decision_to_unpublish_Afro_Samurai_2_and_refund_buyers.php |archive-date=December 31, 2015 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

=== ''Anthem'' ===
{{Main|Anthem (video game)}}
''Anthem'' was an action role-playing game developed by [[BioWare]] and published by [[Electronic Arts]] in 2019. Its seven-year-long development period started after release of ''[[Mass Effect 3]]'', and was envisioned by BioWare to move away from the typical role-playing formats of ''Mass Effect'' and ''[[Dragon Age]]'', and become a type of [[live-service game]]. The game had a difficult development cycle due to shifting staff, technological difficulties in switching to the [[Frostbite Engine]], and demands from EA's management on the direction of the game. Other BioWare projects from its other studios were put on hold to complete ''Anthem'' for release, and according to one BioWare developer, it was only the work of the last fifteen months of development that made it into the game.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://kotaku.com/how-biowares-anthem-went-wrong-1833731964 | title = How BioWare's Anthem Went Wrong | date = April 2, 2019 | accessdate = November 1, 2024 | work = [[Kotaku]] | first = Jason | last = Schreier }}</ref> Due to this rush near the end of the development cycle, the game was considered to be lacking content at release, contained numerous software bugs that plagued gameplay, and was found too similar to other live-service games like ''[[Destiny (video game)|Destiny]]'' and ''[[World of Warcraft]]''. BioWare and EA had stated their intent to revamp the game to meet expectations, but the game struggled to maintain a playbase. Though the game ultimately sold over 5 million copies in its lifetime, EA had anticipated sales to be much higher and comparable to the ''Battlefield'' series, and in 2021, EA opted to terminate further development work on ''Anthem'', with the game's servers closed on January 12, 2026.

=== ''APB: All Points Bulletin'' ===
{{Main|APB: All Points Bulletin}}
''APB: All Points Bulletin'' was a [[multiplayer online game]] developed by [[Realtime Worlds]] in 2010. The game, incorporating concepts from their previous game ''[[Crackdown (video game)|Crackdown]]'' and past work by its lead developer [[David Jones (video game developer)|David Jones]], who had helped create the ''[[Grand Theft Auto]]'' series, was set around the idea of a large-scale urban battle between Enforcers and Criminals; players would be able to partake in large-scale on-going missions between the two sides. The game was originally set as both a Microsoft Windows and Xbox 360 title and as Realtime Worlds' flagship title for release in 2008, but instead the company set about developing ''Crackdown'' first, and later focused ''APB'' as a Windows-only title, potentially porting the game to the Xbox 360 later.
