===Joy-Con{{nbsp}}2===
{{main|Joy-Con 2}}
[[File:Nintendo Switch 2 Joy-Con 2 Blue and Orange.jpg|thumb|upright=0.75|The Joy-Con{{nbsp}}2 controllers]]
The Joy-Con{{nbsp}}2 controllers have an updated design from the original [[Joy-Con]]. Besides being larger to match the console, they attach [[magnetic attraction|magnetically]] by snapping to the sides rather than using a rail system. They are removed using a small button on the Joy-Con{{nbsp}}2 that causes a cylinder inside to extend and push off from the main unit.<ref name="verge everything">{{Cite web |last=Davis |first=Wes |date=April 2, 2025 |title=Here's everything Nintendo has revealed about the Switch 2's Joy-Cons |url=https://www.theverge.com/news/642024/nintendo-switch-2-joy-con-controllers-mouse-magnetic-attach-c-button |access-date=April 2, 2025 |website=The Verge |language=en-US |archive-date=April 2, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250402183502/https://www.theverge.com/news/642024/nintendo-switch-2-joy-con-controllers-mouse-magnetic-attach-c-button |url-status=live }}</ref> Nintendo stated that their [[analog stick]]s would be larger, smoother, and more durable.<ref name="verge everything" /> Early reports suggested the new controller thumbsticks would use [[Hall-effect sensor]]s to address the drift issues that the original models had due to dust collecting within the analog system<ref>{{Cite Q|Q131868494|access-date=January 24, 2025}}</ref> but Nintendo stated in April 2025 that Hall-effect sensors are not used.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://arstechnica.com/gaming/2025/04/switch-2-joysticks-wont-use-hall-effect-sensors-to-avoid-stick-drift/|title=Nintendo isn't using anti-drift Hall effect sensors on Switch 2 joysticks|first=Kyle|last=Orland|date=April 7, 2025|access-date=April 7, 2025|work=[[Ars Technica]]|archive-date=April 10, 2025 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250410222509/https://arstechnica.com/gaming/2025/04/switch-2-joysticks-wont-use-hall-effect-sensors-to-avoid-stick-drift/ | url-status=live }}</ref>

The SL and SR buttons on the side of the controllers have been significantly enlarged, and a new C button is present on the right Joy-Con{{nbsp}}2 to activate the new GameChat feature.<ref name="verge everything" /> The controllers are also able to be used like a [[computer mouse]] in supported games by sliding them across a surface.<ref name="verge everything" /> Both Joy-Con 2 controllers have a 500mAh battery that is estimated to last 20{{nbsp}}hours. The controllers can be recharged by connecting them to the console or by using the Charging Grip.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.videogameschronicle.com/news/nintendo-switch-2-battery-life-confirmed/|title=Nintendo Switch 2 battery life confirmed|first=Chris|last=Scullion|date=April 2, 2025|access-date=April 7, 2025|work=[[Video Games Chronicle]]|archive-date=May 1, 2025 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250501185024/https://www.videogameschronicle.com/news/nintendo-switch-2-battery-life-confirmed/ | url-status=live }}</ref> The [[infrared sensor]] from the first-generation Joy-Con has been removed.<ref name="verge everything" />

===Nintendo Switch 2 Camera===
The Nintendo Switch 2 Camera is a USB-C webcam developed by Nintendo and made specifically for the Nintendo Switch 2. The camera can be used for GameChat and CameraPlay, in-game camera features.<ref>{{Cite web |last=O'Reilly |first=PJ |date=June 20, 2025|title=Nintendo Switch 2: Camera Guide |url=https://www.nintendolife.com/guides/nintendo-switch-2-camera-guide |access-date=February 4, 2026|website=Nintendo Life |language=en-GB |archive-date=February 5, 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260205030412/https://www.nintendolife.com/guides/nintendo-switch-2-camera-guide |url-status=live }}</ref> The camera has an [[aluminium]] body with a rubber grip at its base. The camera includes a 110 degree wide [[lens]] with a 1080p [[image sensor]]. It also comes with a cover for privacy.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Higham |first=Michael |date=June 18, 2025|title=Nintendo Switch 2 Camera Review |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/nintendo-switch-2-camera-review |access-date=June 26, 2025|website=IGN |language=en |archive-date=November 28, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251128065102/https://www.ign.com/articles/nintendo-switch-2-camera-review |url-status=live }}</ref>

While Nintendo allows third party USB-C cameras to function with the Switch 2, they note that not all work with the console. There is an option in system settings to test functionality of a connected USB-C camera. According to Niles Mitchell on [[YouTube]], an [[iPhone]] is compatible as a camera.<ref>{{Cite web |date=June 6, 2025|title=Your iPhone Works as a Nintendo Switch 2 Camera, But Your Webcam Might Not |url=https://www.pcmag.com/news/your-iphone-works-as-a-nintendo-switch-2-camera-but-your-webcam-might-not |access-date=June 26, 2025|website=[[PC Magazine]] |language=en}}</ref>

===Revisions===
According to a report from [[Nikkei, Inc.|Nikkei]], Nintendo is developing a revision of the Switch 2 which includes user-replaceable batteries for the console and the Joy-Con 2. This is to comply with the European Union's [[right to repair]] regulations, which require easy replacement for rechargeable batteries. The revision is only planned to be released in Europe.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Phillips |first=Tom |date=March 20, 2026|title=Nintendo Switch 2 With Removable Battery in Production, Report Reveals — But Only for Europe |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/nintendo-switch-2-with-removable-battery-in-production-report-reveals-but-only-for-europe |access-date=March 24, 2026|website=[[IGN]] |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.engadget.com/gaming/nintendo/nintendo-is-reportedly-making-a-switch-2-with-a-user-replaceable-battery-for-the-eu-172318540.html|title=Nintendo is reportedly making a Switch 2 with a user-replaceable battery for the EU|date=March 20, 2026|access-date=March 24, 2026|website=[[Engadget]]|last=Bonk|first=Lawrence|archive-date=March 22, 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260322051900/https://www.engadget.com/gaming/nintendo/nintendo-is-reportedly-making-a-switch-2-with-a-user-replaceable-battery-for-the-eu-172318540.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Nintendo confirmed that it would start shipping these models across Europe in July 2026, with all regions receiving these by early 2027; at the same time the company announced it was discontinuing the original Switch family in Europe by February 2027.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-07-06 |title=Original Switch consoles are being discontinued in Europe as Nintendo details how EU battery laws will impact its retail strategy for Switch 2 |url=https://www.eurogamer.net/nintendo-switch-2-replaceable-batteries-revision-plans-detailed |access-date=2026-10-02 |website=Eurogamer.net |language=en}}</ref>

===Distribution===
{{See also|Nintendo Game Card|List of Nintendo Switch 2 games}}
As with its predecessor, games for Switch 2 can be obtained in physical and digital formats, with physically distributed games being stored on proprietary Game Cards that share a similar form factor with those used on the first-generation Switch.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Welsh |first=Oli |date=October 3, 2023 |title=Everything we know about Switch 2, Nintendo's next-gen console |url=https://www.polygon.com/nintendo/23899504/nintendo-switch-2-release-date-power-name-games |access-date=January 17, 2025 |website=Polygon |language=en-US |archive-date=May 22, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250522225608/https://www.polygon.com/nintendo/23899504/nintendo-switch-2-release-date-power-name-games |url-status=live }}</ref> Game Cards for Switch 2 games are colored in red to differentiate them from those released for the first-generation Switch, which are grey.<ref name="verge specs" /> Like Switch game cards, Switch 2 game cards are coated in a non-toxic bitterant to prevent children from trying to eat them.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.gamespot.com/articles/switch-2-carts-still-taste-bad-designed-purposefully-to-be-spat-out/1100-6530649/|title=Switch 2 Carts Still Taste Bad, Designed Purposefully To Be Spat Out|first=Eddie|last=Makuch|date=April 7, 2025|access-date=April 8, 2025|work=[[GameSpot]]|archive-date=June 7, 2025 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250607190101/https://www.gamespot.com/articles/switch-2-carts-still-taste-bad-designed-purposefully-to-be-spat-out/1100-6530649/ | url-status=live }}</ref>

Beginning on Switch 2, the physical release of some games may ship with Game Cards that only contain a digital license and no game data ("Game-Key Card"); when inserted, the game's files will be downloaded to the console.<ref>{{cite web |title=Nintendo Switch 2 Game-Key Card Overview |url=https://en-americas-support.nintendo.com/app/answers/detail/a_id/68415/~/nintendo-switch%26nbsp%3B2-game-key-card-overview |access-date=October 2, 2025|publisher=Nintendo}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=April 2, 2025|title=Nintendo Confirms Some Switch 2 Game Cards Will Only Include a Download Key |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/nintendo-confirms-some-switch-2-game-cards-will-only-include-a-download-key |access-date=October 3, 2025|website=ign.com |publisher=IGN}}</ref> Unlike digital purchases, the Game Card must still be inserted to launch the game. Game-Key Cards are an evolution of a similar practice that was used by some third-party Switch games, which only contain a portion of the game's data on their cards due to file size constraints, and similarly required downloading the remainder of the data.<ref name="polygon-legocityinstall">{{Cite web |last=Frank |first=Allegra |date=March 27, 2017 |title=Another third-party Switch game causes uproar |url=http://www.polygon.com/2017/3/27/15078334/lego-city-undercover-download-size-nintendo-switch |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170327235925/http://www.polygon.com/2017/3/27/15078334/lego-city-undercover-download-size-nintendo-switch |archive-date=March 27, 2017 |access-date=March 27, 2017 |website=[[Polygon (website)|Polygon]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Nintendo Switch 2 Game-Key Card Overview |url=https://en-americas-support.nintendo.com/app/answers/detail/a_id/68415/~/nintendo-switch |access-date=April 2, 2025 |website=Nintendo Support |archive-date=April 3, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250403092602/https://en-americas-support.nintendo.com/app/answers/detail/a_id/68415/~/nintendo-switch |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Wales ===Online services===
{{See also|Nintendo Switch Online|GameChat}}
The Nintendo Switch Online service is retained on the Switch 2.<ref name="compatibility" /> Via the subscription-based service, users on the Switch 2 can connect to friends as to play with them in multiplayer games and allow for [[Nintendo Switch Online#Cloud saves|cloud saves]] of their game data. As part of the existing legacy games service on Switch Online, a selection of games from the [[GameCube]] are distributed on the [[Nintendo Switch Online Expansion Pack|Expansion Pack]], exclusively for Switch 2 under the rebranded "[[Nintendo Classics]]" moniker.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Reynolds |first=Ollie |date=April 2, 2025|title=GameCube Games Confirmed For Nintendo Switch Online On Switch 2 |url=https://www.nintendolife.com/news/2025/04/gamecube-games-confirmed-for-nintendo-switch-online-on-switch-2 |access-date=April 5, 2025|website=Nintendo Life |language=en-GB |archive-date=June 4, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250604201806/https://www.nintendolife.com/news/2025/04/gamecube-games-confirmed-for-nintendo-switch-online-on-switch-2 |url-status=live }}</ref> The collection launched in tandem with the console in June 2025, and initially includes ''[[The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker]]'', ''[[Soulcalibur II]]'' (both 2002), and ''[[F-Zero GX]]'' (2003). Other games, such as ''[[Luigi's Mansion]]'' (2001), ''[[Super Mario Sunshine]]'' (2002), ''[[Pokémon Colosseum]]'' (2003) and ''[[Fire Emblem: Path of Radiance]]'' (2005) were added procedurally at later dates.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Pitts |first=Lan |date=April 4, 2025|title=Every GameCube Game Coming To Switch 2's Switch Online Library, Including At Launch |url=https://www.gamespot.com/gallery/every-gamecube-game-coming-to-switch-2s-switch-online-library/2900-6400/ |access-date=April 5, 2025|website=[[GameSpot]] |language=en-US |archive-date=May 22, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250522053439/https://www.gamespot.com/gallery/every-gamecube-game-coming-to-switch-2s-switch-online-library/2900-6400/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Additional features applied across the Nintendo Classics catalog are exclusively supported on Switch 2, namely CRT shaders and a rewind function being added to existing [[Nintendo 64]] games on the service.<ref>{{Cite web |title=What's new with Nintendo Switch Online on Nintendo Switch 2? |url=https://www.nintendo.com/en-gb/News/2025/April/What-s-new-with-Nintendo-Switch-Online-on-Nintendo-Switch-2-2785954.html |access-date=April 5, 2025|website=Nintendo of Europe SE |language=en-GB |archive-date=May 18, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250518034420/https://www.nintendo.com/en-gb/News/2025/April/What-s-new-with-Nintendo-Switch-Online-on-Nintendo-Switch-2-2785954.html |url-status=live }}</ref> Nintendo also released a new iteration of the [[GameCube controller]] alongside the platform's addition to Nintendo Classics, available exclusively to existing Switch Online subscribers.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Barr |first=Kyle |date=April 2, 2025|title=The GameCube and Its Perfect Controller Are Back (on the Switch 2) |url=https://gizmodo.com/the-gamecube-and-its-perfect-controller-are-back-on-the-switch-2-2000584135 |access-date=April 5, 2025|website=Gizmodo |language=en-US |archive-date=June 3, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250603152833/https://gizmodo.com/the-gamecube-and-its-perfect-controller-are-back-on-the-switch-2-2000584135 |url-status=live }}</ref> Switch 2 exclusive games cannot be purchased using earlier Game Vouchers that had been available on the original Switch.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Grant |first=Christopher |date=February 18, 2025 |title=Nintendo Game Vouchers won't work on Switch 2 exclusives, Gold Points discontinued |url=https://www.polygon.com/nintendo/524774/nintendo-game-vouchers-switch-2 |access-date=February 20, 2025 |website=Polygon |language=en-US |archive-date=February 20, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250220002116/https://www.polygon.com/nintendo/524774/nintendo-game-vouchers-switch-2 |url-status=live }}</ref>

A [[voice chat]] service known as GameChat allows users to conduct voice chats and screen sharing with friends. GameChat supports video calls using an optional [[webcam]] accessory. It is accessible via a "C" button on the right Joy-Con 2,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Parrish |first=Ash |date=April 2, 2025 |title=Nintendo's Switch 2 'C' button is a Discord-like GameChat feature |url=https://www.theverge.com/news/24343637/nintendo-switch-2-joy-con-c-button-controller |access-date=April 2, 2025 |website=The Verge |language=en-US |archive-date=April 2, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250402135720/https://www.theverge.com/news/24343637/nintendo-switch-2-joy-con-c-button-controller |url-status=live }}</ref> on the new GameCube controller,<ref>{{cite web | last=Robinson | first=Andy | title=GameCube is officially coming to Switch Online, exclusively for Switch 2 | website=VGC | date=April 2, 2025 | url=https://www.videogameschronicle.com/news/gamecube-is-officially-coming-to-switch-online-exclusively-for-switch-2/ | access-date=April 2, 2025}}</ref> and on the [[Nintendo Switch 2 Pro Controller]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=April 8, 2025|title=Nintendo Switch 2 updates: Release date, price, new games and everything else you need to know |url=https://www.engadget.com/gaming/nintendo/nintendo-switch-2-updates-release-date-price-new-games-and-everything-else-you-need-to-know-175623042.html |access-date=September 10, 2026 |website=Engadget}}</ref> Chat was free to use until March 31, 2026, after which point a paid Nintendo Switch Online membership is required to use the feature.<ref>{{cite news |last= Cardy |first= Simon |date= April 2, 2025|title= Nintendo Switch 2: 23 New Details - Release Date, Price, GameChat and More! |url= https://www.ign.com/articles/nintendo-switch-2-23-new-details-release-date-price-gamechat-and-more|work=IGN |access-date= April 2, 2025|quote= GameChat, of course, comes with a price, though. And that admission fee is a Nintendo Online membership.}}</ref> Smartphones such as the [[iPhone 15]] and [[iPhone 16]], as well as [[Android (operating system)|Android]] phones that support DisplayPort Alternate Mode, can be used as a webcam on the Switch 2 by using a USB-C to HDMI cable, in addition to a HDMI capture cable.<ref>{{cite news |last= Holt |first= Kris |date= June 6, 2025|title= You can use an iPhone as a Nintendo Switch 2 camera |url= https://www.engadget.com/gaming/nintendo/you-can-use-an-iphone-as-a-nintendo-switch-2-camera-142622005.html |archive-date= July 11, 2025|access-date= July 1, 2025|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20250711200311/https://www.engadget.com/gaming/nintendo/you-can-use-an-iphone-as-a-nintendo-switch-2-camera-142622005.html |url-status= live }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last= Hall |first= Zac |date= June 5, 2025|title= iPhone can be used as a Nintendo Switch 2 webcam |url= https://9to5mac.com/2025/06/05/nintendo-switch-2-iphone |archive-date= June 8, 2025|access-date= July 1, 2025|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20250608123420/https://9to5mac.com/2025/06/05/nintendo-switch-2-iphone/ |url-status= live }}</ref>

===Third-party support===
{{rewrite section|date=December 2025}}
A survey conducted at the 2024 [[Game Developers Conference]] in January 2024 inquired 3,000 independent and [[AAA (video game industry)|AAA developers]] on game creation and which platforms they were engaging, of which 250 individuals identified themselves as already producing games slated for Switch 2, and a further 32% of those surveyed expressed interest in developing for the console.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Robinson |first=Andy |date=January 18, 2024 |title=8% of developers in a GDC survey say they're working on Nintendo's next console In May 2024, Nintendo announced their intentions to acquire [[Miami]]-based developer [[Shiver Entertainment]] from its prior parent company [[Embracer Group]], with the company detailing in a statement that the merger enabled them to procure specialized in-house resources for the development and porting of software, while allowing the studio to continue commitments to Switch and other platforms.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Doolan |first=Liam |date=May 21, 2024 |title=Nintendo Announces Acquisition Of Shiver Entertainment News]]'' later reported that the acquisition was for bolstering Nintendo's efforts in securing games from third-party developers on Switch 2, with Shiver assisting external developers in the Microsoft had previously signed an agreement with Nintendo to bring future entries in the ''[[Call of Duty]]'' franchise to their platforms as part of their [[Acquisition of Activision Blizzard by Microsoft|acquisition bid]] for [[Activision Blizzard]], which became legally binding in February 2023.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Reynolds |first=Ollie |date=February 21, 2023 |title=Microsoft's Commitment Publisher [[Ubisoft]] commented that they were "in love" with the console following its reveal, and released ports of ''[[Star Wars Outlaws]]'' and ''[[Assassin's Creed Shadows]]'' for the system during its launch window.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Notis |first=Ari |date=September 14, 2025|title=Star War Outlaws on Switch 2 settles it: Nintendo is in its port era now |url=https://www.polygon.com/star-war-outlaws-switch-2-impressions-ports/ |access-date=November 7, 2025|website=Polygon |language=en |archive-date=October 23, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251023155528/https://www.polygon.com/star-war-outlaws-switch-2-impressions-ports/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Blake |first=Vikki |date=October 24, 2025|title=Assassin's Creed Shadows Finally Has an Official Nintendo Switch 2 Release Date and a Price |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/assassins-creed-shadows-finally-has-an-official-nintendo-switch-2-release-date-and-a-price |access-date=November 7, 2025|website=IGN |language=en |archive-date=October 30, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251030210621/https://www.ign.com/articles/assassins-creed-shadows-finally-has-an-official-nintendo-switch-2-release-date-and-a-price |url-status=live }}</ref> Weicong Wu, producer of ''[[Marvel Rivals]]'', expressed interest in bringing the game to the Switch 2, having stated that the team has already contacted Nintendo and possessed [[Game development kit|dev kits]]. However, he has stated that it will only come to the Switch 2 if the game's performance is satisfactory.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Doolan |first=Liam |date=February 15, 2025 |title=Marvel Rivals Dev NetEase "Already In Contact With Nintendo" About Switch 2 |url=https://www.nintendolife.com/news/2025/02/marvel-rivals-dev-netease-already-in-contact-with-nintendo-about-switch-2 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250215162037/https://www.nintendolife.com/news/2025/02/marvel-rivals-dev-netease-already-in-contact-with-nintendo-about-switch-2 |archive-date=February 15, 2025 |access-date=February 16, 2025 |website=Nintendo Life |language=en-GB}}</ref>

Around August 2025, [[Digital Foundry]] reported that smaller and indie studios had said that Nintendo was not providing Switch 2 hardware development kits, and directing them to focus on releases for the original Switch, which would still be playable on the Switch 2 with backwards compatibility. Nintendo had not made clear what the reasonings behind this was, but this decision was preventing these developers from releasing native Switch 2 games with support for the console's updated hardware or additional functionality like GameChat.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ign.com/articles/nintendo-reportedly-almost-discouraging-switch-2-development-as-studios-told-to-launch-games-on-switch-1-and-rely-on-backwards-compatibility-instead|title=Nintendo Reportedly 'Almost Discouraging' Switch 2 Development as Studios Told to Launch Games on Switch 1 and Rely on Backwards Compatibility Instead|first=Tom|last=Phillips|date=August 26, 2025|access-date=August 29, 2025 | work  =[[IGN]] }}</ref>

===Backward compatibility===
{{See also|List of Nintendo Switch games}}
The Switch 2 is [[Backward compatibility|backward compatible]] with most Switch games, both physically and digitally,<ref name="compatibility">{{Cite web |last=Bankhurst |first=Adam |date=November 6, 2024 |title=Nintendo Switch 2 Will Officially Be Backward-Compatible With Original Switch Games |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/nintendo-switch-2-will-officially-be-backward-compatible-with-original-switch-games |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241106074841/https://www.ign.com/articles/nintendo-switch-2-will-officially-be-backward-compatible-with-original-switch-games |archive-date=November 6, 2024 |access-date=November 7, 2024 |website=IGN |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=McEvoy |first=Sophie |title=Nintendo confirms backward compatibility on Switch 2 |url=https://www.gamesindustry.biz/nintendo-confirms-backwards-compatibility-on-switch-2 |website=Games Industry |date=November 6, 2024 |access-date=November 6, 2024 |archive-date=November 9, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241109044626/https://www.gamesindustry.biz/nintendo-confirms-backwards-compatibility-on-switch-2 |url-status=live }}</ref> allowing certain games to run more stably than they did on the previous hardware.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Feature: 33 Games With 'Secret' Performance Bumps You Should Revisit On Switch 2
|url=https://www.nintendolife.com/features/33-games-with-secret-performance-bumps-you-should-revisit-on-switch-2 |website=[[NintendoLife]] |access-date=30 September 2026 |language=en |first1=Gavin |last1=Lane |first2=PJ |last2=O'Reilly |first3=Ollie |last3=Reynolds |first4=Jim |last4=Norman |first5=Alana |last5=Hagues |date=12 July 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260918141146/https://www.nintendolife.com/features/33-games-with-secret-performance-bumps-you-should-revisit-on-switch-2 |url-status=live |archive-date=18 September 2026}}</ref> Some games are not directly compatible with the hardware changes in the Switch 2 and the Joy-Con 2 controllers, but may still be playable using the Joy-Con from the original Switch, such as games that require [[infrared]] functionality.<ref name="Compatible">{{Cite Q|Q131828115|access-date=January 20, 2025}}</ref><ref name="NintendoCompatibiltyPage" /><ref name="PolygonCompatibility" /> For most other Switch games, they are playable using a type of emulation akin to a translation [[Compatibility layer|layer]] since the Switch 2 does not have the same hardware as the Switch. Hardware director Takuhiro Dohta described the solution as "somewhere in between a software emulator and hardware compatibility" and Tetsuya Sasaki said that the method used is "performed on a [[real-time computing|real-time]] basis as the data is read".<ref>{{Cite web |date=April 2, 2025|title=Ask the Developer Vol. 16: Nintendo Switch 2 — Part 4 |url=https://www.nintendo.com/us/whatsnew/ask-the-developer-vol-16-nintendo-switch-2-part-4/ |access-date=April 5, 2025|website=Nintendo |language=en-US |archive-date=April 5, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250405052115/https://www.nintendo.com/us/whatsnew/ask-the-developer-vol-16-nintendo-switch-2-part-4/ |url-status=live }}</ref> This method allows Switch games to have Switch 2 features added, such as GameChat support, when played on the Switch 2.<ref name="PolygonCompatibility" /> {{as of|2025|05}}, of the 122 Nintendo-developed games tested, all were found to be compatible except the [[Nintendo Labo VR Kit]], due to the Switch 2's larger size being unable to fit inside the accessory.<ref name="NintendoCompatibiltyPage">{{Cite web |date=April 2, 2025 |url=https://www.nintendo.com/us/gaming-systems/switch-2/transfer-guide/compatible-games/ |title=Important information about compatibility of Nintendo Switch games with Nintendo Switch 2 |access-date=April 2, 2025 |publisher=[[Nintendo]] |archive-date=April 2, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250402142029/https://www.nintendo.com/us/gaming-systems/switch-2/transfer-guide/compatible-games/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="VergeCompatibility">{{Cite web |last=Welch |first=Chris |date=April 2, 2025 |title=Nintendo goes in-depth on Switch 2 backward compatibility |url=https://www.theverge.com/news/641578/nintendo-switch-2-backwards-compatibility-games-faq |access-date=April 2, 2025 |website=[[The Verge]] |archive-date=April 2, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250402152025/https://www.theverge.com/news/641578/nintendo-switch-2-backwards-compatibility-games-faq |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="PolygonCompatibility">{{Cite web |last=Sarkar |first=Samit |date=April 2, 2025 |title=Everything we know about Nintendo Switch 2 backward compatibility |url=https://www.polygon.com/nintendo-switch-2/551581/nintendo-switch-2-backward-compatibility-explained |access-date=April 2, 2025 |website=[[Polygon (website)|Polygon]] |archive-date=April 2, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250402230847/https://www.polygon.com/nintendo-switch-2/551581/nintendo-switch-2-backward-compatibility-explained |url-status=live }}</ref> As of 27 May 2025, Nintendo had tested 75% of the more than 15,000 third-party Switch games, finding that "around 170" of them had issues while all the rest were compatible. Some additional software, such as applications for [[Hulu]] and [[Crunchyroll]], were also incompatible.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.videogameschronicle.com/news/nintendo-switch-2-has-no-issues-playing-the-vast-majority-of-nintendo-switch-games-tested-so-far/|title=Nintendo Switch 2 has 'no issues' playing the vast majority of Nintendo Switch games tested so far|date=May 27, 2025|last=Miller|first=Jordan|website=[[Video Games Chronicle]]|access-date=June 5, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250531024741/https://www.videogameschronicle.com/news/nintendo-switch-2-has-no-issues-playing-the-vast-majority-of-nintendo-switch-games-tested-so-far/|archive-date=May 31, 2025|url-status=live}}</ref>

Certain Switch games have upgrades for the console sold separately or available via the Nintendo Switch Online Expansion Pack, with some adding new content. The initial upgrade lineup included ''[[Metroid Prime 4: Beyond]]'', ''[[The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild]]'', ''[[The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom]]'', ''[[Super Mario Party Jamboree]]'', ''[[Pokémon Legends: Z-A]]'', and ''[[Kirby and the Forgotten Land]]'', with both ''Zelda'' games being launch games.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Valentine |first=Rebekah |date=April 2, 2025 |title=Some Nintendo Switch Games Are Getting Nintendo Switch 2 Upgrades, Including Breath of the Wild and Metroid Prime 4 |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/some-nintendo-switch-games-are-getting-nintendo-switch-2-upgrades-including-breath-of-the-wild-and-metroid-prime-4 |access-date=April 2, 2025 |website=IGN |language=en |archive-date=April 2, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250402134613/https://www.ign.com/articles/some-nintendo-switch-games-are-getting-nintendo-switch-2-upgrades-including-breath-of-the-wild-and-metroid-prime-4 |url-status=live }}</ref> Other Switch games, such as ''[[Super Mario Odyssey]]'' and ''[[Pokémon Scarlet and Violet]]'', have free performance updates for the Switch 2, but without additional content.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://arstechnica.com/gaming/2025/04/some-original-switch-games-will-run-better-on-switch-2-some-wont-run-at-all/|title=Some original Switch games will run better on Switch 2; some won't run at all|first=Andrew|last=Cunningham|date=April 2, 2025|access-date=April 2, 2025|work=[[Ars Technica]]|archive-date=April 2, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250402170113/https://arstechnica.com/gaming/2025/04/some-original-switch-games-will-run-better-on-switch-2-some-wont-run-at-all/|url-status=live}}</ref> The games can also be inserted into the original Switch to play the game as if it were a copy of the original Switch game.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Phillips |first=Tom |date=June 5, 2025|title=Nintendo Fans Surprised to Find Switch 2 Edition Game Cartridges Also Work on Switch 1 |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/nintendo-fans-surprised-to-find-switch-2-edition-game-cartridges-also-work-on-switch-1 |access-date=June 6, 2025|website=IGN |language=en}}</ref>

In March 2026, a Switch 2 system update introduced the Handheld Boost Mode function: this function, available in the system settings, forces Nintendo Switch software to play in their TV Mode state whilst played on Nintendo Switch 2 in Handheld and Tabletop Modes. Whilst enabling players with generally improved resolution and performance for most original Switch titles, battery life is affected and handheld-specific functions such as the touchscreen are disabled. <ref>{{Cite web |title=How to Use Handheld Mode Boost on Nintendo Switch 2 |url=https://www.nintendo.com/en-gb/Support/Nintendo-Switch-2/Troubleshooting/How-to-Use-Handheld-Mode-Boost-on-Nintendo-Switch-2-3052417.html |access-date=2026-09-14 |website=Nintendo of Europe SE |language=en-GB}}</ref>

To aid users in bringing their Switch games to the Switch 2, Nintendo introduced Virtual Game Cards for the original Switch system software in April 2025.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theverge.com/news/658511/nintendo-switch-20-0-0-update-virtual-game-card-gameshare-switch-2|title=Nintendo's new Switch 1 update is getting things ready for Switch 2|first=Richard|last=Lawler|date=April 29, 2025|access-date=April 29, 2025|work=[[The Verge]]|archive-date=April 30, 2025 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250430025159/https://www.theverge.com/news/658511/nintendo-switch-20-0-0-update-virtual-game-card-gameshare-switch-2 | url-status=live }}</ref> Virtual Game Cards can be used to virtually transfer digitally purchased games for use on a second Switch or Switch 2 system, or loaned to a family member's Switch for up to two weeks at a time.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Robinson |first=Andy |date=March 27, 2025 |title=Nintendo reveals major Switch and Switch 2 digital games shakeup with 'Virtual Game Cards' |url=https://www.videogameschronicle.com/news/nintendo-reveals-major-switch-digital-games-shakeup-with-virtual-game-cards/ |access-date=March 27, 2025 |website=[[Video Games Chronicle]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Cripe |first=Michael |date=March 27, 2025 |title=Nintendo Unveils Virtual Game Card Update Ahead of Switch 2 Launch |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/nintendo-unveils-virtual-game-card-update-ahead-of-switch-2-launch |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250327160145/https://www.ign.com/articles/nintendo-unveils-virtual-game-card-update-ahead-of-switch-2-launch |archive-date=March 27, 2025 |access-date=March 27, 2025 |website=[[IGN]]}}</ref>

Joy-Con and [[Nintendo Switch Pro Controller]]s are mostly{{efn|Waking the Switch 2 from sleep via an original Switch controller is not supported.<ref name="n076">{{cite web | last=Flores | first=Johnny Jr. | title=Your Original Joy-Cons Will Work With The Switch 2, But They'll Be Missing A Feature | website=TheGamer | date=April 6, 2025| url=https://www.thegamer.com/nintendo-switch-nws-nintendo-switch-2-joy-con-compatibility/ | access-date=June 9, 2025| archive-date=June 20, 2025| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250620142858/https://www.thegamer.com/nintendo-switch-nws-nintendo-switch-2-joy-con-compatibility/ | url-status=live }}</ref>}}<!--Forward compatible is the correct term. While a niche term, please understand that backwards compatibility is incorrect here; backwards means the newer thing accepts an older thing, i.e the game cards for OG Switch will fit in the Switch 2, or the GameCube controllers work on the Wii. FORWARD means the older thing works on a new thing that did not exist when the older thing was created; for example the DualShock 4 is accepted as input by the PS3, or the OG Joy-Con working with Switch 2, even though Switch 2 did not exist when OG Joy-Con were created--> [[Forward compatibility|forward compatible]] with the Switch 2, with some Switch games requiring them in order to be compatible with the Switch 2. Such games include most [[Nintendo Labo]] games, ''[[Ring Fit Adventure]]'' (2019) and ''[[WarioWare: Move It!]]'' (2023).<ref name="PolygonCompatibility" /><ref name="NintendoCompatibiltyPage" />

useful.<ref name="WIREDS2Review" /><ref name="EdgeJuly2024" /><ref name="GSS2Review"/> Critics were unhappy without a solution to [[stick drift]].<ref name="BIS2Review" /><ref name="PCGS2Review" The console's social features were praised.{{refn|According to:<ref name="DTS2Review" /><ref name="WIREDS2Review" /><ref name="BIS2Review" /><ref name="MashS2Review" />}} ''Wired'' described GameChat as "the most notable, wholly new feature" of the console,<ref name="WIREDS2Review" /> and ''[[Mashable]]'' described Nintendo not as reinventing the wheel with a two-decade-old concept, but moving it "beyond pure utility and into the realm of actively being enjoyable to use".<ref name="MashS2Review" /> ''[[Business Insider]]'' felt it was "made for quick, casual multiplayer sessions" rather than specialist communication.<ref name="BIS2Review" /> Critics praised the accuracy of the speech-to-text option and its ability to discern specific speakers.<ref name="MashS2Review" /><ref name="DTS2Review" /> Critics praised the built-in microphone's [[noise cancellation]] capabilities.<ref name="BIS2Review" /><ref name="WIREDS2Review" /><ref name="MashS2Review" /> Many called GameChat's screenshare choppy.{{refn|According to:<ref name="BIS2Review" /><ref name="GSS2Review">{{Cite web |last=Watts |first=Steve |date=June 12, 2025|title=Nintendo Switch 2 Review - The launch game lineup was criticized as lacking;{{refn|According to:<ref name="BIS2Review">{{Cite web |last=Antonelli |first=William |editor-last=Cohen |editor-first=Steven |date=June 13, 2025|title=Nintendo Switch 2 review: A fun console with tons of potential, but where are the exclusive games? |url=https://www.businessinsider.com/guides/tech/nintendo-switch-2-review |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250614153616/https://www.businessinsider.com/guides/tech/nintendo-switch-2-review |archive-date=June 14, 2025|access-date=June 15, 2025|website=[[Business Insider]]}}</ref><ref name="GamerS2Review">{{Cite web |last=King |first=Jade |date=June 13, 2025|title=Nintendo Switch 2 Review: A Predictable Yet Undeniably Impressive Evolution |url=https://www.thegamer.com/nintendo-switch-2-review/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250614160722/https://www.thegamer.com/nintendo-switch-2-review/ |archive-date=June 14, 2025|access-date=June 15, 2025|website=[[TheGamer]]}}</ref><ref name="VergeS2Review" /><ref name="IGNS2Review" />}} ''[[PC Gamer]]'' called it "one of the weakest" of recent times but added that "a new ''[[Mario Kart]]'' certainly eases the blow", referring to ''[[Mario Kart World]]''.<ref name="PCGS2Review" /> Critics criticized Nintendo for charging money for the launch game ''[[Nintendo Switch 2 Welcome Tour]]''.<ref name="GSS2Review"/><ref name="EdgeJuly2024">{{Cite magazine |last=Spencer |first=Alex |date=July 2025 |title=Linked to the Past: Can Switch recapture the original's magic? |magazine=[[Edge (magazine)|Edge]]  |number=411 |pages=68–77}}</ref><ref name="NYTS2Review">{{Cite web |last=X. Nintendo reported on June 10, 2025, four days from release, that the Switch 2 had sold more than 3.5{{nbsp}}million units worldwide, which made it the company's fastest selling console to date,<ref name="initsales">{{cite news |last=Bankhurst |first=Adam |title=Switch 2 Becomes 'Fastest-Selling' Nintendo Hardware Ever With Over 3.5 Million Units Sold Worldwide In Just Four Days |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/switch-2-becomes-fastest-selling-nintendo-hardware-ever-with-over-35-million-units-sold-worldwide-in-just-four-days |access-date=June 11, 2025 |work=IGN |date=June 11, 2025 |language=en |archive-date=June 11, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250611022920/https://www.ign.com/articles/switch-2-becomes-fastest-selling-nintendo-hardware-ever-with-over-35-million-units-sold-worldwide-in-just-four-days |url-status=live }}</ref> while market research firm Niko Partners claimed this made it the fastest-selling console of all time.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theverge.com/news/685162/nintendo-switch-2-sales-figures-record|title=Nintendo's Switch 2 is the fastest-selling game console of all time|first=Tom|last=Warren|date=June 15, 2025|access-date=September 6, 2025|work=[[The Verge]]|archive-date=July 21, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250721234008/https://www.theverge.com/news/685162/nintendo-switch-2-sales-figures-record|url-status=live}}</ref> ''[[Famitsu]]'' reported that the console had sold 947,931 units in Japan within the first four days of its release, surpassing the Switch's launch of 329,152 units sold in the region.<ref>{{cite news |last=Romano |first=Sal |title=Famitsu Sales: 6/2/25 – 6/8/25 |url=https://www.gematsu.com/2025/06/famitsu-sales-6-2-25-6-8-25 |access-date=June 12, 2025 |work=Gematsu |date=June 12, 2025 |archive-date=June 12, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250612135724/https://www.gematsu.com/2025/06/famitsu-sales-6-2-25-6-8-25 |url-status=live }}</ref> ''[[IGN]]'' said that launch sales of the Switch 2 in these first four days were twice as much as the launch sales of the Switch in all regions, and also claimed that the Switch 2 was the fastest-selling gaming hardware in the United States.<ref>{{cite news |last=Valentine |first=Rebekah |title=Nintendo Switch 2 Outselling the OG Switch 2-to-1 Across the Globe |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/nintendo-switch-2-outselling-the-og-switch-2-to-1-across-the-globe |access-date=June 12, 2025 |work=IGN |date=June 12, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250613174904/https://www.ign.com/articles/nintendo-switch-2-outselling-the-og-switch-2-to-1-across-the-globe |archive-date=June 13, 2025 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Valentine |first=Rebekah |date=July 23, 2025|title=The Nintendo Switch 2 Is the Fastest-Selling Gaming Hardware in U.S. History |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/the-nintendo-switch-2-is-the-fastest-selling-gaming-hardware-in-us-history |access-date=September 9, 2025|website=IGN |language=en |archive-date=September 5, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250905193805/https://www.ign.com/articles/the-nintendo-switch-2-is-the-fastest-selling-gaming-hardware-in-us-history |url-status=live }}</ref> By June 30, 2025, the end of Nintendo's first fiscal quarter for 2026, the console had sold over 5.8{{nbsp}}million units worldwide, with sales exceeding 6{{nbsp}}million through the end of July. Over 8.6{{nbsp}}million games had been sold, with ''Mario Kart World'' selling more than 5.6{{nbsp}}million, including copies sold as part of Switch 2 bundles.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ign.com/articles/switch-2-sells-more-than-6-million-in-the-7-weeks-since-launch-nintendo-says-demand-has-surpassed-our-expectations|title=Switch 2 Sells More Than 6 Million in the 7 Weeks Since Launch, Nintendo Says Demand 'Has Surpassed Our Expectations'|last=Yin-Poole|first=Wesley|date=August 1, 2025|access-date=August 1, 2025|work=[[IGN]]|archive-date=August 1, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250801105107/https://www.ign.com/articles/switch-2-sells-more-than-6-million-in-the-7-weeks-since-launch-nintendo-says-demand-has-surpassed-our-expectations|url-status=live}}</ref> Console sales remained strong into the fall of 2025, with 2.4{{nbsp}}million units sold in the US in the 3 months after launch according to industry analyst Mat Piscatella, exceeding the record pace set by the PlayStation 4 by 5%, and exceeding the pace of the original Switch by 77%.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Valentine |first1=Rebekah |title=Video Game Consoles Are Selling for 12% More in the U.S. This Year Than Last Year |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/video-game-consoles-are-selling-for-12-more-in-the-us-this-year-than-last-year |website=IGN |access-date=November 21, 2025|date=October 21, 2025|archive-date=December 21, 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251221222642/https://www.ign.com/articles/video-game-consoles-are-selling-for-12-more-in-the-us-this-year-than-last-year |url-status=live }}</ref>

As of December 31, 2025, the Nintendo Switch{{nbsp}}2 had sold approximately 17.4{{nbsp}}million units since its mid-2025 launch, contributing to Nintendo's strong quarterly profits.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kharpal |first=Arjun |date=February 3, 2026|title=Nintendo keeps Switch 2 forecast as device sales pass 17{{nbsp}}million units |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2026/02/03/nintendo-q3-earnings-switch-2-forecast.html |access-date=February 3, 2026|website=CNBC |language=en |archive-date=February 3, 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260203095823/https://www.cnbc.com/2026/02/03/nintendo-q3-earnings-switch-2-forecast.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

During a February earnings call, Nintendo president Shuntaro Furukawa stated that despite a strong launch and total sales of over 17{{nbsp}}million units since release, "overseas sales were somewhat weaker than expected" and the adjustment was attributed to slower consumer demand rather than cost pressure. The following month, ''[[Bloomberg News]]'' reported that Nintendo had reduced planned production of the Switch{{nbsp}}2 by more than 30% after demand, particularly in the United States, fell short of expectations. The report noted that the company lowered quarterly output to about 4{{nbsp}}million units, down from an initially planned 6{{nbsp}}million, with the reduced pace expected to continue into the following quarter.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Nintendo Cuts Switch 2 Output by Over 30% on Weak US Sales |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-03-24/nintendo-cuts-switch-2-output-by-over-30-on-weak-holiday-sales |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260325021311/https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-03-24/nintendo-cuts-switch-2-output-by-over-30-on-weak-holiday-sales |archive-date=March 25, 2026|access-date=March 31, 2026|work=Bloomberg.com |language=en |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=March 25, 2026|title=Nintendo cuts Switch 2 output by over 30% on weak holiday sales |url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/business/2026/03/25/tech/nintendo-switch-2-output-cut/ |access-date=March 31, 2026|website=The Japan Times |language=en |first=Takashi |last=Mochizuki}}</ref>

Following a surge in sales prior to its price increase, the Nintendo Switch 2 experienced an 87% decline in Japan, with sales dropping to 31,751 units the week after the May 25th price hike. The system's sales had peaked at over 200,000 units weekly in the weeks leading up to the increase, after previously averaging 44,000 to 52,000 units. The price of the Nintendo Switch 2 was raised from ¥49,980 to ¥59,980, which Nintendo attributed to current market conditions.<ref>{{Cite web |last=McEvoy |first=Sophie |date=June 5, 2026|title=Switch 2 sales drop 87% in Japan following surge ahead of cost revisions |url=https://www.gamesindustry.biz/switch-2-sales-drop-87-in-japan-following-surge-ahead-of-cost-revisions |access-date=June 8, 2026|website=GamesIndustry.biz |language=en |archive-date=June 8, 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260608230041/https://www.gamesindustry.biz/switch-2-sales-drop-87-in-japan-following-surge-ahead-of-cost-revisions |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Scullion |first=Chris |date=June 4, 2026|title=Switch 2 hardware sales dropped 87% week-on-week in Japan following price increase |url=https://www.videogameschronicle.com/news/switch-2-hardware-sales-dropped-87-week-on-week-in-japan-following-price-increase/ |access-date=June 8, 2026|website=VGC |language=en-US |archive-date=June 8, 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260608230039/https://www.videogameschronicle.com/news/switch-2-hardware-sales-dropped-87-week-on-week-in-japan-following-price-increase/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Awards ===

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Nintendo video game consoles
======================================================================

{{Short description|List of video game consoles by Nintendo}} <!-- "none" is preferred when the title is sufficiently descriptive; see [[WP:SDNONE]] -->

{{Use mdy dates|date=March 2026}}
{{infobox brand
|name                   = 
|logo                   =
NintendoStack.jpg
|logo_size              = 180px
|logo_caption = Home consoles size comparison of the (top to bottom) [[Wii]] (2006), [[GameCube]] (2001), [[Nintendo 64]] (1996), North American [[Super Nintendo Entertainment System|SNES]] (1991) and the [[Nintendo Entertainment System|NES]] (1985)
|type                   = [[Video game console]]
|currentowner           = [[Nintendo]]
|origin                 = Japan
|introduced             = {{start date and age|1977|06|01}}
|markets                = Worldwide
|website                = {{URL|https://nintendo.com}}
|tagline                = 
}}

[[Nintendo]] has developed eight [[home video game console]]s and multiple [[Handheld game console|portable console]]s for use with external media, as well as [[dedicated console]]s and other hardware for their consoles. {{As of|2026|3|31|df=US}}, Nintendo has sold over 987.81&nbsp;million hardware units.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ir/en/finance/hard_soft/index.html |title=IR Information : Sales Data - Dedicated Video Game Sales Units }}</ref>

The company's first console, the [[Color TV-Game]], was a success in [[Japan]] but was never released in other territories. Their first systems to achieve worldwide success were the [[Game & Watch]] handheld series, before achieving greater worldwide success with the [[Nintendo Entertainment System]] (NES), originally released as the Family Computer (Famicom) in Japan in 1983. The NES restarted the [[video game industry]] after the [[video game crash of 1983]], and was an international success. In 1989, Nintendo released the [[Game Boy]], which became the first handheld console to sell in large numbers. In the early 1990s, Nintendo's market lead began to decrease; although the 1990 [[Super Nintendo Entertainment System]] (SNES) was a strong seller, the [[Sega Genesis]] was a very strong contender. Nintendo and [[Sega]] would both lose a significant portion of the console market towards the end of the 1990s, as [[Sony Interactive Entertainment|Sony]]'s [[PlayStation (console)|PlayStation]] became the most popular console, beating the [[Nintendo 64]], though Nintendo managed to sell more than [[Sega Saturn]].

The [[Dreamcast]], released in 1998, [[PlayStation 2]], released in 2000, and [[Microsoft]]'s [[Xbox (console)|Xbox]], released in 2001, would eventually relegate Nintendo to third place in the international market, despite the release of the [[GameCube]]. However, they retained their lead in the handheld console market, with the [[Game Boy Color]] and [[Game Boy Advance]] models. Towards the middle of the 2000s, Nintendo introduced the first successful handheld device with a touch screen ([[Nintendo DS|DS]]) and the first successful console designed for motion controlled inputs (the [[Wii]]); they became some of the [[List of million-selling game consoles|best-selling consoles]] of all time. In 2011, Nintendo became the first major company to release a handheld game console with [[stereoscopic 3D]] capabilities, with the [[Nintendo 3DS|3DS]], which had very strong sales from the beginning. The [[Wii U]], released in November 2012, was much less successful, and sales were significantly lower than predicted. The [[Nintendo Switch]], by contrast, was released in March 2017 and has become the company's best-selling console and overall second best-selling console of all time. A successor, the [[Nintendo Switch 2]], was released on June 5, 2025.

==Home consoles==
===Color TV-Game (1977–1980)===
{{Main|Color TV-Game}}
[[File:Nintendo-Color-TV-Game-Blockbreaker-FL.jpg|thumb|'''Color TV-Game''' Block Breaker]]'''Color TV-Game''' is a series of five dedicated home consoles released only in Japan. Each of the consoles contained a small number of games and a built-in controller. In total, approximately 3 million units were sold.<ref name="CTGsales">{{cite book |title=[[Game Over: How Nintendo Zapped an American Industry, Captured Your Dollars, and Enslaved Your Children]] |last1=Sheff |first1=David |last2=Eddy |first2=Andy |author-link1=David Sheff |publisher=GamePress |year=1999 |page=[https://books.google.com/books?id=0dK2AAAAIAAJ&q=%22Color+TV+Game%22 27] |isbn=978-0-9669617-0-6|quote=Nintendo entered the home market in Japan with the dramatic unveiling of Color TV-Game 6, which played six versions of light tennis. It was followed by a more powerful sequel, Color TV-Game 15. A million units of each were sold. The engineering team also came up with systems that played a more complex game, called "Blockbuster," as well as a racing game. Half a million units of these were sold.}}</ref> 
The Color TV-Game series consists of:
*''Color TV-Game 6'', released June 1, 1977 with six variations of [[Pong]]: [[Tennis]], [[Hockey]], and [[Volleyball]] in Singles or Doubles mode. Approximately one million units sold.
*''Color TV-Game 15'', released June 8, 1977 with 15 variations of Pong. This was the most popular console in the series, selling just over one million units.
*''Color TV-Game Racing 112'', released June 8, 1978 with one racing game. Notable for being the first Nintendo project that [[Shigeru Miyamoto]] worked on. Approximately five hundred thousand units sold.
*''Color TV-Game Block Breaker'', released April 23, 1979 with one game based on [[Breakout (arcade game)|Breakout]]. Approximately five hundred thousand units sold.
*''Computer TV-Game'', released December 12, 1980 with [[Computer Othello (arcade game)|Computer Othello]]. Few units sold.

{{Clear}}

===Family Computer and Nintendo Entertainment System (1983 and 1985)===
{{Main|Nintendo Entertainment System}}
[[File:NES-Console-Set.jpg|thumb|'''Nintendo Entertainment System''']]
The '''Nintendo Entertainment System''' ('''NES''') is an [[8-bit]] home video game console. It was first released in Japan on July 15, 1983, as the '''Family Computer''' ('''Famicom''') and would become Nintendo's first home video game console released outside Japan. It was released in US test markets as the redesigned NES on October 18, 1985 and fully launched in [[North America]] on September 27, 1986. The NES was distributed in [[South America]], [[Europe]], [[Asia]], [[Oceania]], and [[Africa]] throughout the 1980s under various names.

Selling 61.91 million units worldwide, the NES helped revitalize the video game industry following the [[video game crash of 1983]], and set the standard for subsequent consoles in everything from [[game design]] to business practices. The NES was the first console for which the manufacturer openly courted [[third-party developer]]s. The console also launched many of Nintendo's most iconic franchises, such as ''[[The Legend of Zelda]]'' and ''[[Metroid (series)|Metroid]]''. <!-- NOT the Mario series, which was started in arcades with Donkey Kong in 1981, and not Kirby, which was started on the Game Boy in 1992. --> Nintendo continued to repair Famicom consoles in Japan until October 31, 2007, attributing the decision to discontinue support to an increasing shortage of the necessary parts.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.itmedia.co.jp/news/articles/0710/16/news102.html|script-title=ja:初代「ファミコン」など公式修理サポート終了|access-date=January 20, 2008|date=October 16, 2007|work=ITmedia News|publisher=ITmedia|language=ja|archive-date=October 23, 2007|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071023183833/http://www.itmedia.co.jp/news/articles/0710/16/news102.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.arcade-renaissance.com/2007/10/nintendo-of-japan-dropping-hardware.html |title=Nintendo of Japan dropping Hardware support for the Famicom |access-date=January 20, 2008 |author=RyanDG |date=October 16, 2007 |publisher=Arcade Renaissance |url-status=bot: unknown |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080317164110/http://www.arcade-renaissance.com/2007/10/nintendo-of-japan-dropping-hardware.html |archive-date=March 17, 2008 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Nintendo's classic Famicom faces end of road |url=http://afp.google.com/article/ALeqM5jAJfrC1k8lDKLOCGJu4VonjOYxBg |format=Reprint |publisher=[[Agence France-Presse|AFP]] |date=October 31, 2007 |access-date=November 9, 2007 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071105193128/http://afp.google.com/article/ALeqM5jAJfrC1k8lDKLOCGJu4VonjOYxBg |archive-date=November 5, 2007 }}</ref>

Nintendo released a software emulation-based version of the Nintendo Entertainment System on November 10, 2016. Called the [[NES Classic Edition]], it is a [[dedicated console]] that comes with a single controller and 30 preloaded games.<ref>{{cite web|title=NES Classic Edition|url=http://www.nintendo.com/nes-classic/|access-date=March 15, 2017|author=Nintendo|archive-date=March 16, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170316094026/http://www.nintendo.com/nes-classic|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Super Famicom and Super Nintendo Entertainment System (1990 and 1991) ===
{{Main|Super Nintendo Entertainment System}}
[[File:SNES-Mod1-Console-Set.jpg|thumb|right|'''Super Nintendo Entertainment System''' (North America design)]]
The '''Super Nintendo Entertainment System''' ('''SNES'''), colloquially shortened to '''Super Nintendo''', is a [[History of video game consoles (fourth generation)|16-bit]] home video game console that was released in 1990 in Japan, 1991 in North America, 1992 in Europe and Oceania, and 1993 in South America. It was first released in Japan on November 21, 1990, where it is known as the '''Super Famicom'''. In [[South Korea]], it is known as the '''Super Comboy''' and was distributed by [[Hyundai Electronics]]. In [[Europe]], the console retained the US name, but unlike the NES, used the Japanese-style casing.

The SNES is Nintendo's third home console (second outside of Japan), following the [[Nintendo Entertainment System]]. Whereas the earlier console had struggled in the PAL region and large parts of [[Asia]], the SNES was a global success, albeit one that could not match its predecessor's popularity in Northeast Asia and [[North America]]—due in part to increased competition from [[Sega]]'s [[Sega Genesis|Genesis]] console. Despite its relatively late start, the [[Super Nintendo Entertainment System|SNES]] became the bestselling console of the [[16-bit era]], selling 49.10 million systems worldwide.<ref name="nintendosales">{{cite web|url=https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ir/library/historical_data/pdf/consolidated_sales_e1509.pdf|title=Consolidated Sales Transition by Region|access-date=January 29, 2014|date=January 28, 2014|publisher=Nintendo|archive-date=June 13, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180613134338/https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ir/library/historical_data/pdf/consolidated_sales_e1509.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> The SNES library is known for upgrading some of Nintendo's most famous franchises, and making the games even more critically acclaimed, such as ''[[Super Metroid]]'', ''[[The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past]]'', ''[[Final Fantasy IV]]'' and ''[[Final Fantasy VI|VI]]'', ''[[Kirby Super Star]]'', ''[[Donkey Kong Country]]'', and ''[[Super Mario World]]'', as well starting some popular franchises such as ''[[Star Fox]]'' and ''[[Mega Man X]]''.

Similarly to the NES Classic Edition released prior, Nintendo released a software-emulation-based version of the Super Nintendo Entertainment System on September 29, 2017. Called the ''[[Super NES Classic Edition]]'', it, like its predecessor, is a [[dedicated console]] that comes with two controllers and 21 preloaded games, one of which, ''[[Star Fox 2]]'', is a title originally developed for the system that went unreleased.<ref>{{cite web|title=SNES Classic Edition|url=http://www.nintendo.com/super-nes-classic/|access-date=May 14, 2020|author=Nintendo|archive-date=December 31, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201231012741/https://www.nintendo.com/super-nes-classic/|url-status=live}}</ref>

{{Clear}}

=== Nintendo 64 (1996) ===
{{Main|Nintendo 64}}
[[File:Nintendo-64-wController-L.jpg|thumb|'''Nintendo 64''']] 
The '''Nintendo 64''' ('''N64'''), is a [[Fifth generation of video game consoles|64-bit]] home video game console released on June 23, 1996 in Japan, September 29, 1996 in North America, and March 1, 1997 in Europe and Australia. The Nintendo 64 was Nintendo's third home [[video game console]] for the international market. It was released with three [[launch game]]s in Japan (''[[Super Mario 64]]'', ''[[Pilotwings 64]]'', and ''[[Saikyo Habu Shogi]]'') and two in North America (''Super Mario 64'' and ''Pilotwings 64''). PAL regions also had three launch titles (''Super Mario 64'', ''[[Star Wars: Shadows of the Empire (video game)|Shadows of the Empire]]'' and ''Pilotwings 64'') with ''[[Turok: Dinosaur Hunter]]'' delayed until three days after launch. Other key games included ''[[Donkey Kong 64]]'', ''[[Diddy Kong Racing]]'', ''[[Banjo-Kazooie (video game)|Banjo-Kazooie]]'', two games in [[The Legend of Zelda|''The Legend of Zelda'' series]], ''[[GoldenEye 007 (1997 video game)|GoldenEye 007]]'', ''[[Kirby 64: The Crystal Shards]]'', ''[[Mario Kart 64]]'', ''[[Super Smash Bros.]]'', and ''[[Star Fox 64]]''. The [[Nintendo 64]] sold 32.93 million systems.<ref name="nintendosales"/>

===GameCube (2001)===
{{Main|GameCube}}
[[File:GameCube-Set.jpg|thumb|'''GameCube''']]
The '''GameCube''' was released on September 14, 2001 in Japan, November 18, 2001 in North America, May 3, 2002 in Europe, and May 17, 2002 in Australia. It is Nintendo's [[Sixth generation of video game consoles|sixth generation home video game console]], the same generation as [[Sega]]'s [[Dreamcast]], [[Sony]]'s [[PlayStation 2]], and [[Microsoft]]'s [[Xbox (console)|Xbox]]. Until the console's unveiling at [[Nintendo Space World#Space World 2000|Space World 2000]], the design project was known as ''Dolphin''—this can still be seen in the console and its accessories' model numbers. The GameCube is the most compact sixth generation console. The GameCube is Nintendo's first game console to use [[optical disc]]s rather than [[game cartridge]]s. An agreement with the optical drive manufacturer [[Panasonic Corporation|Matsushita]] led to a DVD-playing GameCube system named the [[Panasonic Q]], which was only released in Japan on December 14, 2001. Much of Nintendo's core line-up centered on sequels to their established hit franchises such as ''[[Super Mario Sunshine]]'', ''[[Super Smash Bros. Melee]]'', ''[[The Legend of Zelda: Wind Waker]]'', ''[[Metroid Prime]]'', ''[[Pokémon Colosseum]]'', ''[[Kirby Air Ride]]'', and ''[[Star Fox Adventures]]'', while new franchises like ''[[Animal Crossing]]'' and ''[[Pikmin]]'' were born, although the former franchise had seen a Japan-exclusive release on the N64. The GameCube has sold 21.74 million units.<ref name="nintendosales"/>

===Wii (2006)===
{{Main|Wii}}
[[File:Wii-console.jpg|thumb|'''Wii''' console (left) and [[Wii Remote]] (right)]]
Nintendo released the '''Wii''' on November 19, 2006 in North America, December 2, 2006 in Japan, December 7, 2006 in Australia, and the following day in Europe, as their [[Seventh generation of video game consoles|seventh generation home video game console]]. Nintendo designed the console to appeal towards a wider audience than those of its main competitors, the [[PlayStation 3]] and [[Xbox 360]], including "[[Casual game|casual]]" players and audiences that were new to video games.<ref name="nyt-backinthegame"/><ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.usatoday.com/tech/gaming/2006-08-14-nintendo-qa_x.htm|title=Nintendo hopes Wii spells wiinner|website=USA Today|access-date=August 20, 2017|archive-date=May 22, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110522150812/http://www.usatoday.com/tech/gaming/2006-08-14-nintendo-qa_x.htm|url-status=live}}</ref>

These aims were emphasized by the console's distinguishing feature, the [[Wii Remote]]—a handheld [[motion controller]] that can [[Motion detection|detect motion and rotation]] in [[Three-dimensional space|three dimensions]], using a mixture of internal sensors and infrared positioning. The controller includes an expansion port that can be used to connect other accessories, such as the Nunchuk—an attachment with an [[analog stick]] and additional buttons, a "[[Classic Controller]]" [[gamepad]] providing a traditional control scheme, and [[Wii MotionPlus]]—an accessory designed to enhance the motion detection capabilities of the original Wii Remote models.<ref name="nyt-backinthegame"/><ref name=":0" />

The Wii's internal hardware is an updated derivative of that of the GameCube; in comparison to its seventh-generation competitors, the Wii had lower overall graphics capabilities, and does not output in [[high-definition television|high-definition]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.ign.com/articles/2006/03/30/revolutions-horsepower|title=Revolution's Horsepower|last=Casamassina|first=Matt|date=March 29, 2006|website=IGN|language=en-US|access-date=August 20, 2017|archive-date=August 28, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170828052537/http://www.ign.com/articles/2006/03/30/revolutions-horsepower|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="nyt-backinthegame">{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2006/11/24/arts/24wii.html|title=Getting Everybody Back in the Game|last=Schiesel|first=Seth|date=November 24, 2006|work=The New York Times|access-date=August 20, 2017|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=January 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210110195457/https://www.nytimes.com/2006/11/24/arts/24wii.html|url-status=live}}</ref> The Wii also featured [[online game|internet]]-enabled features; the [[Nintendo Wi-Fi Connection]] service allowed supported games to offer online multiplayer and other features, while the [[WiiConnect24]] feature allowed messages and updates to be downloaded while the console was in standby. Through [[Wii Shop Channel]], additional [[WiiWare|games]] and apps could be downloaded or purchased for the console, including [[Virtual Console]]—a selection of classic video games [[Video game emulation|emulated]] from older consoles. That service has been discontinued as of January 30, 2019. Early models of the Wii also had backwards compatibility with GameCube games and controllers, but this was dropped from later hardware revisions, namely the [[Wii#Redesigned model|Wii Family Edition]] and the [[Wii#Wii Mini|Wii Mini]].

The Wii was a major success for Nintendo; in April 2007, the ''[[Wall Street Journal]]'' declared that Nintendo had "become the company to beat in the games business", citing the success of the Wii and the portable [[Nintendo DS]] line.<ref name=WSJ041907>Nick Wingfield and Yukari Iwatani Kane, [https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB117691936534774315 Wii and DS Turn Also-Ran Nintendo Into Winner in Videogames Business] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200919184703/https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB117691936534774315 |date=September 19, 2020 }}, ''Wall Street Journal'', April 19, 2007</ref> {{As of|2016|03|31|df=US}}, the Wii has sold 101.63 million consoles worldwide.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ir/en/sales/hard_soft/|title=IR Information : Sales Data – Hardware and Software Sales Units|work=Nintendo Co., Ltd.|access-date=September 9, 2018|archive-date=October 24, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161024140433/https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ir/en/sales/hard_soft/|url-status=live}}</ref> ''[[Wii Sports]]''—a collection of sports minigames that were designed to leverage the Wii Remote, was bundled with the console outside of Japan, and had a major cultural impact as the console's "[[Killer application|killer app]]" among the mainstream audience.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.gamespot.com/articles/study-wii-kids-lose-weight/1100-6166231/|title=Study: Wii kids lose weight|last=Boyes|first=Emma|date=February 23, 2007|website=GameSpot|language=en-US|access-date=August 20, 2017|archive-date=September 9, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180909185427/https://www.gamespot.com/articles/study-wii-kids-lose-weight/1100-6166231/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.gamespot.com/articles/iwata-wii-sports-2-benched-for-now/1100-6178806/|title=Iwata: Wii Sports 2 benched for now|date=September 18, 2007|website=GameSpot|language=en-US|access-date=August 20, 2017|archive-date=January 1, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190101100812/https://www.gamespot.com/articles/iwata-wii-sports-2-benched-for-now/1100-6178806/|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Wii U (2012) ===
{{Main|Wii U}}
[[File:Wii U Console and Gamepad.jpg|thumb|[[Wii U GamePad]] (left) and '''Wii U''' console (right)|alt=]]
The '''Wii U''' was released on November 18, 2012 in North America, November 30, 2012 in Europe and Australia, and December 8, 2012 in Japan, as a direct successor to the Wii, and the first entry in the [[Eighth generation of video game consoles|eighth generation]] of home video game consoles. The Wii U's distinguishing hardware feature is the [[Wii U GamePad|GamePad]], a [[Tablet computer|tablet]]-like controller which contains a resistive [[touchscreen]] that wirelessly streams a video output from the console. The GamePad's display can be used to provide alternative or complementary perspectives within a game, or as the main display instead of a television.<ref>{{Citation|last=Crecente|first=Brian|title=The surprising (mundane) tech behind the Wii U's magical GamePad|date=November 16, 2012|url=https://www.polygon.com/2012/11/16/3653294/wii-u-range-test-gamepad|access-date=August 20, 2017|archive-date=January 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210110175656/https://www.polygon.com/2012/11/16/3653294/wii-u-range-test-gamepad|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="polygon-wiiureview">{{Cite web|url=https://www.polygon.com/2012/11/18/3660470/wii-u-review|title=Wii U review|date=November 18, 2012|website=Polygon|access-date=August 20, 2017|archive-date=November 12, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201112041322/http://www.polygon.com/2012/11/18/3660470/wii-u-review|url-status=live}}</ref> In particular, Nintendo promoted the concept of "[[Asymmetry|asymmetric]]" multiplayer, where a player with the GamePad would have a different objective and perspective than that of other players.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.gamasutra.com/view/news/35102/Nintendo_Unveils_Wii_U_Controller_With_BuiltIn_62quot_Touchscreen.php|title=Nintendo Unveils Wii U, Controller With Built-In 6.2" Touchscreen|last=Caoili|first=Eric|work=Gamasutra|access-date=August 20, 2017|language=en|archive-date=May 9, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120509071032/http://www.gamasutra.com/view/news/35102/Nintendo_Unveils_Wii_U_Controller_With_BuiltIn_62quot_Touchscreen.php|url-status=dead}}</ref> Alongside the GamePad, the Wii U supports Wii controllers and games. A conventional gamepad known as the [[Wii U Pro Controller]] was also released.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.engadget.com/2012/06/05/nintendo-two-wii-u-gamepads-will-work-on-one-system/|title=Nintendo: two Wii U Gamepads will work on one system|author=Jon Fingas|date=June 5, 2012|publisher=Engadget|access-date=June 5, 2012|archive-date=June 7, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120607163120/http://www.engadget.com/2012/06/05/nintendo-two-wii-u-gamepads-will-work-on-one-system/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://kotaku.com/nintendo-unveils-hardcore-wii-u-controller-5915318 |title=Nintendo Unveils Hardcore Wii U Controller |work=Kotaku |date=June 3, 2012 |access-date=June 12, 2012 |archive-date=June 6, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120606004534/http://kotaku.com/5915318/nintendo-unveils-hardcore-wii-u-controller |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="polygon-wiiureview"/>

The Wii U featured more-extensive online functionality than the Wii, using the [[Nintendo Network]] platform; as with the Wii, it supported online multiplayer and [[Nintendo eShop|downloading and purchasing new games and apps]], but also allowed video chat. It previously featured an internal social network known as [[Miiverse]], which allowed users to write and draw posts in game-specific communities, the service was discontinued on November 8, 2017. Players of today can still participate in online usage of Wii U programs through an online service known as "Pretendo", also being available for the 3DS family of systems.<ref name=iw-videochat>{{cite web|title=Nintendo Wii U Adds Video Chat|url=http://www.informationweek.com/nintendo-wii-u-adds-video-chat/d/d-id/1107458?|website=InformationWeek|access-date=December 25, 2014|archive-date=December The Wii U was met with low adoption, attributed by Nintendo executives to a lack of third-party support; poor marketing of the system, which led to a lack of clarity of the Wii U game pad from being a tablet device; and the subsequent release of the [[PlayStation 4]] and [[Xbox One]] the following year.<ref>{{cite magazine|last=Kohler|first=Chris|title=What the Hell Is Wrong With Nintendo?|url=https://www.wired.com/gamelife/2013/12/wii-u-sales/|magazine=Wired|access-date=December 30, 2013|date=December 5, 2013|archive-date=December 29, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131229211610/http://www.wired.com/gamelife/2013/12/wii-u-sales|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Nowak|first=Peter|title=Year in review: The biggest tech flops of 2013|url=http://www.cbc.ca/news/technology/year-in-review-the-biggest-tech-flops-of-2013-1.2467354|work=CBC News|access-date=December 30, 2013|date=December 30, 2013|archive-date=November 11, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201111210538/https://www.cbc.ca/news/technology/year-in-review-the-biggest-tech-flops-of-2013-1.2467354|url-status=live}}</ref> However, some critics argued that the Wii U still had advantages over PS4 and Xbox One, including its lower cost and notable early exclusives such as ''[[Super Mario 3D World]]''.<ref>{{cite web|title=Xbox or PS4?
